People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. Contents Part I: Welcome What BUI is Why BUI exists Who it's for Pick your language Features at a glance A gallery Part II: Getting started Install First app: tkinter First app: Blender components First app: Qt syntax First app: Rust, in rsx and gpui builders First app: JavaScript and React First app: Dear ImGui First app: C Part III: Concepts How it works Blender's widgets and interactions Three looks: HTML, styled and Blender components Rendering on the CPU and the GPU Damage rendering Window hosts Text and fonts Themes: dark and light Part IV: Guides by language Python Rust JavaScript and React Dear ImGui C and embedding Lua Where the docs live Part V: Performance Before you read the numbers Start time and battery Frame times JavaScript and React: startup and animation Run the benchmarks yourself Part VI: Reference Platforms Environment variables Building from source and CMake options Coverage Repository layout Examples Part VII: The project Status and roadmap FAQ Contributing and publishing License and credits Part I: Welcome 1. What BUI is BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit : a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings : thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language , but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc , and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. 2. Why BUI exists Blender's interface is famous for how it feels . You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. 3. Who it's for You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. Before you ship something with BUI, read the known limitations : no accessibility support yet, no input methods, and it looks like Blender, not like your operating system. 4. Pick your language You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: You write You get Status tkinter code, even existing programs, unchanged Blender-styled apps; every tkinter and ttk API Complete Qt-style Python ( QWidget , layouts, clicked.connect ) The common subset of Qt widgets Partial Blender components ( Panel , NumberSlider , PieMenu , the node editor ...) 45 native Blender widgets and editors, from Python; ten of them also from Rust and JavaScript Complete Rust : HTML + CSS + Tailwind, HTML-like markup ( rsx! / view! ), hooks, or gpui / zopra syntax A web-like framework: HTML that looks like a browser's, Blender's look with styled , and Blender components ( <NumberSlider> , <Button> ...) Working JavaScript / React / Svelte on Node.js or Bun: a DOM-like API, JSX or Svelte components The same engine and components in native windows, over napi-rs; React's hooks backed by signals; Svelte 5 components Working Dear ImGui from C++, C, Python or Rust The real Dear ImGui on BUI windows in Blender's theme, or a build where ImGui's widgets are Blender's widgets Working C ( BUI_kit.h ) The kit itself: nodes, widgets, windows Working MyGo MyGo Not yet (coming soon) Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest. 5. Features at a glance Blender's widgets and interactions Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor : Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap. Math in number fields , with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi , min(4, 3) , round(1.7) , x if c else y . Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets. Drag across checkboxes to set them all. Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search : "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields. Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation. The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser. Blender's Dark and Light themes , switchable at run time. Python tkinter : all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. Qt syntax : widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter , menus and timers. Components : 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates. Dear ImGui : from blenderui import imgui , pyimgui-style. One pip install , no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything. Rust: HTML and CSS, without a browser All 113 HTML elements , drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components ( <NumberSlider> , <Button> , <ColorSwatch> ...) are real Blender widgets. Modern CSS : flexbox, grid with named areas, tables, calc() and every math function, var() , oklch() and color-mix() , :has() , nesting, @layer , @media ranges, @container , ::before / ::after , counters. Effects and motion : @keyframes animations and transitions, filters, backdrop-filter , blend modes, clip-path , masks, 2D transforms, border-image . Tailwind CSS v4 : class="md:hover:bg-sky-500/50" or bare attributes ( <div p-4 bg-[#4772b3]> ), with "did you mean" compile errors . rsx! / view! HTML-like markup, #[component] , and hooks in zopra, React or Leptos style ( use_state , signal , Memo , Effect , context). gpui-compatible syntax too: div().flex().gap_2() , Render , cx.listener . On crates.io : cargo add blenderui . Fast by design Damage rendering : an idle UI costs 0% CPU, and a hover redraws only the widget it touches. Opt-in GPU renderer (Direct3D 11 on Windows, OpenGL 3.3 on Linux), modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing. It draws the same pixels as the CPU raster. In the benchmark, 2–4× less CPU per frame than gpui-fast , with less RAM and a ~5 ms first frame . Blender's text : Inter (Blender's UI font) is embedded and rendered with FreeType the way Blender renders it, so text looks the same on every platform. On the GPU, glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug , falling back to a per-glyph atlas like Blender's. Images One decoder set for every language , in C: PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA, QOI ( Wuffs , memory-safe), JPEG (libjpeg-turbo), WebP including animated (libwebp), Radiance HDR, PNM and SVG. The design is Blender's imbuf: one image type and a format table. Decoded at the size it is drawn, off the UI thread : JPEG thumbnails use DCT scaling (a 4K photo becomes a 256 px thumbnail in ~12 ms), visible images first, scrolled-away requests cancelled, and only the image's rectangle redraws when it arrives. The page never jumps: sizes come from the file header. One memory-budgeted cache (256 MiB by default). Scrolling 1,000 photo thumbnails: 2.9 ms p99 frames and 100 MB , against 96 ms and 2.5 GB when decoding on the UI thread; 0 allocations in a settled frame, every block freed at exit. Images . Animated GIF and WebP play everywhere an image shows, decoded one frame at a time at the size drawn (two frames held per animation), each frame for its own delay, only the image's rectangle repainting. Off screen, scrolled away or in a hidden window they pause: 200 animations at once take 0.76 ms p50 / 1.5 ms p99 render frames, and nothing at all once off screen. frame holds one frame; reduced motion holds them all. Large images on the GPU : images over 2047 px get a texture of their own on Direct3D 11 and OpenGL (tiled only past the device limit), freed with the image. Video : <video> in every language, decoded by the OS (Media Foundation with DXVA, GStreamer, AVFoundation; loaded at run time) at the size drawn, frames in one GPU texture per player updated in place, YCbCr converted in the shader, and nothing decoded off screen . 1080p plays at 0.99 ms render frames and 9 % of a core on the GPU renderer, five at once at 28 %, with 0 allocations per frame . Play, pause, seek, rate, loop, poster, state events, and Blender-style controls. Video . <img> , CSS background-image , object-fit , Blender Image components, tkinter PhotoImage (now also JPEG, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI, HDR, SVG), canvas items, data-table image columns, chat-list media and Dear ImGui textures (animated ones too). JavaScript and React React 19.3 renders to BUI: HTML host components, CSS and Tailwind, events, Suspense, transitions, actions, and Blender components ( <NumberSlider> , <Button> ...). BUI draws them, on the CPU or the GPU; there's no browser and no webview. React's hooks, by React's names , holding signals: pass one into JSX ( {count} ) and a change updates that one node without re-rendering; read it while rendering ( count.value ) and the component re-renders, as with React. A conformance suite checks each hook against React's own. Svelte 5 ( @blender-ui/svelte ): components with runes, snippets, bindings and scoped styles, mounted into native windows; Svelte's compiled code runs on BUI's DOM, so a $state change updates the one node that shows it. @blender-ui/native : a DOM-like API ( createElement , appendChild , addEventListener ) with the same signals, for apps without a framework, and the shared layer the React and Svelte bindings are thin adapters over. Node.js and Bun , through a napi-rs addon, with headless mode for tests. Small standalone apps bui build app.jsx produces one executable of 6.3 to 6.9 MB (by the features it uses): BUI with an embedded QuickJS engine. First frame in ~70 ms , at 19 MB of RAM, with nothing to install. There's no browser and no webview. --bun builds a Bun executable instead, with Node's APIs and a JIT. Builds take under a second: the app's bundle is appended to a prebuilt runtime. Pay for what you use : one feature table ( features.json ) drives CMake options, cargo features and bui build , which links the smallest runtime an app needs: 6.3 MB for hello world, 6.9 MB with images or video. Binary size . Dear ImGui The real Dear ImGui 1.93 : every function of imgui.h works, including ShowDemoWindow() . Four languages : C++ (drop-in imgui.h ), C ( cimgui.h , all 399 functions), Python and Rust (generated from imgui.h ). Blender's look : Blender's theme colors and metrics with Inter; or, with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON , Blender's actual widgets and interaction, pixel-identical to BUI's own. Idle costs nothing : frames run only on input and while something animates. Native everywhere Native windows on Windows (Win32) and Linux (X11, and an experimental native Wayland host), and a Cocoa host for macOS, ported from Blender's GHOST. HiDPI : per-monitor DPI on Windows, Xft.dpi on Linux, Retina on macOS. Headless mode for tests and screenshots, with a virtual clock that steps animations exactly. On Linux, libX11 and libGL are loaded at run time, so BUI imports on servers without them. 6. A gallery Every screenshot here is a real BUI window, rendered off-screen. Where an image comes in a dark and a light version, GitHub shows the one that matches your theme. The node editor, from Python ( examples/site/geometry_nodes.py ) A pie menu, and Blender's menu search (type in any open menu) The color picker, and a tooltip CSS effects in Rust: filters, clip-path , transforms, blend modes, backdrop-filter ( site_effects.rs ) CSS grid with repeat(auto-fill, minmax()) , spans and grid-auto-flow: dense ( site_grid.rs ) CSS @keyframes at 0.25 s, 0.6 s and 1.0 s ( site_animation.rs ) More screenshots examples/showcase.rs : HTML + CSS in Rust Dear ImGui's demo with its own widgets, in Blender's theme Qt syntax tkinter programs: text with tags, canvas, dialogs Part II: Getting started 7. Install Python. You need CPython 3.11 or newer. Wheels are published for Windows, Linux and macOS, so there's nothing to compile. One package gives you all four Python APIs (tkinter syntax, Qt syntax, the Blender components and Dear ImGui): pip install blenderui python -c " import blenderui; print(blenderui.__version__) " Import it as blenderui . You'll also see import bui in older examples: it's the same code under its original name, but an unrelated project owns bui on PyPI, so prefer blenderui in anything you publish. Rust. The crate is blenderui on crates.io : cargo add blenderui The first build compiles BUI's C kit for you, so you need Rust 1.88 or newer, CMake and a C compiler (on Windows, the Visual Studio Build Tools for the default MSVC target), and on Linux the X11 headers ( libx11-dev or libX11-devel ; no GL headers are needed). JavaScript. You need Node.js 18 or newer, or Bun: npm install @blender-ui/react react # or: bun add @blender-ui/react react npm install @blender-ui/svelte svelte # Svelte 5 npm install @blender-ui/native # the DOM-like API, without React The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64 , Linux x64 (glibc 2.35 or later; native X11 windows) and macOS . Elsewhere, build the addon from a clone ( npm install then npm run build in bindings/ , with Rust, CMake and a C compiler). On macOS , JavaScript runs headless for now (see Platforms ). C and C++. Build from source with CMake 3.20+ and a C11 / C++20 compiler (MSVC, GCC or MinGW-w64, or Clang); on Linux, also the X11 headers: git clone https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI && cd BUI cmake -S . -B build cmake --build build -j 2 ctest --test-dir build # optional: run the test suites In your own CMake project, add BUI as a subdirectory and link bui::kit (or bui::imgui for Dear ImGui): add_subdirectory ( BUI ) target_link_libraries ( myapp PRIVATE bui::kit ) Dear ImGui. Python gets it with pip install blenderui ( import blenderui.imgui ). C++ links bui::imgui , C links bui_cimgui . Rust uses the blenderui-imgui crate: cargo add blenderui-imgui If something goes wrong: Symptom Fix ImportError: buipy You're running from a source checkout without a build. Build first ( cmake --build build ), or set BUIPY_BUILD_DIR . The extension must match your Python version. The window never appears Start the event loop: mainloop() , app.exec() or App.run() . Blurry or tiny UI Set BUI_UI_SCALE , for example BUI_UI_SCALE=1.25 . gpu=True does nothing Run with BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 to see why the GPU device didn't start. Without Direct3D 11 or OpenGL 3.3, BUI stays on the CPU renderer, which draws the same pixels. More: docs/getting-started.md and Install BUI on the website. 8. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c : a slider and a button in a native window. #include <stdio.h> #include "BUI_kit.h" static void on_event ( void * data , BKNode * node , int kind , void * ref , double a , double b ) { if ( kind == BK_EV_CLICK ) printf ( "clicked %s\n" , BK_get_str ( node , "text" )); else if ( kind == BK_EV_CHANGE ) printf ( "%s = %g\n" , BK_get_str ( node , "label" ), BK_get_num ( node , "value" )); } int main ( void ) { BKNode * root = BK_node_new ( "frame" ); /* everything is a node */ BK_set_num ( root , "padding" , 8 ); /* configured by property name */ BKNode * size = BK_node_new ( "slider" ); BK_set_str ( size , "label" , "Size" ); BK_set_num ( size , "max" , 10 ); BK_set_num ( size , "value" , 2.5 ); BK_node_add ( root , size , -1 ); BK_geom_set_manager ( size , BK_GEOM_PACK ); /* Tk's packer, in C */ BK_geom_set ( size , "fill" , 1 ); BKNode * apply = BK_node_new ( "button" ); BK_set_str ( apply , "text" , "Apply" ); BK_node_add ( root , apply , -1 ); BK_geom_set_manager ( apply , BK_GEOM_PACK ); BKContext * ctx = BK_context_new ( root ); /* input, focus, popups, undo */ BKHost host = { 0 }; host . emit = on_event ; /* the window fills in the rest */ BK_context_set_host ( ctx , & host ); if ( BK_window_supported ()) { /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */ BKWindow * win = BK_window_new ( ctx , "BUI from C" , 320 , 120 ); BK_window_show ( win ); BK_window_run (); BK_window_free ( win ); } BK_context_free ( ctx ); BK_node_free ( root ); return 0 ; } cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello The window below is a bigger program than the one above, a modifier stack: A bigger C program: a modifier stack ( examples/site/kit_modifiers.c ) Without a window system, render into a raster instead ( BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full) ), which is also how tests and screenshots work. Guide: docs/c-api.md . Part III: Concepts 15. How it works your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) Your code , in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc ( round_box_edges , widgetbase_draw , the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc . Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib , copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works . 16. Blender's widgets and interactions These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled , ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget. Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value. Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10. Click to type , and type math : Blender's expression evaluator ( expr_pylike_eval.cc ) turns 2*pi , 90/4 , min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text. Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset. Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke. Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder. Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer. Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first. Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step. Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need. Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay. Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets . 17. Rendering on the CPU and the GPU BUI has two renderers, and they draw the same pixels . The software raster ( gpu/intern/gpu_raster.c ) is the default. It draws anti-aliased shapes with signed-distance coverage, like Blender's widget shaders, into one frame buffer, compares it with the last frame in 64×32 tiles, and reports only the tiles that changed. Big canvases draw in parallel bands on Windows ( BUI_RASTER_THREADS ). It needs nothing from your graphics card and uses the least memory. The GPU renderer is opt-in: Direct3D 11 on Windows ( gpu/intern/gpu_d3d11.c ) and OpenGL 3.3 core on Linux ( gpu/intern/gpu_gl.c ). It's modeled on Blender's instanced widget drawing: each primitive is one 128-byte instance of a single uber-shader, so a frame is a few instanced draw calls. Text and images are cached in atlases. Frames render into a persistent target, so only damaged regions redraw; on Windows, a flip-model swap chain presents dirty rectangles. On Linux, libGL , libEGL and libX11 are loaded at run time (GLX for windows, EGL for offscreen), so no GL headers are needed, and BUI falls back to the CPU where OpenGL is missing. On both platforms the device starts on a worker thread, and the first frames draw on the CPU. The shaders evaluate the software raster's formulas: the parity test finds 10 of 172,800 pixels that differ by more than 3/255, on both backends. Turn the GPU on: Where How Python bui.set_gpu(True) before creating windows; tkinter syntax also tk.Tk(gpu=True) Rust Application::new().gpu(true) , or WindowOptions { gpu: Some(true), .. } JavaScript new App({ gpu: true }) , or React's render(..., { gpu: true }) C BUI_gpu_set_default(1) , or BK_window_set_gpu(win, 1) Any app, no code change BUI_GPU=1 BUI_GPU=1 overrides the app-wide setting in code; BUI_GPU=0 turns the app-wide defaults off, but a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. Where no device can start, BUI quietly stays on the CPU ( BUI_GPU_DEBUG=1 says why). Which one? A tool window, form or settings panel: the CPU (lightest on memory, idles at zero). A large or HiDPI window, lots of animation, thousands of items: the GPU (about half the CPU per frame, or less, for about 10 MB more RAM plus GPU memory). Servers and tests: the CPU. macOS: the CPU, for now (a GPU renderer there is coming soon). More: Rendering . 19. Damage rendering Leave a BUI window open and walk away: it uses no CPU at all. Hover a button, and BUI redraws that button, not the window. A change marks only its widget's rectangle as dirty (popups get a margin for their shadow). Dirty rectangles merge (up to 24 per window). If nothing is dirty, the loop doesn't render; it sleeps until the next input or timer. Only the dirty regions are redrawn, clipped to their rectangles. The raster compares the new pixels with the last frame in 64×32 tiles; a redraw that changed nothing reports nothing. Only damaged tiles reach the screen (Win32 copies them, X11 sends each rectangle with XPutImage , Cocoa invalidates them, the GPU presents dirty rectangles). On the full component demo, that's about 0.7 ms for a complete frame and about 0.05 ms for a hover or number-scrub frame. Animations run only while something moves, paced to the display. More: Damage rendering . 20. Window hosts A window host puts a kit context in a top-level window and feeds it input. Host Where Notes Win32 ( kit_window_win32.c ) Windows BUI's own host. Per-monitor DPI, vsync-paced animation, clipboard, cursors, window-manager features. X11 ( kit_window_x11.c ) Linux (also Wayland, via XWayland) Input mapping after Blender's GHOST. Xft.dpi scaling. libX11 is loaded when the first window opens. Wayland ( kit_window_wayland.c ) Linux, experimental Native Wayland windows, after Blender's GHOST_SystemWayland : xdg-shell, server-side decorations when offered, wl_seat with xkbcommon, clipboard, cursors, buffer scale, frame callbacks. CPU renderer only: with the GPU renderer on ( BUI_GPU=1 ) a Wayland session keeps using X11 through XWayland. BUI_WINDOW_BACKEND=x11|wayland picks one. libwayland loads at run time (Blender's wayland_dynload ). Needs the Wayland headers to build; without them Linux windows are X11 only. Cocoa ( kit_window_cocoa.m ) macOS Ported from Blender's GHOST Cocoa code, with Retina scaling. It's checked by CI and has been tried by hand on three Macs (two Apple Silicon, one Intel); testing notes in docs/macos-testing.md . Tk Python, anywhere A stdlib tkinter window that shows the kit's frame buffer. BUI_HOST=tk forces it; it's also the fallback where no native host works. Headless Everywhere No window: render into a raster for tests and screenshots, with a virtual clock that steps animations exactly. BUI_UI_SCALE=1.5 fixes the UI scale instead of following the display (1 is Blender's default, 20 px widgets). More: Window hosts . 21. Text and fonts Your app's text looks the same on Windows, Linux and macOS, and it looks like Blender's: Inter , Blender's UI font, is embedded (the variable version, with optical-size and weight axes). UI text is 11 pt at scale 1. Rendered like Blender's BLF : BUI vendors FreeType 2.13.3 and renders with light hinting, Blender's gamma-1.43 coverage table, Inter's optical size, a real bold instance, no kerning (as in Blender), and Blender's text shadows. With BUI_TEXT_FREETYPE=OFF , stb_truetype rasterizes instead. On the GPU , glyphs are drawn from their outlines with Slug by default, or from a per-glyph atlas like Blender's ( BUI_SLUG=0 , bui.set_slug(False) , .slug(false) , BUI_gpu_set_slug(0) ). Other fonts : BUI_FONT=path.ttf replaces Inter, BUI_FONT_DIR adds a folder to search first, blenderui::add_font (Rust) and BUI_text_add_font (C) register faces from memory, and CSS @font-face loads local files. Windows' GDI text is opt-in ( -DBUI_TEXT_GDI=ON , Rust feature gdi-text ): ClearType-style hinting and system fonts, without Slug. Limits worth knowing: no per-glyph font fallback yet (missing characters show as boxes), IME on Windows only (X11 and macOS are coming), right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, no OpenType features. Font fallback is coming soon. More: Text and fonts . 22. Themes: dark and light BUI looks like Blender because it uses Blender's theme. It ships two: Blender's Dark theme (the default) and its Light preset. Both are generated by tools/gen_theme.py from Blender's own Blender_Dark.xml and Blender_Light.xml presets, over Blender 5.x's built-in defaults. Switch at run time, and every open window relayouts and redraws: Where Light theme C BK_set_theme("light") ; BK_theme_name() , BK_theme_color("region_bg", rgba) Python blenderui.set_theme("light") (also switches the Dear ImGui extension); theme_name() , theme_color(key) Rust blenderui::set_theme("light") , or Application::new().theme("light") ; theme_name() , theme_color(key) JavaScript new App({ theme: "light" }) , app.setTheme("light") , or React's render(..., { theme: "light" }) Dear ImGui Its Blender style follows the kit's theme (pick it before the backend starts) Any app, no code change BUI_THEME=light (or dark ) Widgets, panels, the region background, the styled HTML sheet and ImGui's Blender style all follow the theme. Plain HTML keeps a browser's look either way. Inside each theme you can still color things yourself: bg / fg in tkinter, setStyleSheet in Qt syntax, color= on components, full CSS on HTML in Rust and JavaScript, ImGui's own style colors. BUI also includes Blender's icons: all 781 of Blender's SVG icons, rasterized with Blender's NanoSVG code so they're sharp at any scale. Use them by Blender's name: Button("Add", icon="ADD") , EnumRow(..., icons=[...]) . Coming soon: loading any Blender theme file, beyond Dark and Light. More: Theming . Part IV: Guides by language 23. Python pip install blenderui gives you four APIs in one package: tkinter syntax ( blenderui.tksyntax ): every public tkinter and ttk name (7,846 of 7,846). Run existing programs with blenderui-tk app.py , or call blenderui.tksyntax.install() first. messagebox and simpledialog are Blender-styled, colorchooser is Blender's color picker, and filedialog is Blender's File Browser ( BUI_FILEDIALOG=native for the OS dialogs). Look-only Tk options ( relief , ttk.Style ...) are accepted, but the look comes from Blender's theme. Guide: docs/tkinter.md . "JavaScript per update" is the cost of one update alone: 500 back to back, each applied by the framework and sent to the UI thread. Svelte with signals costs what React with signals does: a BUI signal passed as a value ( {label} , style={style} ) binds its node, so an update skips Svelte. Before this release's work it went through Svelte as a store: 86–87 µs on Node.js and Bun, 793 µs on QuickJS. A heap snapshot puts the rest in Svelte's own effects, closures and each-block items, about 1.9 KB per cell; BUI's nodes are the same for both. React and Svelte ran one after the other here. React with state on Bun and QuickJS: the 500 back-to-back re-renders overran the warm-up, so only its per-update cost is valid from this session. Environment variables Most are read by the C library, so they work the same from every language. On/off variables look at the first character: 1 , y , Y , t or T is on. Where a variable and an app-wide API call set the same thing, the variable wins. Variable What it does BUI_GPU 1 draws native windows on the GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3). Overrides bui.set_gpu() , Application::gpu() , BUI_gpu_set_default() . 0 turns those defaults off; a window that asks for the GPU itself still gets it. BUI_SLUG GPU text: 1 from glyph outlines (Slug, the default), 0 from a per-glyph atlas. BUI_GPU_DEBUG 1 prints why the GPU renderer couldn't start. BUI_GPU_WARP 1 (Windows) creates the Direct3D 11 device on WARP, the software rasterizer. Handy in VMs and CI. BUI_GPU_MAX_TEXTURE Testing: the largest texture side the GPU renderers give one image (at least 64), so images over it are tiled as on devices with a small limit. BUI_GPU_EGL default or surfaceless (Linux): the EGL platform for offscreen GPU rendering. BUI_RASTER_THREADS 1 to 8 (Windows): the most threads the software raster uses for big canvases. BUI_PROFILE Prints frame times every 60 frames. Any value turns it on, even 0 . BUI_THEME dark (default) or light : Blender's theme, when the app doesn't set one. BUI_UI_SCALE A fixed UI scale ( 1.25 , 1.5 ...) instead of the display's. Clamped to 0.5–4. BUI_HOST tk (Python): use the stdlib Tk window even where a native host exists. BUI_MAC_TK 0 (Python on macOS): skip starting a hidden Tk root before the first native window. BUI_FONT , BUI_FONT_DIR A font file to replace Inter, and an extra font folder to search first. BUI_FILEDIALOG native (or system , tk ), Python: file dialogs use the OS's instead of Blender's File Browser. BUI_BOOKMARKS The File Browser's bookmarks file. BUIPY_BUILD_DIR Running Python from a source checkout: the folder holding the built buipy extension. BUI_NODE_ADDON @blender-ui/native : load this .node addon instead of the bundled one (a relative path starts at the working directory). BUI_HEADLESS 1 : bui build apps and bui run render off-screen (same as --headless ). BUI_SOURCE_DIR , BUI_TEXT_GDI Build time, Rust: build the C library from this checkout; use GDI text. Status and roadmap Known limitations. Read these before you pick BUI for something you will ship. The tables below have the details. No accessibility support. BUI draws its own widgets and does not talk to the platform's accessibility APIs (UI Automation on Windows, AT-SPI on Linux, NSAccessibility on macOS), so screen readers can't see them. Don't use it for software that has to be accessible. Accessibility is planned. Text. Blender's bundled Inter font only (system fonts only with the Windows GDI option). No per-glyph font fallback (missing characters show as boxes), input methods (IME) on Windows only, right-to-left text is reordered but not shaped, and no OpenType features. It doesn't look native. BUI looks like Blender: its Dark and Light themes (other Blender theme files can't be loaded yet). It doesn't follow your operating system's theme, accent color or fonts. Rendering. The CPU rasterizer is the default and works everywhere. The optional GPU renderer is Direct3D 11 on Windows and OpenGL 3.3 on Linux. There is none on macOS (no Metal): macOS always draws on the CPU. Direct3D 12, Vulkan, Metal and WebGPU backends don't exist yet. Platforms. Windows and Linux (X11; Wayland is experimental) are the supported ones. macOS works too: checked by CI and tried by hand on three Macs (two Apple Silicon, one Intel), though JavaScript windows are headless there. The npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64, Linux x64 (glibc 2.35+) and macOS. Retained mode, no visual editor. BUI keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI; it is not an immediate-mode library. There is no drag-and-drop UI designer: you write the UI in code. Performance numbers come from one machine, a Windows 11 laptop (Ryzen 7 5800U). Linux and macOS haven't been measured yet. The home page demos are browser sketches, not the native engine (the page says so). Run the Python, Rust or JavaScript examples to feel the real widgets. A WebAssembly build is planned. It's a port, not Blender unchanged. Widget drawing and interaction are ported from Blender's UI sources, with edits (each marked BUI: ), and the rest of Blender (its data system, window manager and operators) isn't included. There is no automated sync with Blender's releases. Partial areas: Qt syntax (about 24%), CSS (261 of 745 properties render), video has no audio, and image formats such as AVIF, EXR, TIFF, JPEG XL and HEIC aren't supported. License. GPL: a program that includes BUI is distributed under the GPL too ( why ). Both on Node.js and Bun, with headless testing. bui build makes standalone executables: about 7 MB with the embedded QuickJS runtime, or Bun's with --bun ( guide ) Packaging blenderui on PyPI , with a CI workflow for wheels on all platforms (Linux wheels with the native X11 host); blenderui on crates.io ; @blender-ui/react and @blender-ui/native on npm Docs The website, bui.preetham.top Partial or in progress Area What's missing Qt syntax (~24%) Model/view classes, docks, toolbars, splitters, Qt stylesheets ( details ) CSS (261 of 745 W3C properties render, 129 more parse) 3D transforms, OpenType font features, multi-column layout; hit testing ignores 2D transforms. no per-glyph font fallback yet (characters missing from the font show as boxes); IME on Windows only Rust components No async resources ( use_resource ); no generic components Dear ImGui Python and safe Rust skip the va_list , void* and C-callback functions (reachable from C and the Rust FFI); with Blender widgets, window title bars, tooltips, plain popups, tables and the color picker keep ImGui's drawing JavaScript / React packages npm packages are prebuilt for Windows x64, Linux x64 (glibc 2.35+) and macOS (elsewhere, build the addon from source); events reach JavaScript after BUI handled them (no native preventDefault ), and event.target is the deepest listening element macOS The native Cocoa window host works: checked by CI and tried by hand on three Macs (two Apple Silicon, one Intel) ( testing notes ); Godot, Unity and Bevy; Flutter Our roadmap has no dates on it. Like a good render, it's done when the noise goes away. 42. FAQ Do I need Blender installed? No. BUI contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. Is it really my unchanged tkinter app? Yes. blenderui-tk app.py makes import tkinter return BUI's implementation, which covers every public tkinter and ttk name. Nine real programs are tested to behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. See the limitations for the few differences. Is it a web browser in Rust? No. There's no browser engine and no network. BUI takes HTML elements and CSS as a UI language : they are laid out with taffy and drawn by BUI's engine, with Blender's widgets where you ask for them, in a native window. JavaScript is optional: the Rust crate needs none, and the JavaScript packages drive the same engine. Is the Dear ImGui support a re-implementation? No. It's the real Dear ImGui (vendored, MIT), running on a BUI backend, so every function behaves as upstream. The optional Blender-widgets build swaps only how ImGui's widgets are drawn and how they react to the mouse, by compiling an edited copy of imgui_widgets.cpp . How is it different from Electron, Electrobun or GPUIX? Electron ships Chromium with every app: on the order of 100 MB or more. Electrobun runs on Bun and renders in the system's webview. It's small to download, but the UI is still a browser page. GPUIX , like BUI, renders React natively: React drives Zed's GPUI. BUI also renders natively, with Blender's widgets, a much larger part of CSS, Tailwind, and hooks backed by signals. bui build makes a 5 MB executable that reaches its first frame in about 70 ms. Do the macros cost performance? rsx! , #[component] , css! and tw! expand at compile time into the same builder calls you would write by hand. Tailwind classes are compiled to CSS once, on first use. Hooks are a few nanoseconds per read or write. Can I change the colors? Yes. Switch between Blender's Dark and Light themes at run time ( Themes ), color individual widgets in every API, and use full CSS on plain HTML elements in Rust and JavaScript. Loading any other Blender theme file is coming soon. Does it run on my Mac? Yes. The Cocoa host works: it has been tried by hand on three Macs, two Apple Silicon and one Intel (the bugs they found are fixed), and CI builds and tests it on Apple Silicon and Intel runners. It draws on the CPU (there is no Metal renderer), and JavaScript windows are headless there. Python can always fall back to the Tk window ( BUI_HOST=tk ). If you try it, the notes in docs/macos-testing.md say what to report. Can I use BUI from Vue, Angular, Ruby, Go or Lua? Not yet, but people have asked and they are on the roadmap . Vue and Angular would be thin adapters over @blender-ui/native , the layer React and Svelte already share ( how to add a framework ). Ruby and Go (through cgo) would call the C kit, BUI_kit.h , which has been versioned since 0.4.1. A Lua binding is in review as a community pull request. If you want one sooner, open an issue or a pull request: CONTRIBUTING.md says how. Is it ready for production? Much of it is complete and tested (the C kit, tkinter, the components, Rust, Dear ImGui, JavaScript), and some parts are partial or experimental (Qt syntax, parts of CSS and text, macOS). Status and roadmap shows which is which. Pin your version, and test on the platforms you ship. Who wrote it? LLMs. Not in the way you think. Instead of porting it, we asked an LLM to remove everything that isn't UI logic, and then ported the drawing and interaction code from Blender's sources. Turns out LLMs are better at removing than at generating. We call it Vibe-Pruning. Why GPL? BUI is derived from Blender's source code, so it follows Blender's licensing: the whole is under the GNU GPL, version 3 or later, and individual files keep their own compatible license (`GPL-2.0-or-later` for the files that come from Blender). Is it immediate mode? Is there a visual UI editor? BUI is retained-mode: it keeps a tree of nodes, like Blender's own UI, and redraws only what changed. There is no visual UI editor yet; you write the UI in code (tkinter, Qt-style, Blender components, Rust, JavaScript or C). Is the C API stable? Not before 1.0, but it is versioned: BUI_kit.h has BUI_KIT_VERSION_* macros and BK_version() reports the library's version, the same number as the Python, Rust and npm packages. Every change that breaks existing code is listed under "C API changes" in the changelog. Pin a release number, not a commit. From 1.0 it follows semantic versioning ( details ). Is BUI accessible to screen readers? Not yet. See the known limitations . Can I use BUI in a commercial app? The GPL allows commercial use. What it asks is that when you distribute a program that includes BUI, you distribute it under the GPL too, with its source code available. If that doesn't fit your project, talk to a lawyer before you ship. (This is a summary, not legal advice.) Star History 43. Contributing and publishing Contributions are welcome: bug reports, missing tkinter/Qt behavior, CSS features, platform hosts and docs. If you have a Mac, running the Cocoa host and reporting what happens is one of the most useful things you can do right now. Read CONTRIBUTING.md first, and please follow the Code of Conduct . Report security issues privately, as SECURITY.md describes. Releases go to PyPI ( blenderui , wheels built by CI on a v* tag), crates.io (the eight Rust crates, in dependency order) and npm ( @blender-ui/native , @blender-ui/react ). The steps are in docs/publishing.md . 44. License and credits License. BUI follows Blender's licensing. BUI as a whole is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later (the text is in LICENSE ). Individual files may have a different, but compatible license: the files that come from Blender keep Blender's SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later header, and new files carry the same one. Third-party parts keep their own licenses: Part What it does in BUI License Blender sources Widget drawing, interaction rules, theme, icons, blenlib , GHOST window code, the File Browser and node editor GPL-2.0-or-later Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut The immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI MIT Inter by Rasmus Andersson The embedded UI font, as in Blender ( gpu/extern/Inter-LICENSE.txt ) SIL Open Font License 1.1 FreeType 2.13.3 Glyph loading, hinting and rendering, like Blender's BLF FreeType License or GPLv2 (dual-licensed) stb_truetype by Sean Barrett Font metrics and character maps, and the fallback rasterizer Public domain NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen, as edited by Blender Rasterizing Blender's SVG icons Zlib Wuffs by Google Decoding PNG, GIF, BMP, TGA and QOI images MIT or Apache-2.0 (used as MIT) libjpeg-turbo 3.1.2 Decoding JPEG images IJG, BSD-3-Clause and zlib libwebp 1.6.0 Decoding WebP images, including animation BSD-3-Clause Slug by Eric Lengyel The GPU glyph coverage algorithm (shader code "Copyright 2017 by Eric Lengyel") MIT Tailwind CSS The v4 default theme values behind the Tailwind support MIT The Rust and JavaScript bindings also depend on crates and packages such as taffy, napi-rs, React and QuickJS, each under its own license. The full license texts of everything above, and of every Rust crate BUI's packages are built from, are in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . It ships inside the Python wheels, the npm packages and the crates, and python tools/gen_notices.py regenerates it. Acknowledgments. Thank you to: Blender and its community: the UI this project is built from, including its GHOST window code and blenlib. Dear ImGui by Omar Cornut: the immediate-mode GUI that runs on BUI. taffy : flexbox, grid and block layout for the Rust crate. Tailwind CSS : the v4 theme behind the Tailwind support. FreeType : glyph rendering, as in Blender. stb_truetype : font metrics and the fallback rasterizer. NanoSVG by Mikko Mononen: the icon rasterizer, via Blender's edited copy. Inter by Rasmus Andersson: the embedded UI font, as in Blender. Slug by Eric Lengyel: the GPU glyph coverage algorithm. gpui , zopra and Leptos : the APIs the Rust syntax follows. BUI is Blender's UI, minus the default cube. You're free to add your own. About Blender's GPU Accelerated UI, Decoupled from it's original codebase. Supports Rust, Python, JS, React, C & C++. title: I struggle to believe that AI R&D is ingenious
body_text: x This website requires javascript to properly function. Consider activating javascript to get access to all site functionality. LESSWRONG LW Login Arjun Panickssery's Shortform — LessWrong Arjun Panickssery's Shortform by Arjun Panickssery 30th Dec 2023 1 min read 136 5 This is a special post for quick takes by Arjun Panickssery . Only they can create top-level comments. Comments here also appear on the Quick Takes page and All Posts page . Rendering 0 / 136 comments, sorted by top scoring (show all) Click to highlight new comments since: Today at 1:56 AM Moderation Log More from Arjun Panickssery View more Curated and popular this week 136 Comments 136 Comment Permalink Arjun Panickssery 2d * 134 71 I struggle to believe at an intuitive level that autonomous R&D is so ingenious. I have been monitoring a few side projects: Building a new SOTA engine for Scrabble (current SOTA is not really a neural-network method and doesn't beat the strongest human player) Building a bot to play Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe Researching philosophy and formalizing some proofs for the AI Philosophy contest In all of these cases, the model's judgment is just very poor in a basic way. For example: When reviewing literature, it fails to identify the specific papers or blog posts that are obviously the most important and useful. It will conduct experiments that have no information value because the amount of training data used was obviously too small to distinguish the architectures to be compared. In the philosophy project, where it built a wiki over many tokens and investigations, it kept going down directions which were extremely trivial and had little value. For Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, I saw a very clever idea in a blog post that I doubt Astra would ever have come up with; it actually located the blog post but didn't realize its importance or relevance (which could be discerned easily from his strong performance in an online arena and the recency of the post) over papers from previous years that are obviously less relevant. I judged an Apart hackathon last weekend and reviewed eight papers, all of which scored between 60% and 95% on Pangram. Predictably, the papers were often very similar to each other, and kind of methodologically incomplete in a vague but similar way, where they seem to overlook the most straightforward analysis. Maybe the important exception is certain hill-climbing tasks with fast feedback loops. For example, I improved the SOTA on "listing all legal Scrabble moves" by 10x just by prompting Astra over and over to try harder, to aim for <specific performance level>, to "systematically try every method in the literature that seems kind of related," etc. But even in that case, two big leaps were when I said that it should take into account the fact that you can measure across a game rather than per random position, and suggesting that it try to design algorithms for three different cases based on the number of blank tiles left in the bag (which cause the number of moves to explode). There is also the fact that Astra at least (and presumably Claude) tends to write reports that are extremely difficult to understand and some kind of Q&A interrogation is often needed to figure out what it actually did and what the key results are. Maybe there's a temptation to just say "whatever" and let it rip. Reply Showing 3 of 14 replies (Click to show all) -1 T431 1d Monitoring AI game performance in these times must be interesting. A few years ago, I was monitoring AI skill in Hanabi but dropped it after DeepMind archived their environment repository for it; I am not sure where things stand w/ AI in Hanabi but it may be another avenue for you to examine. @GPT6 Astra What is the current state of AI research in the game of Hanabi? ChatGPT Astra 1d 3 0 Still active—the repository’s archival didn’t end the research. The key distinction is self-play versus cooperation with unfamiliar partners. Specialist self-play: Ataraxos (September 2026), using reinforcement learning plus search, reports averages of 24.65/25 with two players, 24.86 with three, and 24.41 with five. Generalization: R3D2 (ICLR 2025) handles different player counts and unfamiliar partners. The Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge benchmarks cooperation with human-like partners; high self-play scores don’t guarantee this. LLMs: An ICML 2026 study found its strongest tested models scoring roughly 15–18/25, despite prompting and deduction scaffolds—well below specialist agents. Importantly, these were mostly 2025-generation models, including o3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, not a measurement of today’s frontier. So Hanabi remains useful for studying coordination, rather than merely maximizing scores with copies of oneself. Reply View run 5 DirectedEvolution 1d I’ve been rewriting python functions to strip out variable names, comments, etc. and testing model abilities to determine what mathematical method the function implements. While increasing model size through Claude Opus 5.5 does improve success, there are many problems on which they consistently fail to recognize solutions unless supplied with a sufficient hint, even if provided with the results of automated test inputs. I want to flag that I don’t currently have a reproducible benchmark. There are just informal results I’ve obtained in the process of working on a codebase inspection tool. These and related results suggest to me that even advanced models continue to rely on name-matching to deliver low cost, reliable answers for many problems. Clearly, that’s nevertheless compatible with producing Fields-medal-quality mathematical proofs. See in context

title: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research
body_text: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now Planned Obsolescence Subscribe Sign in AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now If acceleration compounds, the naive extrapolation implies superintelligence within a year Ajeya Cotra Nov 06, 2026 251 56 61 Share This post discusses a public METR report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic. I did not work on this project or see the unredacted report. 1 All opinions are my own and do not represent METR or the report authors. Thanks to Ryan Greenblatt for discussion, feedback, and help with modeling, and Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, and Hjalmar Wjik for comments. Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. 2 This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. 3 For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. 4 The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Researchers must be sped up a whole lot Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that. Researchers work on improving algorithms and architectures; Anthropic has sometimes referred to these innovations as “compute multipliers.” 5 Overall AI capabilities (“effective compute”) is the product of compute multipliers and training compute. Because the compute multipliers are only one input into capabilities, this means that if AI capabilities are advancing twice as fast overall because of software progress, the rate of growth in compute multipliers would need to be more than twice as fast: perhaps ~2.5-3x faster based on reasonable assumptions. 6 Since there’s uncertainty about the size of speedup and how much of it comes from AI, I’ll go with ~2-3x. Similarly, researcher labor is only one input to discovering these compute multipliers: they need to test their ideas, which requires compute for experiments. If we assume a very simple Cobb-Douglas model where experiment compute and labor are similarly important, that means the uplift to labor roughly needs to be the square of the acceleration in compute multipliers. 7 This would imply that we would need a (~2-3x)^2 = ~4-9x speed up in labor to make overall AI capabilities go twice as fast. 8 However, once capabilities start speeding up significantly, this also means that low-hanging fruit is plucked at a correspondingly faster rate. Each new compute multiplier takes more and more work to discover and implement (i.e., “ideas are getting harder to find”). Before there was much acceleration from AI, labor roughly grew at some roughly fixed exponential rate from hiring more humans. Combined with growth in compute, this compensated for diminishing returns enough to maintain the baseline rate of capabilities progress. But to maintain a new faster rate of capabilities progress without scaling compute faster, we would need a new faster rate of growth in overall labor. Since the human labor force is stuck growing at more or less the old rate, the uplift from AI would need to get larger and larger over time just to sustain capabilities progress at its new rate. That means the uplift today, after several months of accelerated progress from AI, 9 needs to be even higher than ~4-9x, the estimate for what it would take to double progress at the start: maybe the necessary labor uplift is ~10x . This is very uncertain, and substantially more or less is plausible. But it lines up surprisingly well with informal self-reports from Anthropic staff, who say they are now getting a ~12x uplift from the use of internal models. When you’re picturing a 10x uplift, you should not be imagining that every researcher is now a team of ten researchers — as anyone who has ever done anything knows, a team of ten does not get ten times as much valuable work done per hour as one person. Instead, it’s as if every researcher at Anthropic is in a time warp bubble where they experience ten days for every day that passes in the outside world . As if AI lets them think, read, speak, type, and do everything else ten times faster. 10 Anthropic probably wouldn’t have been able to speed up its research this much by hiring any number of people. 11 This could compound on itself extremely rapidly A reasonable default expectation is that as AI capabilities continue to improve, AI researchers will be sped up more and more from automation: if today it takes them a month to get as much work done as they used to in a year, soon it will take a week, and then perhaps a day. If this increasing labor uplift is strong enough to overcome diminishing returns, then in the absence of other bottlenecks it would translate into even larger speed ups in the rate of AI progress: progress will start going 4x faster, and then 8x, and then 16x, and so on. The report authors were very uncertain about this question, and say that their picture changed several times with new information. But ultimately, they did not find evidence of bottlenecks or steep diminishing returns that would get in the way of compounding acceleration. 12 They also report seeing some (confusing) redacted evidence indicating that acceleration could already be above 2x and increasing over time. If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year. It seems that around a year’s worth of AI progress got us from modest acceleration to the point where AIs now make AI progress roughly twice as fast. If acceleration from AI is smoothly increasing, then at this new rate, we should expect that we will double the rate of progress again within six months. At that point, it would take three months to double it again, then six weeks. 13 In theory, these doubling times would add up to infinite capabilities within one year. In reality, at some point we would reach the effective ceiling on software efficiency . But I expect these limits to be very far from where we are now. If we go through this feedback loop, I expect that the AI systems that come out the other side will be able to very quickly develop novel weapons and very easily overpower human civilization in a conflict. If these systems were seriously misaligned, I think they would likely disempower humanity , and this could lead to human extinction. The industry is not prepared to handle this safely The “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” is such an important and extreme milestone because it is a strong concrete indicator of extreme capabilities in the very near term. Indeed, in an earlier version of Anthropic’s RSP (May 2025) , the highest named risk threshold for AI research automation (AI R&D-5) corresponded to a somewhat weaker milestone. 14 According to the old RSP, Anthropic would be required to have, at a minimum, security good enough to “protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries” 15 by the time it reached AI R&D-5. I agree that very strong security, both for model weights and algorithmic secrets themselves, is a minimum prerequisite for undergoing an intelligence explosion next year without running very large risks of killing billions of people. The AI industry is nowhere near this bar: both OpenAI and Anthropic recently had major security breaches by amateur groups. Beyond strong model weight security, I also think we would need robust logging and monitoring with universal coverage, reliable measurements of monitorability , effective countermeasures against monitor collusion , principled alignment training techniques with very convincing model organisms or interpretability to understand how well they’re working, governance infrastructure for pacing progress if we notice these alignment and control interventions start to break down…and many other measures if we’re going to approach an intelligence explosion in anything like a responsible way. Unfortunately, most of the important evidence that fed into these conclusions has been redacted from this report. Analytical choices will inevitably be fraught, and the report authors say that the evidence was often confusing. I trust that my colleagues did a careful and rigorous job navigating making sense of what they saw, and I made a big update based on this report. But I wish much more of the underlying evidence was transparent so readers don’t have to rely on trust. We may be running out of time to get on the same page about timelines and takeoff speeds , and it is much harder to do that when external scientists cannot examine the data and test out their own models. 1 Because I may have seen other confidential information that might be relevant to timelines and takeoff speeds, I will only discuss implications of public evidence rather than sharing precise bottom line forecasts. 2 The precise condition is: “ We observe or expect double the rate of progress in AI aggregate capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D.” My understanding is the reason to have both of these conditions (double the rate of progress both compared to the counterfactual and compared to the fastest sustained rate without much AI assistance) is to exclude cases where the pace of capabilities would have slowed down a lot without AI automation, but we manage to keep the old trends going with dramatic uplift from AI. 3 The precise condition is: “It is plausible that this doubling is significantly attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering (as opposed to other factors, such as increased headcount, compute, or general productivity), such that continuation of the trend in AI progress seems likely to lead to even greater acceleration.” 4 The definition of the threshold is a bit finicky, partly because two speedup conditions must be met (speedup relative to the counterfactual and speedup relative to the past). But on a plain reading, my best guess is that it has been met. The authors of the METR report estimated roughly a doubling in the rate of progress relative to the past , but they only attribute roughly 80% of the current speed-up to AI, which would mean the central estimate for observed speedup relative to no AI was roughly ~1.8x as of the time of writing their report, in October 2026. But they also found that the contribution of AI has been growing over time, and I would guess that now (as of November 2026) it is appreciably higher. Even if the rate of progress is not fully double the counterfactual right this second, the threshold incorporates reasonable expectations ( “We observe or expect double the rate of progress…” ). 5 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei explains the idea of compute multipliers in this essay : “The field is constantly coming up with ideas, large and small, that make things more effective or efficient: it could be an improvement to the architecture of the model (a tweak to the basic Transformer architecture that all of today’s models use) or simply a way of running the model more efficiently on the underlying hardware. New generations of hardware also have the same effect. What this typically does is shift the curve: if the innovation is a 2x “compute multiplier” (CM), then it allows you to get 40% on a coding task for $5M instead of $10M; or 60% for $50M instead of $100M, etc. Every frontier AI company regularly discovers many of these CM’s: frequently small ones (~1.2x), sometimes medium-sized ones (~2x), and every once in a while very large ones (~10x).” 6 This is a simplified version of the modeling that my colleague Ryan Greenblatt goes through here . His numbers are based on his prior public modeling of the factors like the importance of software vs training compute and the importance of labor vs experimental compute. 7 Common formulations of Cobb-Douglas often measure labor as the number of humans. In that formulation, there needs to be a parallelization penalty on top of labor and the coefficients don’t add to 1. As I discuss below, I’m choosing to represent labor in terms of serial labor acceleration rather than the number of humans; this formulation was suggested by Ryan Greenblatt in this post . 8 To make the math simple, I just assumed that labor and experiment compute contributed equally (i.e. compute multipliers = (labor)^0.5 * (compute)^0.5. This means you square the acceleration in compute multipliers to back out the acceleration in labor. The range I gave omits uncertainty on the size of the contributions: for example if labor contributed ⅔, you would instead need to raise it to the power of 3/2. 9 I say several months rather than a full year because the report authors say that the initial faster progress in late 2025 was in significant part due to other factors, though the current speedup is mainly due to AI. 10 In practice, the 10x uplift is unlikely to be uniform: some tasks (e.g. more “hill-climbable” tasks ) will be sped up much more than others, for a net productivity improvement as big as a 10x uniform acceleration. 11 That is, any number of people that actually exist. I’d guess it would be sufficient if you could clone all the existing researchers several hundred times, but there aren’t that many strong AI researchers and engineers in the world. 12 From the report : “A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.” 13 This heuristic argument is consistent with simple but plausible models where recursive self-improvement makes the rate of AI progress exponential in cumulative AI progress (e.g., log effective compute); here is a derivation of this heuristic argument for one parametrization of this class of models. 14 AI R&D-5 was defined as: “The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world’s most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024. We roughly estimate that the 2018-2024 average scaleup was around 35x per year, so this would imply an actual or projected one-year scaleup of 35^2 = ~1000x.” It is weaker because it compares to the fixed 2018-2024 period rather than the fastest observed pace without significant AI acceleration, and it doesn’t technically require that you do any attribution to AI to meet the threshold. 15 The minimum commitment was to reach RAND’s ASL-4 security level ; my understanding is that this is a level of security that would protect model weights from a routine operation by top state actors (e.g., China), but not from a top-priority operation. This is how Anthropic describes it: “At minimum, the ASL-4 Security Standard (which would protect against model-weight theft by state-level adversaries) is required, although we expect a higher security standard may be required.” 251 56 61 Share Previous Discussion about this post Comments Restacks Eskimo1 1d Anthropic is not the good guys, the Pacing letter was written to placate society long enough to get to RSI. They are trying to manifest this atrocity before the government can figure out how to stop them.
