title: Deus Ex
body_text: » Deus Ex The Digital Antiquarian The Digital Antiquarian A history of computer entertainment and digital culture by Jimmy Maher Home About Me Ebooks Hall of Fame Table of Contents RSS ← This Week on The Analog Antiquarian Deus Ex 06 Nov This article tells part of the story of Warren Spector . A slight shift of focus, and the future could still turn out like Deus Ex after all… — Deus Ex lead writer Sheldon Pacotti, speaking in 2014 The reviews that greeted Ion Storm’s Deus Ex upon its release in June of 2000 ranged along a continuum from cautiously to wildly positive. Computer Gaming World , the Gray Lady of the hobby, came with one of the most nuanced takes. Reviewer Thierry Nguyen spoke of “loving” the game in the abstract, but lamented “deep flaws that sometimes frustrated me, as they detracted from its ambitious design”; these included performance issues, poor artificial intelligence on the part of the enemies, and a sense of contrivance that clung to some of the environments and plot points. The excitable lads at Australia’s PC Powerplay , on the other hand, placed no such qualifiers on their declaration of love for Deus Ex . In a special feature published when the game was not yet three months old, they declared it to be quite simply The Best Game Ever: “Every action within Deus Ex’ s expansive environments has far-reaching consequences, making it seem like the player is ensconced within a living, breathing world.” For better or for worse, the critical consensus over the quarter-century since Deus Ex was a brand-new game has hewed more to PC Powerplay than Computer Gaming World . As the years have passed, it has been praised more and more fulsomely, not only for its gameplay but for being a full-blown work of interactive speculative fiction, full of uncanny insights into the ways the world has changed since it was released just as the Dot-com Bubble was bursting. YouTube in this Year of Our Lord 2026 is overflowing with videos that declare it to be “The Most Important Videogame Ever Made,” the game that “predicted the future,” the proud home of “some of the most insightful philosophy that you will ever witness in the gaming medium.” It’s become fodder for a certain species of painfully earnest commentator who desperately wants games to be culturally relevant true-blue art, whilst also continuing to allow him to run around and blow shit up in the manner to which he’s become accustomed. All too often, this causes such folks to make claims for Deus Ex that have only a tangential relationship with its reality, lacking the necessary grounding in the cultural circumstances that produced it. Which is no surprise really; some of these folks weren’t even born yet when Deus Ex was new on store shelves. My favorite anecdote in this vein involves the name of the protagonist: J.C. Denton. It was theorized for years that the “J.C.” stood for “Jesus Christ,” pointing to the literal deus ex machina (“God in the machine”) of one of the game’s three possible endings, in which Denton merges with an artificial intelligence — in the Singularity sense, not that of the algorithms controlling the enemies who run through the game’s corridors shooting at you — to take over the world. At a Game Developers Conference postmortem in 2017, Deus Ex’ s mastermind Warren Spector, who had always stayed mum on the subject prior to this event, brought forth a revelation that caused jaws to drop almost audibly throughout the room: the initials really did stand for “Jesus Christ.” But then came the deflating coda. Rather than having any deeper thematic or philosophical implications, the name of the protagonist came from a friend of Spector’s with the first name of Denton, who was so nice and helpful that it could become downright “irritating,” as Spector put it. “Jesus Christ, Denton!” he would say at these junctures. When production on Deus Ex began, Spector thought that the phrase had a nice ring to it. So much for philosophy. Like Planescape: Torment and to some extent even Alpha Centauri , Deus Ex has become as much an aspirational ideal as a concrete artifact. And that’s fine; we all need things to which to aspire, after all. Still, in this article I’m going to do my best to drill down on the less hyperbolic reality of Deus Ex . If this meaning pushing back at times against its popular reputation as a sui generis masterpiece, know that that doesn’t mean it isn’t a fine and groundbreaking game, a game which dares to attempt to do a lot of difficult things and manages to succeed at a remarkable number of them. One of the nefarious actors in Deus Ex is the Federal Emergency Management Agency. How’s that for a deep state? As I’ve already implied, discussions of Deus Ex tend to break down along two axes: the innovations of its gameplay and the statements it makes — or seems to make — about the very future in which we are now privileged or condemned to be living. The gameplay is both the easier subject to get a handle on and the one where the more grandiose claims require less qualification, so let’s start there. Whatever else it happens to be, Deus Ex is the greatest game that Looking Glass Studios never made, steeped in that creative collective’s ethic of the “immersive sim.” As longtime readers of this site know, Looking Glass’s very first game, Ultima Underworld , appeared in 1992, right about the same time that id Software released Wolfenstein 3D , their dry run for DOOM . For the balance of the decade, Looking Glass was the yin to id’s yang. Both studios worked with first-person 3D, but, while id emphasized straightforward shooter gameplay, Looking Glass stubbornly stuck to a much more complex, multi-variant gameplay model that strove to drop the player right into a believable 3D world. It was a far more difficult path to walk, with far fewer commercial rewards to be found along the way, yet it resulted in a catalog of games that are still well remembered and widely recognized as formative to what gaming has become in the decades since. It might not be going too far astray to call Looking Glass the Velvet Underground of gaming. In my opinion, the greatest, most quintessential Looking Glass game of all is System Shock , which was released in 1994, still fairly early in the studio’s run. It casts you as the sole surviving human aboard a space station where an evil central computer, the chillingly iconic SHODAN, has killed everyone else and turned their corpses into bloodthirsty zombies. You have to shoot, sneak, hack, and engineer your way to victory against her, in combinations that can and will vary from player to player. The game is less a fixed story than an emergent playground of problems and possibilities that yields a story, if the player is doing it right. System Shock so impressed Warren Spector, who was serving as Looking Glass’s producer and liaison at the publisher Origin Systems at the time it went into development, that it caused him to quit his job there and join Looking Glass full-time. System Shock . One of its design principles was a thoroughgoing commitment to diegesis; you aren’t privy to any information which the character you play isn’t also privy to. What you see onscreen is exactly what the protagonist sees through his neural implant. (Valve’s Half-Life would famously employ the same approach four years later.) All told, System Shock was the most uncompromising implementation of an immersive sim that Looking Glass ever created — for that matter, one of the most uncompromising that anyone has ever created, right up to the present day. Confronted by feedback from players who found the scope of possibility which System Shock allowed them less bracing than confusing, Looking Glass shrank it just slightly in their later games. Their 1998 game Thief , for example, made it clear to the player that stealth was the only real route to success. Yet Spector found the early builds of that game, which is at least as critically lauded as System Shock today, to be more frustrating than freeing. What happened if you were discovered in one of the dark corners of the game, despite all of your best efforts to stay hidden? It usually just led to a swift game-over screen, so inept was your character in a straight-up sword fight. Spector wondered why he couldn’t be allowed to take a different approach to the game’s problem space than that of pure stealth, if he so chose. After having worked on System Shock , Thief felt too constrictive. This was the direction his thoughts were traveling when John Romero called him up to offer him $3 million to make “any game you want to make.” Deus Ex was a return to the ethic that had produced System Shock , and thus cannot be fully understood without reference to that earlier game. Like System Shock , it gives you a goal and sets you loose to try to achieve it in any way you can conceive and pull off. The core of Spector’s mission statement to his team was just three words long: “Problems, not puzzles.” Instead of insisting that you work your way to solutions that have already been thought up by the designers — the definition of puzzle-based gameplay — it’s content to offer up a selection of challenges and affordances and then trust in the multi-variant simulation to do the rest. This gives emergent possibilities for problem-solving — as opposed to puzzle-solving — that even the designers may never have imagined. If this approach wasn’t quite as breathtakingly new in 2000 as some of the YouTube commentariat seem to think it was — again, see System Shock — it was most definitely the road less traveled in 3D gaming at the time. That said, Deus Ex is more willing than System Shock to compromise on the ideology of the immersive sim in order to satisfy other goals. It’s slightly less committed to diegesis, being willing to foreground information that System Shock prefers to keep hidden. The changes which the protagonist of System Shock undergoes all happen organically, as a result of his actions in the world. In Deus Ex , while you will always play an agent with the code name of J.C. Denton, your identity is less intimately bound up with his. You’re free to make your own version of him by explicitly choosing which skills to invest in initially and which ones to improve as the game goes on, from a modest menu of same that includes Computers, Electronics, Environmental Training, Lockpicking, Medicine, Swimming, and an array of Weapons competencies. (Interestingly, a 1999 direct sequel to the original System Shock that was developed by Irrational Games rather than Looking Glass themselves made the same choice to crack open the black box, as it were, and expose the CRPG elements.) Deus Ex’ s character-creation screen. Instead of taking place in one contiguous space like System Shock — albeit a space with plenty of locked doors and balky elevators to be sorted out — Deus Ex embraces a more typical first-person-shooter campaign structure, giving you a set of twelve missions that are played out one after the other. Each mission is, we might say, a kind of mini- System Shock , a self-contained simulation space that must be “solved” in one way or another in order to proceed to the next one. In terms of its overarching narrative, then, Deus Ex is really a quite traditionalist game. The campaign structure does allow Deus Ex to present a far broader array of environments than it otherwise could, the polar opposite of the relentlessly uniform, suffocating corridors of System Shock . You hopscotch from New York City to Hong Kong to Paris among many other destinations, ending up — inevitably, given the nature of the story — at good old Area 51. But what is gained in cosmopolitan diversity is lost in the ability of players to make their own story. While each mission can be solved in a huge number of ways, it will always lead to the same mission afterward; the game will always dance to the tune of the same set of fixed plot beats. The “living, breathing world” that so delighted PC Powerplay back in the day is an illusion outside of the granular frame of how you complete each individual mission. Whether you choose to make your J.C. Denton a hyper-violent super-soldier who assassinates moral niceties along with everyone else he meets or a tormented soul engaged in what he suspects more and more to be a bad business, he will always arrive there at Area 51 via the same basic series of steps. Yes, one might argue that System Shock as well has a somewhat linear, deck-by-deck instead of mission-by-mission progression, but the ability — indeed, the necessity — to periodically go back to decks you might have thought you had “cleared” gives it a verisimilitude that Deus Ex can’t quite match. So, for all its reputation for innovation, well-deserved in many respects, Deus Ex’ s wide-frame approach to storytelling is almost as old as digital games themselves. At the climax of the linear campaign, you are given a choice between three pre-crafted endings. Other than by dying and failing to reach the climax at all, you have no more control than this over the final outcome of the story. This could be construed as a weakness, given the stakes of the plot, which is vastly more complicated than System Shock’ s personal zero-sum game between yourself and SHODAN. Still, I do understand why it was done this way, and don’t really blame anyone for it: because truly interactive storytelling, especially on a scale like this one, is hard , as decades of experience have taught us all too well. As I’ve written many times, game design is an art of the possible; having made their bed by choosing to tackle such an ambitious story, the designers of Deus Ex had to lie in it as best they could. Try to pick the lock or blow it open? The choice is yours… or maybe you can do something else, perhaps something totally unexpected, instead. At the level of the individual missions, however, the game does do an admirable job of living up to its goal of letting you figure things out for yourself. If you want to go for maximum lethality, you can do that, although the limited quantity of ammunition to hand will make it a daunting task. (Just why does the organization you work for spend a fortune to turn you into an augmented super-soldier and then scrimp on bullets like a corporate Karen in charge of an office-supply cabinet?) If you want to rely on stealth and technological trickery, reserving your kill shots for the people who really deserve them, you can do that too. The best way to know if an immersive sim is successful at what it has set out to do is to imagine that you — the real you, that is — are actually in the situation it depicts, ask yourself how your real-world self would react, and then find out if the game allows you to do that. If the answer is yes, then the game is probably onto something. And by this standard, Deus Ex acquits itself pretty darn well, all things considered. Indeed, for many years after the game’s release, the designers were regaled with tales of players who had devised solutions to the missions’ problems that they had never even thought of — another sign of a successful immersive sim. One of the most famous examples emerged when the game was still in testing. It involves magnetic explosive charges that can be attached to doors and windows for the purpose of blowing them open, or to make booby-traps for enemies. The testers discovered that they could use these in a whole different way: to make a kind of staircase for climbing a wall by attaching them one after another at increasing heights, hopping from one rung to the next. It was a clever and totally unanticipated way to reach high balconies and rooftops. Informed of this exploit, many a design team would have contrived some way to block it and moved on to the next bug on the list. But Warren Spector’s team took it as a challenge to make their virtual realities that much more airtight, such that even climbing to someplace you “shouldn’t” be couldn’t break them. An improvised ladder made from magnetic explosive charges. The worst thing you can say about this aspect of Deus Ex is that the simulation of the real world sometimes leads to situations where behaviors are entirely emergent, but a long way off from believable. Deus Ex goes so far in simulating a logically functioning environment in comparison to most games of its era that it occasionally falls into a kind of uncanny valley of realism, amenable to “cheap” solutions on the player’s part that remind her all too clearly that she’s merely playing a game. The most notorious examples of this phenomenon tend to revolve around the behavior of the various guards, terrorists, and other enemies in the spaces, who act more like confused herd animals than trained operatives. There are lots of ways to lead these clowns astray in order to avoid and/or kill them, ways that would never fly in the real world. But they stand out only because so much else has raised our expectations so high… One of the many choices which Deus Ex largely leaves up to its player is how much to engage with its convoluted, much-discussed story line. You can treat the game as nothing more than a series of tactical scenarios to overcome, if you’re so inclined. Or you can really dig into the lore by exhausting every possible line of interrogation with the people you meet and carefully reading through the many documents you stumble across. It’s to this side of the game, which is increasingly described as prescient if not downright prophetic by people looking back from these dystopic-feeling current times of ours, that I’d like to turn now. The most infamous and chilling “proof” of Deus Ex’ s alleged facility for predicting the future is a view of the New York City skyline that you can see in the very first mission. This game that was released fifteen months before the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, nonetheless shows only empty sky where the twin towers of the World Trade Center ought to be. As the people who made the game have always been quick to explain, this was not intended as a conscious statement of any sort, much less a prophecy. The towers were left out due to a shortage of texture memory. But still… what a coincidence! It’s almost enough to make you believe that the ghost of the Oracle of Delphi really does haunt Deus Ex . The game that follows that disconcerting skyline view is littered with quotes that seem almost as unnervingly prescient, especially when pulled out of context. They seem to apply all too well to our present age of ever greater disparities of wealth, all but unchecked corporate power, solipsistic social media, and widespread surveillance in both digital and physical spaces. Add to all of that the claim that our computers are on the verge of waking up to sentience and taking over the world… For 100 years, there’s been a conspiracy of plutocrats against ordinary people. In 1945, corporations paid 50 percent of federal taxes. Now they pay about 5 percent. In 1900, 90 percent of Americans were self-employed. Now it’s about 2 percent. It’s called consolidation. Strengthen governments and corporations, weaken people. With taxes, this can be done imperceptibly over time. This is real freedom: freedom to own property, make a profit, make your life. The West, so afraid of strong government, now has no government. Only financial power. All taxes are social engineering. That’s always been their real purpose. What happens is that politicians get money from big companies, so all the social engineering is for making big companies. The need to be observed and understood was once satisfied by God. Now we can implement the same functionality with data-mining algorithms. The human organism always worships. First it was the gods, then it was fame (the observation and judgment of others), next it will be the self-aware systems you have built to realize truly omnipresent observation and judgment. But before we get too hot and bothered over this 26-year-old game that seems to have so accurately captured the world we live in today, we should perhaps take a step back to ask ourselves where its ideas actually came from and what its makers were actually trying to do with them. This supposed engine of prophecy is in reality one of the last enduring artifacts of 1990s conspiracy culture, that virulent Petri dish of vanished civilizations, crash-landed aliens, hidden historical overlords, secret societies, and more government coverups than an army of Boy Scouts could shake their sticks at. While the guiding ethic of Deus Ex’ s gameplay was “problems, not puzzles,” that of its story was almost as simple: “What would the world be like if every conspiracy theory — every single one of them — was true?” It’s the trashcan cocktail of conspiracy culture, with some of just about everything thrown in. This was done not because its makers earnestly believed in most of what they wrote into their game, but for the most typical reason that any group of game developers do anything: because they thought it would be fun in a game that was to be, as Warren Spector described it, “James Bond meets The X-Files by way of Neuromancer .” To that list of influences can be added Blade Runner , The Terminator , and Snow Crash , along with a small library’s worth of dodgy books about aliens and pseudo-history. As anyone who has been reading these histories of mine for a while will readily recognize , this is not a strikingly original collection of gaming source material. Deus Ex stands out more for its maximalist approach and utter commitment to its subject matter than for the subject matter itself. What follows may be a fool’s errand, but I’m going to try to summarize — in extremely abbreviated fashion, mind you — the conspiracy-addled backstory of Deus Ex as I understand it. (Credit where it’s due: the script of Deus Ex is primarily the work of Sheldon Pacotti and Austin Grossman, with much input from Warren Spector and the rest of his 30-person team.) It all goes back at least as far as the Knights Templar — it’s always the Knights Templar , isn’t it? — who during the Crusades set up a banking system that would help them to rule the world, money being power and all. They morphed via several intermediate steps into the Illuminati, the hidden hand behind the last three or four centuries of human history, who numbered among their ranks the Founding Fathers of the United States. (Their symbol is right there on the American dollar bill!) In 1947, this strand of conspiracy theory collided violently with another one, when a UFO crash-landed in Roswell, New Mexico. The Illuminati suppressed news of the close encounter, setting up a new and ultra-secret arm of the American government, known as Majestic 12, to study the alien artifacts that were recovered. All was more or less well in the national-security state for the better part of a century thereafter; some of the information gleaned from Roswell was strategically leaked to the scientific establishment, other parts held back as instruments of social engineering and mind control. Some decades into the 21st century, however, the Illuminati fell victim to infighting within their own ranks. Bob Page, a filthy-rich industrialist who was one of the Illuminati’s ruling Council of Five, decided to assassinate his colleagues and take over the organization all by himself. This plan only partially came off, resulting in two dueling would-be Earth-dominating secret societies. Page, who was quite a piece of work even by Illuminati standards, tried to consolidate his power by unleashing a massive pandemic to kill off billions of people and destabilize the world’s governments. (Have I mentioned that this game really can feel unnervingly prophetic?) Then he deployed an artificial intelligence by the name of Icarus to invade and subsume the entire Internet. (Have I mentioned… oh, yes, I have, haven’t I?) While he was about all of this, Page genetically engineered himself and a small team of agents into supermen. Among these agents was one J.C. Denton, the player’s avatar in the game proper. There’s much, much more to it, including a second rogue AI that sets about fighting the first one on the highways and byways of the Internet, but that will have to do for our purposes. The game itself kicks off in 2052 on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, which has been occupied by a gang of “terrorists” — freedom fighters by other people’s definition — as part of an operation to steal a shipment of a vaccine against Page’s genetically engineered disease. J.C. Denton is called in to stop them. He does so, but while he’s about it he’s given cause to wonder whether he’s been told the whole truth about the organization he works for, which he had heretofore believed to be completely benevolent. The plot takes many twists and turns thereafter, with J.C. Denton bouncing from team to team — including not only the two feuding dominant secret cabals, but others who oppose them both. As I wrote earlier, it all comes to an end at Area 51, where J.C. Denton is confronted with a choice of three solutions to the chaos. One is to blow up the Internet and all other global communications systems and throw humanity into a new “Dark Ages” for at least the next few hundred years, in the hope that his descendants will make less of a mess of things when they get around to reinventing the technology that he is about to destroy; one is to join with the original Illuminati who have been fighting Bob Page all along and help to rule the world as one of them; and one is to join with the AI to form a true superintelligence combining the best parts of humans and computers, and rule the world alone that way. Warren Spector has often said that he wanted the choices the player makes in Deus Ex to say less about J.C. Denton than they did about the person behind the monitor; this choice of endings is surely the ultimate expression of that impulse. (For the record, I’d have to go for the Dark Ages as the least bad choice in this situation. There’s even a part of me — possibly the most morbid one, granted — that thinks this might not be such a bad thing. Maybe we could use a few centuries to rediscover our humanity: to learn to breathe real air, eat real food, do real work, and talk to one another face to face again.) So, it’s not as if the story of Deus Ex gives no food for thought. Yet it’s better understood as an exercise in pastiche than philosophy, much less prophecy. The relationship of past, present, and future is actually a quantum one: the act of predicting or warning us about the future can itself produce the very outcomes it depicts. Novelist Thomas M. Disch cottoned onto this inverse relationship in the pages of his Hugo-winning nonfiction book The Dreams Our Stuff is Made Of already a couple of years before Deus Ex was released, in chapters with titles like “The Future as a Lifestyle,” “Science Fiction as Religion,” and “Republicans on Mars.” Not long afterward, the ubiquitous “flip phones” of the aughts, modeled on the communicators found in the original Star Trek television series of the 1960s, provided an indubitable example to everyone of what can happen when engineers who have been raised on vintage science fiction are placed in charge of product design. More recently, manifestations of the same phenomenon have begun to feel more and more sinister. We live in a world today in which Mark Zuckerberg — admittedly, not one of the brighter bulbs in the Silicon Valley firmament — renamed one of the largest and most profitable companies on the planet after the virtual-reality network found in Neal Stephenson’s Snow Crash , having apparently failed to understand that the novel in question was intended as satire. We live in a world in which Sam Altman and Dario Amodei are constantly arguing over which one’s statistical pattern-matching and probabilistic text-generating machine will spontaneously wake up to consciousness and enslave us all first, all because the novelist Vernor Vinge has told us this is inevitable. We live in a world in which seeing is no longer believing, because any photograph or even video clip we see may be AI-generated. In short, we are all struggling to discern reality through an ever thicker fog of what Jean Baudrillard dubbed “hyperreality” back in the 1980s. Large-language models have become the perfect symbols of the age, what with their congenital inability to separate fact from fiction. Small wonder that some people have convinced themselves that life itself is probably just a giant videogame. The conspiratorial view of history fits so neatly into this milieu because it actively encourages us to substitute what might be true — or what we would like to be true — for what we can know to be true. Once upon a time, it was easy to see it as just good fun. Certainly most of the makers of Deus Ex never thought they were making a grand statement about the way the world really was or would become as they piled trope upon trope to create their grand conspiratorial edifice, any more than did the makers of The X-Files , the television show from which they drew so much inspiration. But, as literary theorists have long told us, you are still saying something about our world even when you insist that you’re saying nothing at all. Betwixt and between the quotations that have come to seem so prescient, Deus Ex also bangs away on tired old anarcho-libertarian drums about the evils of the United Nations and the so-called “deep state.” These quotations have aged rather less well than the ones I included above, coming across more like prescriptions for than descriptions of our current problems, revealing Deus Ex to be a game that is as much of its time as timeless. One can all too easily imagine these sentences coming straight from the mouth of Alex Jones, back in the days when he could still be dismissed as just another reactionary nutcase crackling through the ether on the further reaches of the AM-radio dial. The whole project of world government — going back to the League of Nations — has been funded and manipulated, mainly by wealthy bankers. Remember that the U.N. itself was built on land donated by John D. Rockefeller. The U.N. was founded, not to end war, but to gradually replace national governments with a globalist meritocracy. The entire executive branch is hand-picked. Nineteen of the last 23 U.S. presidents have been members of the Trilateral Commission. The Trilateral Commission is financed by the Rockefellers and the Rothschilds. I find the way that Deus Ex turns honest attempts to improve our world — for instance, on the part of the founders of the United Nations and at least some American presidents — into yet more nefarious conspiracies to be as personally aggravating as it is unhelpful to our modern political discourse. Lurking in the accusations against “wealthy bankers” is the oldest, ugliest conspiratorial trope of all, the idea — stemming from the 1903 forgery “The Protocol of the Elders of Zion” — that a cabal of Jews secretly run the world. “Famous conspiracy theories always turn out to be just antisemitism,” this website’s regular commenter Ross theorized after reading a piece I wrote about the thoroughly unpleasant Pierre Plantard , the man behind some of the most outlandish tales surrounding the French village of Rennes-le-Château . The more conspiracy theories I examine in depth, the more true this proposition seems. The writers of Deus Ex might respond, reasonably enough on the surface, that all of the most controversial statements come from its various feuding characters; it would be as unfair as it would be schizophrenic to claim that the writers are in agreement with every word these characters say. In case I haven’t made myself clear, know that I don’t accuse anyone who worked on this game of being personally antisemitic. The thing is, though, that even explicitly fictional conspiracy theories — heck, even explicitly satirical ones — have a way of overflowing the vessels that are meant to contain them. Take, for instance, all of this business about the Illuminati, a staple of decades of conspiracy culture that naturally made its way into Deus Ex . The original wellspring of it all, in a modern context at least, is the Illuminatus! trilogy of novels, published in 1975 by Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson. They are convoluted, endlessly discursive, and filled with unexpected and eye-opening connections… and also a giant joke in the same style as Umberto Eco’s later novel Foucault’s Pendulum , being an intellectual shell game and a parody of the fever dreams of the hippie generation. And yet there were people who decided it was all real, worked it into their worldview, and refused to be dissuaded from belief even by the very authors who had made it all up. It seems to me that there are two principal dangers here. One is the way that, as our friend Ross so cogently noted, all or almost all conspiracy theories tend to wind up in dark places by the time they reach maturity, no matter how harmless they start out. The other one is still more insidious: by teaching us to look for all of the world’s ills in secret cabals of consciously evil people, conspiracy theories mislead us as to how history fundamentally works, thereby leading us to seek simple solutions to complicated problems. Way too often, the result is demagoguery. Again, we can see this all around us today; I trust that I don’t need to belabor the point further. Suffice to say then that the story of Deus Ex does make me a little uncomfortable, for all of the reasons I’ve just listed. Even if we acknowledge that it puts its fingers on many of the ailments besetting us today with improbable accuracy, the reasons it posits for those ailments, and thus the ways of combating them that it might lead us to adopt, are deeply misguided. But that’s just me, viewing it with the benefit of a quarter-century of hindsight. Setting aside sociopolitical concerns, I still wouldn’t call Deus Ex’ s story a great one; the best drama does not arise from merely piling backstory complication upon complication, as television shows like The X-Files and Lost proved when their unwieldy conspiratorial edifices finally collapsed into weary incoherence. Thankfully, though, a videogame seldom needs a great story in the way that so much linear media does; in some cases, it may even be an unnecessary distraction. The story of Deus Ex is effective enough within the frame of this particular videogame, lending it a memorable atmosphere and gravitas while only modestly compromising its bona fides as an immersive sim. I just wish we could all agree not to force it to punch above its weight by assigning it a profundity it hasn’t earned and doesn’t even really aspire to. This fiction is pulp, not prophecy. Having chewed my way through all of the above, I’m left with just one more question on my docket: what do I think of Deus Ex? You know, just as a computer game? I must admit that I approach this question with some trepidation. I know that some of you think highly of it indeed; more than one of you have told me that it’s your favorite game of all time. Many years ago now, during one of those occasional discussions we have around here about where these histories of mine ought to end, one or two of you suggested that Deus Ex might be a good place, an argument predicated on the assertion that it brings together all of the strands of narrative and interactivity that I’ve spent so many years running down and wraps them up in a neat little bow. (For the record: I don’t actually plan on stopping. I can already hear the sighs of relief raining down on me from the galleries, along with perchance a few disgruntled grumbles from the Statler and Waldorf types.) Personally, I wouldn’t go so far in praising Deus Ex . However, let me state very clearly that Deus Ex is a landmark game that is in most ways brilliantly conceived and executed. There is good reason that it struck many folks as a revelation upon its release all those years ago, what with its rich breadth of player possibility and its compelling atmosphere of tension and betrayal. This was the immersive sim’s breakthrough moment, the one that Looking Glass, the inventor of the approach, ironically never got to enjoy. Deus Ex sold over 1 million copies, spawned a series of equally commercially successful if never quite as critically lauded sequels, and influenced the design conversation in games for two and a half decades. Deus Ex knows exactly what it wants to be, and realizes most of its ambitious goals smoothly while avoiding a Kenyan motorway worth of potential potholes. So, when I tell you that it left me somewhat less thrilled than it did many of you, know that it wasn’t really the game but the player who was at fault. My central stumbling block with a game like this is that it asks a little bit more from me than I’m prepared to give it at this point in my life. My sweet spot of an evening these days is sitting on the sofa next to my wife, bantering about the game I — usually “I,” but sometimes “we” — play on the television screen. This is not the way that Deus Ex wants to be played; it wants me to put on headphones and burrow my way deep down into its hermetic virtual world, where I can start at every shadow and react to every passing footfall. The experience it wants to give me just isn’t the one I’m looking for these days. (In light of that reality, I do wonder how I would respond today to System Shock , a game I still want to rate above this one…) It’s awful to say, I know, but when I play Deus Ex I can’t escape a certain sense of ennui, not only with all of the tactical energy it demands of me, but with its all too typically “gamerdark” aesthetics and laundry list of influences that I’ve become just a bit too familiar with by this point. On the whole, I prefer some more light to accompany my shade. I’m afraid my favorite Warren Spector joint remains The Worlds of Ultima: Martian Dreams , that delightfully quirky and totally original journey to Edwardian Mars. But that’s just, like, my opinion, man. You should absolutely try Deus Ex for yourself to form your own. At best, you might discover your new favorite game. And even if you’re a sourpuss like me, you’ll walk away with a better understanding of why it holds that status for so many other people. Did you enjoy this article? Add to that the atmospheric, memorable music and you get locations that you can really breath in and have a sense of truly being there. And that was what I was doing during my first two playthroughs, in 2004 and 2008: I was taking my time, not rushing things, slowly examining the levels, finding different ways to do stuff, carefully reading datacubes and emails. Later, in 2019, I tried replaying Deus Ex and while I was still having a great time, I noticed something about my playstyle: I was much more impatient, I was blazing through levels, not paying this much attention to hidden details. All the time I had this sense that I want to dive deep in, but at the same time, I had this weird feeling that it would be… too much of a time waste? Maybe it’s my familiarity with the game, maybe it’s the dreaded “adulthood”, maybe the shortening of my attention span? Whatever it was, I completely agree with this sentiment, quoting the article: “it wants me to put on headphones and burrow my way deep down into its hermetic virtual world, where I can start at every shadow and react to every passing footfall. The experience it wants to give me just isn’t the one I’m looking for these days.” This is the exact way of playing in which I fell in love with this game and will remember it forever. Reply   Hresna November 7, 2026 at 1:29 pm You appear to have an uncommon masculine generic gendered pronoun when you refer to a “painfully earnest commentator” early on. I’m surprised I even noticed… I guess I’ve gotten used to your style over the years. Love the content, thanks. Reply   Jonathan November 7, 2026 at 2:37 pm There’s a Warren Spector anecdote that succinctly sums up the messy pastiche that *is* the game’s politics. he said at some conference – I can’t locate the video now, but it may be that very same 2017 one you mention, Jimmy – that he once went out with fans after speaking at some event. He claimed that at the bar, one drunken fan asked, “Amazing game, but really, how could you publish such right-wing propaganda?” Spector claims that *another* fan butted in with, “what are you talking about? It’s left-wing propaganda from start to finish!” Spector then claims he excused himself to let the two fans argue about whether Deus Ex is “left-wing” or “right-wing” propaganda. Spector was winkingly implying that this game is ideologically flexible and open-ended, but one could fairly attribute this anecdote to Deus Ex’ thematic *incoherence* as well. You captured that messiness a bit in your article here, Jimmy. Some characters complain about how corrupt billionaires are supplanting the rule of law everywhere……. others drone on about how multilateralism / globalism are bad. Characters in Silhouette are clearly left-wing anarchists; meanwhile the bartender in Hong Kong is allowed by the game to make a strong (strong-sounding?) case for authoritarian Communism. As another commenter noted, the game doesn’t seem too cognizant of the fact that without the threat of Majestic 12, Silhouette (French anarchists) and the NSF (a right-wing secessionist U.S. militia) would NOT be friends. So all in all, it’s a smart but thematically messy experience – which is perfectly okay, I think! So long as you allow the game to be “pulp” and “pastiche,” not “prophecy” (to paraphrase your article). Reply   Infinitron November 7, 2026 at 3:04 pm That one of the members of Silhouette was the daughter of an Illuminati bigwig who grew up in a mansion was a nice touch. What they did with her character in the sequel shows that Ion Storm’s writers knew what they were doing there. Reply   Veronica Connor November 7, 2026 at 8:02 pm Claiming that his incoherent soup of hundred-year-old conspiracy theories and clichés magically appeals to everyone in a deeply introspective way is a very Warren Spector thing to say. His little bar anecdote probably never even happened. Reply   Todd November 7, 2026 at 3:01 pm Great article! I’m one of those readers who would call Deus Ex the greatest of all games, but I readily admit that says as much about me — having been at the right impressionable age when it came out — as it does about the game. I think you gave it a fair hearing. The moment when I fell in love with it was after completing the first assignment, capturing the NSF leader in the Statue of Liberty. From my experience with all the other games I’d played until then, I expected the game to cut to a “mission complete” screen with some kind of score and then teleport me to the next mission. I was shocked when, instead, I was just told “good job, report back to base” and left free to walk back through Liberty Island over to the office, chat with colleagues, check in with the boss, and eventually walk back outside to catch a boat ride to the next mission. CRPGs have towns, but I hadn’t ever played an FPS that invested in making the exploration of friendly areas just as immersive and compelling as hostile areas. This is still a big difference between Deus Ex and its peers in the “immersive sim” category like System Shock, Thief, or Dishonored. Deus Ex is unfocused compared to its peers and successors, with both the gameplay systems and the story having elements that can feel like they were thrown in half-baked without much effort to integrate them with the whole, and would have been cut by a disciplined editor. There are items and skills of dubious value like pepper spray or environmental training, while the story has dangling references to content that was planned but never created, like a war in Texas, and also dips its toes into a lot of philosophical and political topics without deeply exploring any of them. But I’d argue this lack of focus actually became a strength, and this becomes evident when comparing the original game to the later ones. The sequel, Deus Ex: Invisible War, drastically simplified the game mechanics to eliminate anything the designers considered superfluous and inelegant, including the skill system and even different weapons using different ammo, but this took away some of the fun, as Harvey Smith would admit in later interviews. And for their prequels/reboots, Deus Ex: Human Revolution and Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, the writers at Eidos Montreal decided to zero in on cybernetic augmentation as the only theme their stories would explore. The result is tighter and more coherent writing, but it lacks both verisimilitude and breadth of interest compared to the original game, because everyone in the world is constantly talking about nothing but cybernetic augmentation. I’d rather play a game where I can debate the future of democracy with an AI and then have a bartender try to get me to read Olaf Stapledon — it might be shallow but it’s still thought-provoking and it’s a lot of fun. Some corrections and comments. Others may have beaten me to them, since I’ve taken a long time writing this: – JC doesn’t work for FEMA, but for UNATCO, which is part of the United Nations and not under the authority of the US government. So when Walton Simons as director of FEMA swaggers into UNATCO and orders everyone around like he owns the place, this is an early hint to JC that all is not as it seems. – The NSF terrorists on Liberty Island aren’t threatening to blow up the Statue of Liberty — it already had its head blown off long before the game started. They’re occupying it and holding a hostage to buy time while their compatriots smuggle away the shipment of vaccine they captured. – I believe the issue with NYC skyline wasn’t polygon count but texture size. It isn’t 3D modeled but a texture on a flat plane, and if I recall correctly they made its two halves mirror images of each other to save memory, which made it impossible to include the WTC. Reply   Jimmy Maher November 7, 2026 at 4:49 pm Thanks for the clarifications! (Hopefully I finally have the World Trade Center story right…) Reply   Hunter November 7, 2026 at 3:19 pm That was an insightful article, although you do leave with several misunderstandings about the game and its plot. Also, you are just too hard on it. Why does the deliberate choice to name the character JC after Jesus Christ and its only coincidental philosophical value have to be zero? There is a lot to be said about a savior figure, how he is received, and how it fits into the game not just as a element of philosophy, but as a game design choice. You can interpret the hell out of JC’s presence, that is what critical analysis is. All of these ideas about how Deus Ex relates to real world issues, including ones from long after Deus Ex’s time, are our projections on it, but they are created by the storytelling framework that it creates. You could argue that your filling in the blanks on what the vague political situation in the game REALLY means is entirely intentional. Then your hammering the game for not having multiple fully fleshed out plots is ridiculous. If a game has a plot, it’s linear. Of course it would be nice to have a “non violent plot” that doesn’t go to Area 51 and a “UNATCO plot” that keeps JC working for the conspiracy. But it’s a harsh and undeservéd review of a game that gives you more choices than most working through an inevitably linear set of levels; what they were able to achieve in time and budget and still make a coherent story out of a mish mash of nonsense is remarkable. And that bit about antisemitism – give me a break. Not every line hits the mark – a lot of that guy’s presentation and some characters just seem to be completely off – but I never thought of dredging antisemitism up in favor of considering the argument seemingly being made, whether this character has some kind of naiive belief, or whether in this game where “the Illuminati” are real, there is some backstory involving bankers that need not be a referendum on the beliefs and ethics on the original real world origins of the conspiracy, whatever century that was in. Stop grasping at straws. Reply   Kaarel Jakobson November 7, 2026 at 8:13 pm I find the author’s cultural criticism of the game perplexing. Most of it, I disagree with, but some of it, I simply do not understand. For example, the claim that it’s “better understood as an exercise in pastiche than philosophy, much less prophecy” is beyond me, because these angles don’t exist in opposition to one another. It’s true that the game’s narrative is a somewhat cheesy soup of conspiracy theories, but it’s also true that it touched on a number of social and technological nerves that have increased in relevance and therefore amplified the meanings it presents to the player. Simply saying Deus Ex predicted the future is a banal observation in itself, but the author fails to examine the compelling ideas that underpin such observations. I would also say that the game’s politics are much more sophisticated, or at least multi-faceted, than the author portrays them as. Without knowing much anything about the author, my out of pocket assumption about them is that they are an American liberal who’s by necessity familiar with destructive 21st century conspiracism, but has huge blind spots about leftist political and economic analysis. Reading the game’s localist and anti-elite messaging as primarily right-wing rather than left-wing is at best incomplete. The game has a definite libertarian flavor, but it’s progressive as well. One of the most interesting things about Deus Ex’s politics is that the anti-techbro coalition includes both right-wing militias and quasi-socialist intellectuals (among others). I think a modern reading of the game would do well to consider this, especially in when and where it was conceived and written – in Texas in the 90s, at a time when the American left was all but dead and most Americans lacked even the most basic vocabulary to engage with socialist ideas. On the topic of conspiracies, I have two other comments: Firstly, mentioning the Protocol of the Elders of Zion in the context of this review is a tasteless bit of innuendo. It’s little better than intimating that “Deus Ex portrays conspiracy theories, and antisemitism is influential in conspiracy theories, so isn’t Deus Ex a little antisemitic by association?” Warren Spector is himself Jewish as far as I know, and the game never points to Jews as the primary drivers of its plots. If anything, it’s magnates of all colors and creeds. Secondly, the author already references some other postmodern interpretations of conspiracy theories, but I would absolutely place Deus Ex in their ranks. I think portraying a world full of conspiracies rather than any single conspiracy being responsible for all the world’s ills fundamentally shifts how the concept of portrayed and interpreted. The spirit of this incisive quote by Alan Moore is present in Deus Ex, where so many plots and secrets collide against each other: “The main thing that I learned about conspiracy theory, is that conspiracy theorists believe in a conspiracy because that is more comforting. The truth of the world is that it is actually chaotic. The truth is that it is not The Iluminati, or The Jewish Banking Conspiracy, or the Gray Alien Theory. The truth is far more frightening – Nobody is in control. The world is rudderless.” Reply   DarkMage November 7, 2026 at 11:38 pm Amazing article as usual, Jimmy. Reading your take on Deus Ex immediately made me think of THE other game from that same moment that the modern internet routinely hails as a “prophetic masterpiece”: Metal Gear Solid 2 (2001). You already warned us we won’t be reading about Solid Snake’s adventures featuring labyrinthine plot twists and over-the-top storylines here since Kojima’s gloriously convoluted, operatic storytelling is a rather different beast from the design sensibilities you tend to champion. Nevertheless, the way both games’ legacies have mutated is fascinating. Nowadays, video essayists and internet commenters — as you noted, many of whom weren’t even around when these games came out — approach both with almost reverential seriousness. Their themes of AI, surveillance, and information control are routinely extracted from their original context and presented as evidence that the games somehow foresaw the 21st century. With Deus Ex, this can obscure how thoroughly its story was steeped in the conspiracy-pulp culture of the 1990s: Illuminati, Area 51, aliens, cyberpunk, The X-Files, and just about every other trope thrown into one gloriously overstuffed blender. Even Tomb Raider III (1998) had an Area 51 level! MGS2 is a somewhat different case, since its anxieties about information control and the circulation of ideas were very much deliberate. But its retrospective reputation can still flatten an often ludicrously theatrical, B-movie action game into a solemn prophecy. The game’s finale was substantially altered in the wake of 9/11: the original version had Arsenal Gear crashing through Manhattan. A rather literal reminder that these games were commercial products of their own cultural moment, not untouchable prophecies. There’s something strange about the way the internet’s memeification of a game’s supposedly prophetic elements can overwhelm the memory of what it was actually like to play it at the time. I was in my mid-twenties when Deus Ex came out; I loved every minute of it, and it remains one of my favorite games ever. Reading you put such a great game back into its historical and cultural context, rather than the myth it has become online, somehow makes those memories even better. (Also, MGS2 was an absolute technical marvel in 2001, but I digress.) Reply   Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Markets & Policy See all Sodium-ion batteries approach cost parity with LFP, with 70 GWh covered by supply agreements Sodium-ion batteries are approaching cell-level cost parity with LFP technology, with supply agreements exceeding 70 GWh worldwide. Despite higher upfront costs, they could offer a 21% lower total cost of ownership over 20 years, according to Wood Mackenzie. By Pilar Sánchez Molina 06 Nov 2026 Markets & Policy Batteries Energy Storage Singeng sodium-ion battery project in Hubei | Image: Sineng Advertisement Sodium-ion battery technology is entering the commercial production phase and emerging as an alternative to lithium-ion batteries, driven by supply chain diversification, strong low-temperature performance, and the potential for lower total cost of ownership. According to an analysis by Wood Mackenzie, supply agreements totaling more than 70 GWh are already in place. The study, which examines markets in China, the United States, Germany, and India, identifies sodium-ion batteries as the most promising emerging alternative to lithium-based technologies for stationary energy storage. Leading manufacturers are expected to achieve cell-level cost parity with lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries by late 2026, while parity at the module and system levels is not expected until after 2030. China is leading the commercialization of the technology. BYD plans to reach 30 GWh of sodium-ion battery manufacturing capacity, while CATL aims to exceed 1 GWh in sodium-ion battery shipments by the end of 2026. Supply agreements for sodium-ion batteries are already in place in China, the United States, and Europe, while India remains in the early stages of commercial validation. For the 2026–2035 period, Wood Mackenzie estimates a learning rate of 18% to 20% in China, reflecting the greater maturity of its industrial supply chain. Planned manufacturing capacity currently exceeds demand, although the growing number of supply agreements points to the technology’s gradual adoption in the market. Higher upfront costs, lower total cost of ownership Sodium-ion batteries currently have higher upfront costs than LFP batteries. The global average stands at $229/kWh, compared with approximately $200/kWh for LFP batteries. However, Wood Mackenzie estimates that sodium-ion batteries could achieve a 21% lower total cost of ownership over a 20-year project lifetime. The difference is primarily attributed to the elimination of capacity expansion cycles and lower operating costs. The economics of sodium-ion systems remain relatively stable across storage durations of two to four hours. The study identifies raw material supply security, service life, and a wider operating temperature range as key technical advantages of sodium-ion batteries. The latter could make them particularly suitable for applications in cold climates, where lithium-ion batteries may require additional thermal management systems. Regulation accelerates development Industrial and trade policies are playing an increasingly important role in the competitiveness of different battery chemistries. In July 2026, China reintroduced a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries while exempting sodium-ion batteries until the end of 2028. LFP batteries became subject to a 2% levy in September 2026, which is set to increase to 4% in September 2027. In the United States, tariffs of approximately 58% on energy storage cells imported from China, combined with production tax credits under Section 45X of the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), are encouraging domestic sodium-ion battery manufacturing. In Europe, carbon footprint declaration requirements under the EU Battery Regulation could favor technologies with supply chains that are less dependent on certain critical raw materials. Meanwhile, India is supporting domestic manufacturing through a $1.25 billion incentive program and tariff exemptions for certain types of manufacturing equipment. Wood Mackenzie expects the 2030–2035 period to be decisive for sodium-ion batteries to achieve economic competitiveness. For energy storage projects currently under development, LFP remains the most commercially mature option for storage durations of two to four hours. title: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS
body_text: So my ISP was hijacking my DNS - Karthikey Hegde / karthihegde / contact / posts So my ISP was hijacking my DNS Published on November 3, 2026 It was just a boring Saturday afternoon, and I thought I'd fix some of the problems with my homelab. One of those problems was that an external site my Podman container was trying to talk to just wasn't working. I kept getting "Site cannot be reached" almost immediately. This made me suspect something was wrong with my DNS setup, so I started doing a dig on the domain. I tried different providers, Google DNS, Cloudflare, pretty much everyone. Almost all of them returned the same IP address. But as soon as I tried Cloudflare's DoH endpoint, I got a completely different IP address. "Huh?" was my exact reaction. I took the IP I got from the first DNS resolution and tried to look up who owned it. Lo and behold, it was my goddamn ISP. That's when I realised my ISP was hijacking my DNS queries and returning a tampered IP address. Well, the obvious answer was DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS). I made a tweet about this, and it somehow blew up . But going through the replies, I noticed quite a few misconceptions and questions that I couldn't answer one by one. So I figured I'd use this article to address some of those questions and clear up a few misconceptions along the way. I self host Unbound I am safe For those of you who don't know, Unbound is basically a DNS resolver, kind of like what Cloudflare runs at 1.1.1.1 . The difference is, you can run it locally. It works by querying DNS servers to figure out the IP address for a domain, starting at the root nameservers and eventually making its way to the domain's authoritative nameserver. Now here's the catch. DNS resolution doesn't happen over a single connection. Your resolver might have to talk to multiple nameservers to figure out an IP address, and these queries are traditionally sent over plaintext DNS, usually UDP. Which means, you guessed it, your ISP can snoop on or even tamper with your DNS traffic. But you can also configure a forward-zone in Unbound. Instead of resolving DNS queries itself, Unbound can forward them to another DNS resolver. And if that resolver supports DoT, the connection to it is encrypted, which means your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS queries in transit. Just use DNSSEC It's understandable why someone would assume DNSSEC is what protects them here. I mean, it has DNS and Security right in the name. And in a way, it does, but it works through verification, not encryption. You see, DNSSEC doesn't encrypt your DNS traffic before sending it to a resolver. It uses cryptographic signatures to verify that the DNS data is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. But the problem here remains the same: your DNS traffic is still unencrypted in transit. Which means, your ISP can still snoop on it or mess with the responses. And for DNSSEC validation to work, the domain you're querying needs to have DNSSEC properly configured, with valid signatures and a chain of trust. And here's another problem: according to the October 2026 Defaults.Exposed census , only 7.03% of graded domains have a valid, fully validating DNSSEC chain. If a tampered response fails DNSSEC validation, your resolver will return SERVFAIL instead of handing you that bogus IP address. DoH and DoT are not Tamper free And yes, this is true. DoT and DoH rely on you trusting the DNS resolver you're sending your queries to. They encrypt the connection, so your ISP can't casually snoop on or tamper with your DNS traffic in transit. But that doesn't mean the resolver itself can't mess with your responses. You're still putting your trust in whoever runs that DNS server. Your ISP can snoop on the sites regardless Indeed. Although your regular internet traffic is encrypted with TLS, your ISP can see the hostname during the TLS handshake (SNI). They can also figure out which site you're visiting just from the destination IP sometimes. Unless, of course, you tunnel your traffic through a VPN. I use Mullvad through Tailscale's exit node feature. Of course, this just shifts some of the trust to your VPN provider. But that's a story for another day. So what does my setup look like? I've been using Pi-hole/AdGuard for over 3 years now. That's actually what got me into self-hosting in the first place. But there's another reason I don't route every single container through my local DNS server. When I'm updating containers, if something goes wrong and my DNS server goes down, I don't want that to take down DNS resolution for other containers that depend on it. So for some containers, I wanted an external DNS resolver as a fallback. Right now, I use AdGuard for my DNS, with dnscrypt-proxy handling the upstream DNS queries over DNSCrypt, so my DNS traffic is encrypted in transit. For containers where I really can't afford DNS failures, I also have Cloudflare configured as a fallback. My local AdGuard is still the primary DNS for them, though. I also run NixOS on my servers, and my dotfiles are open source if you're interested

title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
body_text: PhobosLab Blog Games Projects Dominic Szablewski, @phoboslab — Tuesday, November 3rd 2026 Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64 Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time. But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited. Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it. Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer. This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB. So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question. Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay. Audio in the Open Source Libdragon Similar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon , the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space. Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this “obsolete” hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay. What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse. QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize. A simple transform codec, something like MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work… The Ultra Low Complexity Codec During some late-night “research” , I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare. ulcplayer-gba by Aikku93, recorded in a Game Boy Advance emulator Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU . For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill. So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC). ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax. In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it. The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change: -7 … -2 , 2 … 7 - coefficient value 0 - zero run, run length ( 1 … 16 ) follows in the next nibble 1 - long zero run, run length ( 17 … 288 ) follows in the next two nibbles -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C . Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is . ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications. Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then! ULC on the N64 I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch. The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU. Float to 16-bit Fixed Point Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer. That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point. While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving at 3072 bytes : 32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14). After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is. Cramming it into the RSP Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor. This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job. (Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now) So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL . Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer. The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP. The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all. My ulc64 demo demonstrating quality at various bitrates To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio. ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects. The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago. Addendum A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. The README states: [...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image. ~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. body_text: MCP Explained Â· how the Model Context Protocol works MCP Explained What is MCP? by Model Context Protocol What is MCP? An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back. Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope.
