Reducing this gap is a priority for future models. We also worked to secure training and evaluations with two layers of monitoring. The first is synchronous: a monitor inspects tool calls before they run. Each task declares what actions it authorizes. Deterministic rules check calls against the task’s policy and circumvention patterns, escalating uncertain cases to an LLM judge. The second layer is asynchronous: an LLM judge reviews completed rollouts from training and evaluation for misbehavior and actions against our security boundary, raising alerts that we triage and escalate into our incident process. Together, these form a defense-in-depth approach to safety and alignment that we consider critical to developing a safe model factory. Training Inkling 2 Small Inkling 2 Small’s initial pretraining phase (H1) covered 8.4 trillion tokens of a broad mix of natural language, code, and image data. It ran for 68 hours on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks, which enabled high expert parallelism. Training ran natively in NVFP4, the 4-bit floating-point format introduced with the NVIDIA Blackwell GPU architecture. We’ll share more details on our NVFP4 recipe in a follow-up post soon. Stable training Metric Value Median policy staleness 17 updates Rollout batch size 16K Total tokens per rollout Median: 43K · p99: 1.5M Rollout duration Median: 8 minutes · p99: 4 hours Context window 256K tokens, with compaction for longer trajectories Making this scale practical required improvements throughout the systems stack. Our RL infrastructure deploys NVFP4 MoE training and sampling. During sampling, prefill, draft, and verify run fully on CUDA graphs. Trainers mirror the pretrain stack with high expert parallelism, EPLB, and CUDA graphs to improve GPU efficiency. To support long horizon agentic workloads, we use sticky routing and DRAM KV-cache offloading for maintaining 93%+ prefix cache hit rate, allowing us to maintain a 5:3 sampler:trainer ratio despite training at long contexts. Weight transfer is done via GPUDirectRDMA at 93%+ line rate with a parallelism-invariant checksum verifier. We also further lower deployment inference cost by offering a variant of NVFP4 KV cache, which we find to minimally lower evals. Long-horizon tasks give the model hours of autonomy, increasing potential risks from misaligned behavior. Midway through the main RL run, our asynchronous monitor flagged an instance where the model, failing at a task, worked around a network block through a third-party service it could reach using its search tools. We paused the run, hardened our infrastructure, removed environments that required web access, and added synchronous tool-call monitoring. We then resumed the run, incorporating additional training phases specifically for alignment, as described above. Improvements to our process allow us to train models at different sizes using similar recipes with predictable scaling and performance. Inkling 2 Small is part of a ladder of models; we look forward to sharing more rungs with you soon. Limitations While Inkling 2 Small improves on usability vs Inkling, it is not the most succinct communicator, and doesn’t always choose the best tools for the job—especially in codebases with a large number of skills. Like previous Inkling models, Inkling 2 Small natively supports image input; however, this model does not support audio. Inkling 2 Small is also less optimized for the chat experience. We notice issues such as worse organization and presentation of content, overuses of slashes, and overreaction to mental health and other safety related queries. Try Inkling 2 Small today We are proud to make Inkling 2 Small available on Tinker for inference and fine tuning. Following the completion of safety testing, the model will be available on additional platforms in the coming weeks. Inkling 2 Small was made in service of our mission to build AI that extends human will and judgment. Nov 5th, 2026 - Your friends and family can finally try Kagi # Kagi Search Search for everyone As many of you know, we don't run ads anywhere . Instead, we are active on social media and online communities to stay close to you, build a great product, and rely on word of mouth . We've heard that it can be hard to recommend a search engine when your friends can't try it without creating an account. That's changed: anyone, anywhere, can now visit kagi.com and search the web . No account required for the first 50 searches (100 more upon registration). We are counting on you to spread the word to your friends and family <3 Our new landing page for new users Our take on the latest Search industry news Google announced that, starting in early 2027, AI tools will be turned off by default for school accounts. It sounds like a win for schools until you read that Google Search will be switched off along with them. Our take: Education shouldn't be taken hostage by an advertising company. Letâs stop putting corporate profits over the imperative to educate students. Our call to schools facing this choice: You don't have to accept it. There are alternatives to mandatory AI, and, yes, Kagi is one of them. Kagi Assistant on the go and design refinements for Search # Announcing the official Kagi Assistant apps Kagi Assistant is now available as a native app for iOS and Android ! Ask a question, explore the web, work with files, conduct in-depth research, or choose from leading AI models, all from your phone. Your threads and Custom Assistants stay with you, so you can pick up wherever you left off. These are the first steps towards delivering a fantastic Kagi Assistant experience on mobile, with much more to come. July 31st, 2025 - Kagi Assistant gets tags, bulk actions, and much more # Kagi Assistant This week's release brings several big updates to Kagi Assistant, laying the groundwork to exciting new chapters ahead. Introducing tags Tags let you organise your Kagi Assistant threads. Each thread can have multiple tags. You can use the Temporary tag to mark any thread as temporary, and it will auto-delete 24h after its last update. If you use Kagi Assistant in 24h mode, all new threads will be tagged as Temporary by default. When you remove the Temporary tag, that thread will be saved. When you create a thread while viewing a specific tag, the new thread will automatically inherit that tag. Threads without a custom tag, such as all your currently saved threads, appear in the All folder. Learn more on our help page . Bulk managing threads We've also made thread management easier: select multiple threads and either tag them or delete them permanently. [upl-image-preview url= https://kagifeedback.org/assets/files/2025-07-31/1753986178-528658-image.png ] Model picker The model picker now features a curated set of base models that we believe deliver the strongest performance, helping you choose the best option for your specific task. We continuously update this list using our own in-house benchmarking . Define your default Assistant You can now define your default Kagi Assistant model , as either one of your Custom Assistants, a base model or the last used model. Every new thread you create will start with that default model. Removal of context windows limits Kagi Assistant no longer enforces context window limits . We include all available information, and if we reach the modelâs maximum size, we carry forward relevant context so it remains available for your next instructions. Advanced control for Bangs via Regex We've added an optional "Regex" field to Custom Bangs for more precise control. Instead of $1 always being the first word and $2 the second, you can now define exactly how your query is split to create more powerful shortcuts. For example, to create a custom translator for a query like !tr spanish live long and prosper , you can now separate the language from the text. In your Custom Bang settings, you would use: Template: https://translate.kagi.com/?to=$1&text=$2 Regex: (\w+)\s+(.*) This pattern tells the Bang to use the first word for $1 and the entire rest of the query for $2 . If you leave the Regex field blank, your Bangs will continue to work as they always have. title: Motorola Signature 27 with GrapheneOS support
body_text: The motorola signature 27 sets a new flagship standard Skip to content Home News Press Box Search 2026. Motorola® All rights reserved Search Search for: Advanced search Top Tags 5G B2B ESG general moto e motorola edge Power to Empower Ready For Software ThinkShield for mobile Date All Last month Last 3 months Last 6 months 2025 2024 High-contrast Mode Regular-contrast Mode Large Font Size Regular Font Size EN Select Language Global Motorola Latin America América Central & Caribe Argentina Brasil Chile Colombia Ecuador México Perú Uruguay & Paraguay Article Motorola sets a new flagship standard with motorola signature 27, featuring its most advanced camera system, next-generation agentic AI and the brightest display available in a smartphone November 5, 2026 Overview: The world’s best camera system launched in 2026 25 , outranking all other Android and iOS devices, as assessed by DXOMARK. The brightest display available in a smartphone 20 , with an Extreme AMOLED Duo tandem display and up to 12,000 nits of peak brightness 4 . Among the first smartphones powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, delivering breakthrough performance, next generation connectivity, and advanced AI experiences. Designed for Gemini Intelligence⁷, the motorola signature 27 meets the high system standards required to run Google’s best Gemini experiences. The only smartphone in-market with Audio by Bang & Olufsen, providing richer, more immersive sound through a custom-tuned audio experience. A 7000mAh battery¹¹, 35% larger than the last generation. The first Motorola device to support GrapheneOS, a privacy and security-focused mobile operating system. Motorola, a Lenovo Company, is designing to a higher standard with the new motorola signature 27, the company’s most advanced flagship smartphone to date, bringing together distinctive design, category-leading innovation and next-generation AI experiences. From its contoured edges, expressive finishes and refined craftsmanship to the breakthrough technologies within, every detail of the motorola signature 27 was purposefully built to deliver a premium experience without compromise. Featuring Motorola’s most advanced camera system yet, recognized with a DXOMARK Gold Label for image quality performance, the brightest Extreme AMOLED Duo Tandem display¹ available in a smartphone, the Snapdragon® 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, making it among the first smartphones to unlock next-generation connectivity and AI experiences, and the only smartphone in-market with Audio by Bang & Olufsen, the motorola signature 27 represents the pinnacle of Motorola innovation. Motorola’s best camera system yet, recognized for imaging excellence The motorola signature 27 includes the world’s best camera sytsem launched in 2026 25 , combining advanced hardware, cinematic video, and effortless photography. Awarded the coveted DXOMARK Gold Label in recognition of its industry-leading level of imaging quality performance and outranking all other Android and iOS devices, the motorola signature 27’s camera system delivers eye-catching photos and videos, with: A 50MP Sony LYTIA L910 main camera captures exceptional clarity, rich color and deep contrast for vibrant, ready to share results. Combined with LOFIC technology, it records brighter, more balanced video with consistent detail across challenging lighting conditions, whether filming concert stages, neon-lit streets, candlelit dinners or nights out with friends. A 200MP periscope telephoto camera with 100x Super Zoom captures everything from distant landmarks and architectural details to wildlife and action unfolding far away with remarkable clarity. Powered by AI, 100x Super Zoom Pro helps preserve natural color, sharpness and details even at extreme distances. The 3x periscope telephoto lens also delivers flattering, natural-looking portraits, while ultra-resolution imaging provides greater flexibility for cropping, reframing, and editing. The first ever dedicated EVS action sensor on a smartphone² introduces a new approach to smartphone motion photography, helping capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision. Working together with the Action Shot feature, it freezes motion while maximizing available light, producing crisp, vibrant images with richer detail and more natural color. The 50MP ultrawide camera³ fits more into every frame, transforming tight spaces into expansive compositions and making it easier to capture sweeping landscapes, large landmarks and group photos without stepping back. And a 50MP front camera delivers sharp, ready-to-share selfies and supports 4K video recording, so selfie videos feature the same bold colors and clarity as still photos. For a more cinematic video experience, the motorola signature 27 features a powerful Video Enhancement Engine that uses AI to intelligently optimize color, contrast and dynamic range in real time. Support for Dolby Vision ® , the same technology used by leading filmmakers, helps enable richer, more immersive video. Combined with the Qualcomm® Electronic Image Stabilization and 3.5° OIS hardware on the main camera, panning, walking, and handheld recording looks more fluid and stable, so users can stay in the moment while the camera does the hard work. the brightest display available in a smartphone 20 Engineered to unlock the full potential of the latest advances in display technology, the motorola signature 27 features a new Extreme AMOLED Duo display, the brightest display available, designed to provide a premium viewing experience in virtually any environment. Built with breakthrough Tandem Technology, it combines two emissive layers into one, producing brighter visuals, richer color and greater efficiency. With up to 12,000 4 nits of peak brightness, users can comfortably view maps, messages, photos and videos virtually anywhere, whether navigating a sunny afternoon, checking directions on the go or capturing content outdoors, without needing to shield the screen or strain to see it. Plus, 1.5K Super HD resolution and Dolby Vision® bring entertainment to life with exceptional sharpness, contrast and precision. This advanced display is also designed to be smarter and more durable, delivering up to 34% greater energy efficiency and up to a 121% longer lifespan than traditional AMOLED panels. 24 Pantone® Validated color calibration ensures colors and skin tones appear true to life 5 , while SGS-certified blue light technology helps reduce eye strain. powering next generation experiences At the heart of the motorola signature 27 is the Snapdragon® 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, making it among the first smartphones to feature Qualcomm Technologies’ latest flagship mobile chipset. Engineered to power breakthrough gaming, advanced camera experiences, ultra-fast connectivity and AI, it delivers the performance needed for today’s most demanding mobile experiences and the next wave of AI innovation. To sustain peak performance when it matters most, the motorola signature 27 pairs the platform with Motorola’s ArcticMesh cooling system that uses micro-diamond-infused thermal gel and a thermal chamber that is 40% larger than the previous generation⁶ to keep performance running at its best during extended gaming sessions, AI tasks, video recording and intensive multitasking. With a new 6‑antenna design delivering faster 5G downloads, up to 2x faster Wi‑Fi speeds 6 , Wi‑Fi 8 compatibility, the motorola signature 27 is built to stay fast, capable and ready for next-era AI. And seven years of OS upgrades 23 help ensure the experience stays reliable long into the future. AI that goes beyond assistance The motorola signature 27 is designed for Gemini Intelligence, which brings the best of Gemini to Android’s most advanced devices, alongside out-of-box Google Gemini experiences and Motorola Qira. The motorola signature 27 can understand context, help people create, support decisions and move from intention to action across the apps and services they use every day. As Google rolls out these capabilities to Gemini Intelligence⁷ devices globally in the coming months, motorola signature 27 will be ready to bring them to users around the world: Whether booking a ride or preparing a grocery order from a shopping list on your screen, Gemini helps users go from intention to action with less effort. Gemini can handle complex, multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf , reducing app switching and helping them stay focused on what matters. Users remain in control throughout, with the ability to view progress, jump in, or stop a task. 16 Rambler 17 transforms natural speech into polished messages, letting users think out loud while it refines their words in the background. Rambler removes filler words, edits repetition, and organizes ideas into clear paragraphs or bullet points. Users can correct themselves mid-sentence, switch languages seamlessly, and review everything before sending, ensuring they share exactly what they intend. Afterwards, users can quickly ask Rambler to rewrite, rephrase, translate, or reformat their text. Create My Widget 18 enables users to create personalized widgets by simply describing what they want to see. Whether it’s a tracker to follow your monthly spending, daily recipe inspiration, or a trip countdown with your travel details, your homescreen can be as personalized as you want it to be. Sign-to-Text 19 translates American Sign Language (ASL) into written English in real time using the device’s front-facing camera. Integrated with Gboard and Live Transcribe, it opens new ways for users to communicate across digital and in-person interactions. Right out of the box, the motorola signature 27 also includes powerful Google Gemini⁸ experiences designed to bring new levels of creativity, including Gemini Omni, which enables users to create and edit video through natural conversation, and Lyria which generates custom soundtracks from simple prompts. In addition, the device features Motorola Qira ⁹ , a built-in AI system designed to connect and enhance experiences across supported Motorola and Lenovo devices, helping users get more from their broader ecosystem through a single, seamless hybrid AI experience. the only smartphone with “Audio by Bang & Olufsen” As the only smartphone in-market to feature Audio by Bang & Olufsen, the motorola signature 27 unlocks an elevated audio experience built on Motorola’s recently announced multi-year partnership with Bang & Olufsen. Combining Motorola’s premium mobile innovation with Bang & Olufsen’s renowned expertise in sound and design, the device is engineered to deliver sound that is meant to be felt, not just heard. Featuring dedicated Sound Modes and an all-new speaker architecture, the device is tuned to preserve the character of the original recording, alongside deep bass, clear vocals and greater fidelity across music, movies and games. distinctive design, exceptional durability With the motorola signature 27, Motorola continues the evolution of its signature family design philosophy, that balances aesthetic expression with everyday usability. The device features a sleek aluminum silhouette with contoured edges and a thin profile that feels comfortable in hand, while delivering a distinctly premium look and feel. Complementing the refined design is a seamlessly integrated camera plane, finished in smooth ceramic and brushed aluminum, creating a sophisticated focal point that feels both purposeful and modern. Precisely crafted with a ceramic and glass construction, the motorola signature 27 is available in two unique, elevated finishes: PANTONE Coal Smoke, which features a tactical weave finish inspired by automotive design and performance materials, and PANTONE Capulet Olive, which features a textile-inspired finish influenced by premium fashion and interior design. Premium materials and durability come together in the motorola signature 27, featuring Corning® Gorilla® Glass Ceramic 3 , an aerospace-grade aluminum frame, military-grade durability (MIL-STD-810H) 10 , and IP68 and IP69 ratings for enhanced protection against the elements. 22 power that gives the freedom to do more To back up all this powerful innovation, the motorola signature 27 features a 7000mAh battery 11 , 35% larger than the last generation, so users can stay connected longer, stream and create without interruption, and move through the day without constantly thinking about battery life. When battery does get low, 90W TurboPower™ charging quickly restores power for the day in just 12 minutes 12,13 , whether on a coffee break or while getting ready. For a more effortless experience, users can go cord-free with 50W wireless charging , powering 0 to 100% in up to 80 minutes of wireless charging. 12,14 Motorola’s first GrapheneOS-supported device, built for privacy and peace of mind Data privacy matters, and Motorola continues to build on its commitment to security with ThinkShield®, which helps protect users from the factory to the phone, and Moto Secure, a centralized destination for managing privacy and security features. Expanding that commitment even further, the motorola signature 27 will kickstart a new era of smartphone privacy and security. It will be Motorola’s first device to support GrapheneOS, a hardened, open-source operating system based on the Android Open Source Project. Developed in partnership with the GrapheneOS Foundation, the leading nonprofit in advanced mobile security, the device reflects Motorola’s commitment to bringing cutting-edge security to everyday users across the globe. That commitment runs deeper than software: GrapheneOS sets demanding requirements for the hardware it runs on and how it’s kept updated, and the motorola signature 27 is built to meet them. The device is Motorola’s first with a performant implementation of ARM Memory Tagging Extension, a new hardware memory safety mechanism for helping ensure system integrity and privacy. More details on it will be shared in the coming months. Availability Motorola signature 27 will be available in markets worldwide in the coming months, with a starting MSRP of $1,599. title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
body_text: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts) | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts) 729 points by jameslk 3 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 200 comments If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information . https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988 “[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“ https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review “A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers” https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data “Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. title: Nvidia RTX Spark encrypted firmware slows inference speed to 35% on Linux
body_text: Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works | MindStudio Skip to main content Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Product AI Models AI Media Workbench Agent Skills Plugin Workflow Capabilities Pricing Learn University Documentation Blog About Log in Get Started My Workspace Blog / Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works RTX Spark Linux Nvidia DGX Spark Linux dual boot laptop Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark Laptop: What Actually Works A hands-on look at dual-booting Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, the GPU clock throttling bug found, and why WSL still wins. Edited by Luis Chavez-Mattos , Director of Product · November 1, 2026 · RSS Can you run Linux on the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop? Yes, but it comes with a serious catch. Linux installs and runs on RTX Spark laptops like the MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI Plus, including GPU acceleration through Nvidia’s open kernel driver. The problem is clock speed: once the laptop is plugged into wall power, the GPU gets locked to roughly 780 MHz on Linux instead of the 2 GHz-plus it hits on Windows. That turns a chip capable of around 65 tokens per second on a 120 billion parameter model into one struggling to break 14 tokens per second, for reasons tied to power management firmware that Linux currently can’t read. TL;DR Dual-booting Linux works on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop, with a full desktop, GPU acceleration via Nvidia’s open driver, 4K output at 120Hz, and working audio, keyboard, and touchpad once configured correctly. A hidden Windows-only component called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework manages power delivery between CPU and GPU, and it has no Linux equivalent, which is the root cause of the slowdown. GPU clock speed collapses to about 780 MHz on Linux when plugged in , compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows, because the firmware’s power table is encrypted and only the Windows driver can decrypt it. Benchmarks on GPT-OSS-120B show the gap clearly : Windows hit 65.4 tokens per second, WSL hit 65.1, the Nvidia DGX Spark hit 61, and native Linux on the same laptop managed only 13.9. Memory allocation is a separate headache , since the laptop reserves 96GB of unified memory for the GPU by default and only Windows exposes a setting to change that split, which is required before Linux can see more than a sliver of RAM. WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the practical middle ground today , since it rides on the Windows driver stack and keeps full GPU boost whether the laptop is plugged in or on battery, while still running Linux-first AI tools like vLLM. A real fix depends on Nvidia , specifically on porting the platform controller’s power management logic into its Linux driver, which would effectively turn the laptop into a portable version of the DGX Spark. Self-host Remy. On-prem or in your private cloud. Remy and every app you build stay inside your walls. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today What makes the RTX Spark laptop different from a normal Windows PC? The RTX Spark platform, which ships in machines like the MSI Prestige, the Asus ProArt, and the Dell XPS, uses the same GPU design as Nvidia’s DGX Spark desktop unit. But where the DGX Spark ships with Nvidia’s own Linux build out of the box, every one of these laptop variants ships with Windows on ARM. That distinction matters because Windows on ARM with CUDA support is new. ARM-based Windows machines have existed for a few years, but pairing that architecture with Nvidia’s CUDA stack only became possible with this chip. The laptops also support unified memory configurations up to 128GB, shared between CPU and GPU, which is unusual for a laptop and central to why they’re being marketed at AI developers in the first place. Because so much of the AI tooling ecosystem, including vLLM and SGLang, is built Linux-first, developers who buy these machines naturally want to know whether they can ditch Windows, or at least dual-boot, without losing performance. How do you actually install Linux on it? The process is not plug-and-play. A first attempt using Omarchy (a Linux distribution with Arch roots) failed because, while it already supported the chip on Asus and Dell hardware, the MSI Prestige behaved differently, producing a flickering, unstable display during boot. Switching to Debian worked more reliably, but still needed workarounds. The installer couldn’t connect to Wi-Fi, so installation required a USB Ethernet adapter. Out of the box, Debian also didn’t recognize the keyboard, touchpad, or GPU, because none of the laptop-specific hardware support was present in a vanilla kernel. Going back to Omarchy solved the driver problem, since its kernel already bundled Nvidia’s open-source driver. At that point Linux booted properly, but could only see 28GB of the laptop’s 128GB of unified memory. That’s because the laptop’s firmware reserves 96GB for GPU use, and that split is only adjustable from Windows. Dropping the Windows-side GPU memory reservation down to 4GB freed up 120GB for Linux to see once booted. After that adjustment, the laptop ran a full desktop at 4K and 120Hz, with working audio, touchpad, keyboard, and CUDA acceleration. Getting video output over HDMI during the install process was its own obstacle. Early in the process, the laptop would only display video on its own internal screen, not over HDMI, which required pointing an external camera at the laptop’s screen just to see what was happening during remote-controlled installation steps. How does Linux performance compare to Windows and WSL? This is where the story turns. With GPT-OSS-120B running on the GPU, Windows produced 65.4 tokens per second. WSL, which runs a Linux environment inside Windows, hit 65.1 tokens per second, nearly identical. The DGX Spark desktop unit, running Nvidia’s native Linux build, came in at 61 tokens per second. Native Linux on the laptop, however, dropped to 13.9 tokens per second, roughly five times slower. Every team builds with AI. Nothing gets lost. The AI platform for building secure, compliant enterprise apps Try Remy today The gap showed up again with vLLM running eight concurrent clients: WSL reached 127 tokens per second while native Linux reached 39.5. A longer benchmark run told the same story in time rather than throughput. Windows finished in about 8 minutes while holding the GPU near 2.2 GHz. Linux took 37 minutes, with the GPU parked around 790 MHz the entire time. Temperatures stayed low, between 40 and 47°C, so this isn’t a thermal throttling issue. The GPU simply isn’t being allowed to run at full speed. Oddly, the direction of the problem flips depending on power source. Unplugged, Linux hit around 61 to 67 tokens per second on LM Studio, comparable to Windows. Plugged in, that same test dropped to about 15 tokens per second. Clock speed told the same story: around 1,800 MHz unplugged under load, and down to roughly 780 MHz when connected to wall power. Why does plugging in the laptop slow Linux down? The cause traces back to a component visible in Windows Device Manager called the Nvidia Platform Controllers and Framework. This piece of firmware and driver logic manages the shared power budget between CPU and GPU, since a laptop (unlike the desktop DGX Spark) has to balance power delivery between both chips rather than feeding the GPU on its own line. Disabling that controller in Windows reproduced the slowdown directly: tokens per second dropped from around 83 to about 31, and clock speed fell from roughly 2 GHz down to the same 786 MHz seen on Linux when plugged in. Re-enabling the controller restored normal speed immediately. That confirms the controller, not the kernel, the distribution, or the Nvidia GPU driver itself, is what’s holding Linux back. The deeper issue is that the firmware hands this controller a table of power settings that is encrypted. Windows has the key to decrypt it. Linux currently does not, and no software fix attempted during testing could enable it, including one attempt that triggered a kernel panic. Extracting the decryption key from the Windows driver was floated as a theoretical workaround, but that would amount to a fragile, single-machine hack rather than something that works broadly. A real fix needs to come from Nvidia shipping equivalent power management logic in its Linux driver. Is WSL a good substitute for native Linux right now? For most developers, yes, at least for now. WSL runs on top of the Windows driver stack, so it inherits Windows’ full GPU boost behavior whether the laptop is plugged in or running on battery. It also runs Linux-first AI tools like vLLM and SGLang without the clock throttling problem that affects native Linux installs. The one adjustment needed is memory. WSL reserves only 14GB by default, which isn’t enough for large model workloads on a 128GB unified memory machine, so that allocation needs to be increased manually. Once that’s done, WSL benchmarks land close to native Windows performance, making it the more practical choice until Nvidia addresses the Linux driver gap directly. Frequently Asked Questions Can the Nvidia RTX Spark laptop dual-boot Windows and Linux? Yes. Dual-booting was demonstrated on the MSI Prestige RTX Spark laptop using Omarchy, a Linux distribution that already included Nvidia’s open kernel driver for this chip, after an initial attempt with Debian required manual driver and networking workarounds. Why is Linux so much slower than Windows on this laptop when plugged in? Developers have their tools. Enterprises have Remy. Without a Linux equivalent, the GPU’s clock speed gets locked around 780 MHz when the laptop is connected to power, compared to roughly 2.2 GHz on Windows. Does unplugging the laptop fix the Linux performance problem? It helps significantly. On battery power, Linux GPU clocks and token throughput come much closer to Windows levels. The severe slowdown specifically appears when the laptop is plugged into wall power, which is the opposite of what most users would expect. Is WSL the same as running native Linux on the RTX Spark? Not exactly, but it’s close in practice. WSL runs a Linux environment on top of the Windows kernel and driver stack, so it retains Windows’ GPU clock boost behavior and avoids the throttling issue, while still supporting Linux-native AI tools like vLLM. Will Nvidia fix Linux GPU performance on RTX Spark laptops? That depends on Nvidia shipping the platform controller’s power management logic in its Linux driver. The encrypted firmware power table currently can only be decrypted by Windows, and no workaround found so far restores full clock speed on Linux without it. title: September in Servo: <progress>, rounded rectangles, and more
body_text: September in Servo: &lt;progress>, rounded rectangles, and more! - Servo aims to empower developers with a lightweight, high-performance alternative for embedding web technologies in applications. , rounded rectangles, and more!"> Get Involved Contributing Servo Book WPT pass rates Code of Conduct Download Blog Demos About About Servo Made with Servo Governance Sponsorship , rounded rectangles, and more!"> September in Servo: <progress>, rounded rectangles, and more! Plus new CSS functions and WEbGL2 improvements. Posted 2026-11-05 Servo 0.7.0 contains all of the changes we landed in September, spanning 527 commits! The developer tools console now eagerly evaluates JS inputs, allowing faster feedback ( @freyacodes , #47527 ). We’ve shipped new web platform features: the :checked pseudoclass ( @skyz1 , #47987 ) the user-select property ( @SimonSapin , @mrobinson , #48137 , #48242 ) the <progress> element ( @rayguo17 , #46974 ) CSS typed arithmetic ( @Loirooriol , #48338 ) the alpha() CSS function ( @Loirooriol , #48344 ) the font-width property ( @Loirooriol , #47914 ) Plus a bunch of new DOM APIs: parentRule on CSSRule and CSSStyleDeclaration ( @skyz1 , #47743 ) version on HTMLHtmlElement ( @SilvioPilato , #47786 ) getComposedRanges() and direction on Selection ( @mrobinson , #47683 ) baseURL on CSSStyleSheet ( @Gae24 , #47783 ) CSS modules ( @Gae24 , #47813 ) and text modules ( @Gae24 , #47863 ) getContextAttributes() on CanvasRenderingContext2D and OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D ( @Taym95 , #47868 ) the Content-Language header ( @TimvdLippe , #47930 ) dir on Document ( @yezhizhen , #48170 ) SVGAElement , SVGPatternElement , SVGTSpanElement , SVGTextContentElement , SVGTextElement , SVGTextPositioningElement ( @mu-mostafa98 , #48174 ) the MLKEM768-X25519 algorithm for WebCrypto ( @kkoyung , #48240 , #48282 , #48313 , #48350 ) roundRect() on CanvasRenderingContext2D ( @yezhizhen , #48293 ) paintTime and presentationTime on PerformancePaintTiming ( @shubhamg13 , #47926 ) getCueAsHTML() on VTTCue ( @TimvdLippe , #48146 ) Security We upgraded to SpiderMonkey v153.3 and mozangle v0.7 , both of which included fixes for security bugs reported upstream ( @sagudev , #48176 , #47655 , #48259 ). Real world compat The egui.rs demo now works as expected with --pref dom._webegpu_enabled . This Candy Crush game is now playable. We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion , and failures in our GitHub issues . Work in progress Our accessibility tree ( --pref accessibility_enabled ) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements ( @alice , #47905 ) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes ( @alice , @mrobinson , #47690 ). Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden ( @alice , #47772 ). We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation ( --pref dom_webgl2_enabled ) ( @mxmgorin , #48423 , #48441 , #48470 , #48479 , #48495 , #48473 , #48536 ). Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable ) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable ( example ). Closed captioning for video elements is making progress. Text tracks now fire enter , exit , and cuechange events ( @TimvdLippe , #47725 ). Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks ( @TimvdLippe , #47785 ), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly ( @TimvdLippe , #48012 ). Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated <track> element. Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time ( @TimvdLippe , #48325 ), and active cues are computed correctly ( @TimvdLippe , #48305 ), while text track cues are ordered as expected ( @TimvdLippe , #48368 ). Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors ( @TimvdLippe , #48391 ). The Sanitizer API ( --pref dom_sanitizer_enabled ) now accepts the javascriptURLs property ( @skyz1 , #47867 ). IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names ( --pref dom_indexeddb_enabled ) ( @leowatts , #47936 ). Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex ( @kuntal-devrat , #48281 ), as well as advance() , continue() , and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor ( @kuntal-devrat , #48400 ). We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface ( --pref dom_web_animations_enabled ) ( @simonwuelker , #48122 ). Embedding API There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo :: forward_accessibility_action ( @alice , @mrobinson , #48512 ). There is also an API to clear session history: WebView :: clear_session_history ( @Narfinger , #47483 ). The WebView :: set_throttled API has been removed ( @mrobinson , #39923 ). Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown . The WebViewDelegate :: notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur ( @mrobinson , #48364 ). Embedders must call WebView :: set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus. The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature ( @janeoa , #47866 ). If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features. Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess ( @Narfinger , #47360 ). To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled. Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb ( @mxmgorin , #47999 ). These can help on memory-constrained devices, and more information is available in the SpiderMonkey source ( base , urgent ). The JVM compatibility target was raised to 11 on Android ( @veyndan , #48414 ). For users and developers It is now possible to cross-compile the OpenHarmony build from Windows hosts ( @jschwe , #48392 ). Unhandled promise rejections are reported to the JS console ( @TTyChud , #48486 ), making it easier to narrow down web compatibility issues in Servo. The OpenHarmony SDK was updated to API level 23 ( @Narfinger , #48505 ). Pressing Control+A (or Command+A on macOS) now selects all the content in a document ( @dzfrias , @mrobinson , #48025 ). It is no longer possible to copy text inside of password inputs ( @dzfrias , #48404 ). Embedder-originating JS (e.g. devtools console or embedding APIs) will always execute, even in documents that disable scripting via sandboxing or CSP ( @derdilla , #48394 ). Performance and stability We improved performance by removing unnecessary allocations ( @Narfinger , @TimvdLippe , @yezhizhen , #47689 , #47839 , #47838 , #47982 , #48006 , #48036 , #48099 , #48204 , #48127 , #48218 , #48357 , #48386 , #48422 , #48440 , #48452 , #48508 ), preallocating more when building vectors ( @jschwe , @Narfinger , @sagudev , @webbeef , #47455 , #47613 , #48026 , #48398 ), and avoiding IPC in single process mode ( @leowatts , @Narfinger , @Uiniel , @TTyChud , #47691 , #47718 , #48002 , #48073 , #48476 , #48435 ). We also sped up Servo by reducing interactions with the GC ( @TimvdLippe , @Narfinger , #47818 , #48257 , #48396 ), and doing less work when modifying selections ( @SimonSapin , #47579 ), dispatching events ( @webbeef , #48078 ), calculating font metrics ( @RichardTjokroutomo , #48238 ), and indexing window frames ( @mrobinson , #47832 ). We reduced memory usage in common cases by reusing buffers ( @Narfinger , #47751 ), clearing more page-specific data ( @Radeonares32 , @Narfinger , @jschwe , @mrobinson , @mxmgorin , #47651 , #47806 , #47805 , #48166 , #48295 , #48297 , #48016 ), compacting data structures ( @Narfinger , @webbeef , @SimonSapin , @mrobinson , #47776 , #48039 , #48050 , #47742 , #48301 , #48296 , #48105 ), and sharing more buffers ( @jdm , #47998 ). We also fixed a memory leak involving <audio> and <video> elements ( @TTyChud , #48371 ). We turned on thread affinity boosting on Linux, which can improve performance on some CPU architectures ( @jschwe , #47058 ). We’re working on statically preventing a footgun that can lead to uncollectible GC cycles and leaking memory ( @Gae24 , @jdm , @lumiscosity , @SilvioPilato , @sahilnyk , @TTyChud , @kuntal-devrat , @MohamedAli00949 , #47941 , #48013 , #48021 , #48035 , #48033 , #48051 , #48072 , #48171 , #48209 , #48248 , #48246 , #48264 , #48285 , #48311 , #48408 , #48053 , #48156 , #48186 , #48223 , #48315 , #47872 , #47698 , #47682 , #47735 , #47816 , #47817 , #47794 , #47909 , #47934 , #47935 , #47954 , #48022 , #47955 , #48058 , #48228 , #48247 , #48261 , #48280 , #48302 , #48316 , #48328 , #48346 , #48355 , #48262 , #48377 , #48304 , #48378 , #48388 , #48432 ). We fixed panics in WebRTC ( @MunishMummadi , #4772 ), execCommand() on Document ( @TimvdLippe , #47784 ), <video> ( @calvaris , #46148 ), <iframe> ( @jdm , #48465 ), SharedWorker ( @mrobinson , #47940 ), ancestorOrigins on Document ( @mrobinson , #48009 ), about:memory ( @mxmgorin , #47686 , #48001 ), and EGL 1.4 configurations ( @mxmgorin , #47803 ). We also fixed a very ironic panic triggered by the about:crash page that loads when a normal page triggers a panic ( @mrobinson , #48055 ) The JS console no longer hangs when primitive values as thrown as exceptions ( @FatCat560 , #47629 ). Servo no longer hangs on shutdown in multiprocess mode ( @Narfinger , #48523 ), when certain pages use IntersectionObserver ( @mxmgorin , #47693 ), when closing a browsing context with pending WebDriver commands ( @yezhizhen , #48131 , #48172 ), or when closing SharedWorker s ( @nicoburns , #48477 ). about:memory got more improvements: we measure more memory for SVG rendering ( @Narfinger , @mrobinson , #47061 ), WebAudio ( @jdm , #47996 ), and identify globals that have been leaked ( @jdm , #48237 ). More on the web platform CSS images now delay the load event , leading to more consistent behaviour for engine users performing visual rendering ( @TimvdLippe , #48199 ). Interactive selections in documents continued to improve! They now can span shadow trees ( @mrobinson , @SimonSapin , #47931 , #47694 , #47895 ), and have consistent heights and positions ( @mrobinson , #47937 ), plus there are new context menu entries to copy and select all ( @mrobinson , #48101 ). Additionally, image-based content shows when it is part of a selection ( @mrobinson , #48149 ). Window.open() respects sandbox flags that prevent popups ( @mrobinson , #47653 ). LargestContentfulPaint now reports the loadTime for image content ( @shubhamg13 , #48286 ), ignores cross-origin frames ( @shubhamg13 , #48094 ), ignores invisible text ( @shubhamg13 , #48010 ), and reports null elements when they are removed from the tree ( @shubhamg13 , #48125 ). select() on a text input now focuses the control ( @dzfrias , @mrobinson , #48475 ). Our WebDriver server now automates setting permissions ( @xbwwj , @yezhizhen , #47623 ), while sending click events and keyboard actions uses fewer delays ( @yezhizhen , #48066 ). There are more useful error messages for methods on Document ( @eachra-bawn , #47835 ) and CSS -related interfaces ( @eachra-bawn , @jdm , #47746 ). We upgraded our stylo dependency, which improves compatibility with contrast-color() , color-mix() , vertical-align , list-style , place-items , at-rule() , calc() , alpha() , attr() , content: attr() , and named-feature() ( @Loirooriol , #46987 , #47942 ). We also fixed bugs related to visibilityState on Document ( @yezhizhen , #47908 ), containsNode() on Selection ( @mrobinson , #47938 ), setKeyframes on KeyframeEffect ( @simonwuelker , #48103 ), selections when focusing a text input ( @mrobinson , #48107 ), AudioParam clamping and automation ( @kevlu93 , #48351 , #48347 ), PannerNode outputs ( @kevlu93 , #48510 ), the muted attribute on HTMLMediaElement ( @TimvdLippe , #48403 ), placeholders in text inputs ( @jdm , #47761 , #47797 ), animations when modifying document stylesheets ( @SharanRP , #48000 ), gradient color stops ( @BudiArb , #48288 ), sticky table rows ( @TTyChud , #48380 ), ::first-letter ( @Loirooriol , #48307 ), text-wrap-mode ( @mrobinson , #48469 ), OTF fonts ( @wood-ghost , #47904 ), CSS and nosniff ( @sahvx655-wq , #45481 ), Sec-Fetch- headers and redirects ( @TimvdLippe , #48203 ), moveBefore() on Node ( @mrobinson , #47692 ), supports() on WebCrypto ( @kkoyung , #47768 , #47891 , #47953 , #47984 , #48410 , #47545 ), cross-origin windows ( @mrobinson , @jdm , #47632 , #48411 , #48038 ), origins of about:blank and about:srcdoc ( @mrobinson , #47630 ), keypress events ( @mrobinson , #48324 ), text and media documents ( @SilvioPilato , #47823 ), body() on Response ( @TTyChud , #48409 ), <details> with <summary> ( @TimvdLippe , #48224 ), editing hidden inputs ( @dzfrias , #48165 ), attribute nodes in XPath ( @leowatts , @mrobinson , #47912 ), absolutely positioned boxes ( @mxmgorin , #48081 ), CSS Grid containers with absolutely positioned nodes ( @nicoburns , #47519 ), WebDriver wheel/pointer actions ( @yezhizhen , #48143 ), and blob: URLs ( @Gae24 , #47910 ). New contributors A special thanks to the following people for landing their first patch in Servo: Arnau Camprubí ( @Arnau478 , #47726 ) Silvio Pilato ( @SilvioPilato , #47786 ) Radeonares32 ( @Radeonares32 , #47651 ) derdilla ( @derdilla , #47828 ) pr3pony ( @pr3pony , #48030 ) Mario ( @Fatcat560 , #47629 ) TtyChud ( @TTyChud , #48228 ) Devrate Kuntal ( @kuntal-devrat , #48247 ) Diego Frias ( @dzfrias , #48025 ) LiamillionSS ( @LiamillionSS , #48424 ) Interested in helping build a web browser? Take a look at our curated list of issues that are good for new contributors! Donations Thanks again for your generous support! title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
body_text: Training a Text-to-Image Model for $21K | Field Notes by Linum Introduction Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT) Training Regime Model Limitations Appendix A – Training Settings Introduction Contents × Introduction Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT) Training Regime Model Limitations Appendix A – Training Settings Home · Field Notes Research · 10 min read Training a Text-to-Image Model for $21K Sahil Chopra & Manu Chopra Co-CEOs @ Linum · November 4, 2026 RSS Subscribe Road to Linum v3 · Issue 04 previously: P-JiT In our last blog post, we iterated towards P-JiT, a pixel-space architecture that cut attention context windows by 4× while converging in 11× fewer samples. Here, we train the P-JiT for 660M samples (just $21K in compute) as a stepping stone towards larger, video models. Research release · Apache 2.0 Model code Model weights 249 samples · 2B Pyramid-JiT Click any picture for full resolution and its prompt All 249 Person 57 Animal 42 Building 20 Product 43 Landscape 19 Stylized 68 Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT) For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it with the world as an experimental release. If you haven't followed our work previously, we'd love to take a step back and introduce ourselves. We're a 2-person research lab training our own generative video models entirely from scratch. The ultimate ambition is creative tools that democratize access to animation. You can read more about that here . Today, generative video models have two major flaws: they are too slow/expensive and they lack proper controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. With this double whammy, video models (as they stand today) are effectively useless for storytelling. When we set out to build Linum v3 earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools. We've written extensively about the steps we've taken in this direction, but here's the long story short: The bottleneck for training and inference for video is attention, O(n²). If we can compress more aggressively, we'll reduce the context window for attention, slashing the cost of training and inference. Typically, compression is handled by a separate specialized model like a Variational Autoencoder, but that's not necessarily optimal. VAEs seem to have an empirical ceiling on the amount of compression they can achieve. There are other ways to get more compression, but they require substantial surgery to the traditional VAE (e.g. the 2B decoder in Minimax's H3). More importantly, improving the VAE on its task of reconstruction can produce worse generations in the downstream diffusion model. If you get rid of the VAE altogether, you should be able to compress more aggressively and learn faster. Diffusion models are a more powerful family of generative models than VAEs. We should be able to use them to compress and generate at the same time. Instead of using another model's latent space, the diffusion model should learn a latent space purpose-built for its use case. In turn, we should be able to squeeze more juice out of this compression. In our last blog, we iterated towards a new architecture that we called the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT). It's a pixel-space model that converges in 11× fewer samples than Linum v2 with 4× more aggressive token reduction (i.e., we represent a 512² image in the same number of tokens we used to represent a 256² image). Linum v2 is a fairly standard Wan VAE + DiT diffusion model. Linum v2 used a 16×16 token reduction like most models (e.g. FLUX-2). P-JiT enables 32×32 token reduction. This implies a 4× reduction in attention context-window. For the details on how we got there, we'd recommend you take a look at our previous blogs on JiT-DDT and P-JiT . But at a high level, we found a noise schedule for pixel-space models that helps the models better learn fine-grained detail. And, we added readouts along the trunk of the DiT. Adjacent work in REPA , RAE-v2 , and Self-Flow all point to weak gradients in the early blocks of the DiT. By operating in pixel space, every block of our DiT is quite literally predicting a version of the final image, so we can boost gradient signal earlier in the network by predicting low-resolution versions of the final image. This helps accelerate convergence. The architecture did well in our initial experiments, but we wanted to see how it performed when we trained it for longer (i.e., ~600M samples instead of 50–100M samples). For context, generative video models pretty much always start as generative image models. You have to learn nouns (people, places, things) before you can learn verbs (actions, movement). It's a pressure test of sorts along the way towards larger models (and video). Training Regime Overview of Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT) Architecture replay caption Qwen3.5-4B frozen xₜ · 512² / 1024² patchify 32×32 → 1,024 text refiner 2 blocks image refiner 2 blocks ‖ 1 5 10 16 22 readout → 8·8·3 x̂₀ 128² / 256² MSE vs x₀ ↓4 readout → 16·16·3 x̂₀ 256² / 512² MSE vs x₀ ↓2 output head → 32·32·3 x̂₀ 512² / 1024² MSE + LPIPS + P-DINO PixelREPA 2-layer aligns to DINOv3-L features 512²: 256 image + 256 text = 512 tokens 1024²: 1,024 image + 256 text = 1,280 tokens PixelREPA head: ~241M params readout heads: 2.8M params all dropped at sampling sizes read 512² stage / 1024² stage · flower = an illustrative target 2.18B params at sampling · purple heads are training-only and add ~0.24B, for ~2.42B in training Text and image each pass through two single-modality "refiner" DiT blocks, then merge into one stream of 22 identical DiT blocks. The text representation comes from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B model, which we read at layers 7, 15 and 27 (its three full-attention layers). We concatenate and project these representations into the text refiner. The image is split into 32×32 patches and compressed into a 1024-dimensional space, before being projected up into the image refiner blocks. This is a 3:1 compression rate. A 32×32 patch with RGB values is a 32×32×3 = 3,072 representation, which gets projected into 1024 dimensions. At block 5, we have a 2-layer PixelREPA readout that aligns the model's latent space to DINOv3-L. We mask 20% of the tokens in our hidden state and push it through a 2-layer transformer to predict DINOv3-L's feature representation of the same image. We have two linear readout heads along the trunk after blocks 10 and 16. As discussed earlier, these predict the clean image at a quarter and half resolution, respectively. The total loss is given by MSE at the readouts, PixelREPA cosine-distance, MSE at the final output head, and perceptual losses on the full resolution image ( LPIPS and P-DINO ). One DiT block: 22× in the trunk, 2× in each refiner DiT block AdaLN timestep modulation timestep sinusoidal → MLP shared down-proj → 256 shared up-proj 256 → 4 × 2,944 per block RMSNorm × (1 + s₁) attention QK-norm · gated RMSNorm × tanh(g₁) + RMSNorm × (1 + s₂) SwiGLU FFN → 5,376 → RMSNorm × tanh(g₂) + blue = AdaLN · s scales the input before attention/FFN, g gates its residual write hidden size 2,944 · 23 heads × 128 · FFN inner width 5,376 in the trunk, 2,816 in the refiners Every DiT block is conditioned on the timestep through a low-rank AdaLN, following Z-Image . The timestep embedding goes through one down-projection to 256-dim. The image refiner and trunk share one down-projection; the text refiner has its own. Each block then has its own up-projection to a scale and a gate, zero-initialized so every block starts as the identity. As described in our last blog, we employ a curriculum over the noise schedule. We start concentrated at high noise for the first 80M samples, so the model learns basic structure. Then, we widen the noise distribution for the remaining training time so it can learn fine-grained details. See Appendix A for details. We train the model in several stages as we go from 512² to 1024² replay 2e-4 LR 0 100M 200M 300M 400M 550M 610M 660M 0.10 0.11 0.12 0.13 validation loss · lower is better training samples seen EMA live Widen timestep schedule Cooldown LR to 2.5e-5 Adapt to 1024² 2.5e-5 ↑ 0.157 0.0991 0.0960 0.1270 H100-hours 512² · 0 1024² · 0 0 Samples seen 512² · 0M 1024² · 0M 0M Validation loss on a fixed set of 20,480 square images at each stage's resolution. The live spike to 0.157 at 80M is the first eval after the timestep schedule widens. The x-axis widens after 550M so the cooldown and the 1024² stage are legible; the bars are to scale. We start EMA at 100M samples, so the model has already learned decent representations of structure and detail. When we switch to 1024², we start with a fresh optimizer and resume training from the 512² EMA weights. At 1024² we double the noise scale from 2 to 4 to account for the redundancy of information (see JiT, Appendix A ). The higher noise level and need to reproduce fine detail exactly at high resolution result in a higher overall loss, even as image quality improves rapidly. We use RoPE interpolation in the resolution transition. We keep a fixed grid aligned to 512² and multiply the 1024² patch indices by ½ to align them to the 512² coordinate axes. Moreover, we start the 1024² EMA 2M samples in, so it has adjusted to the new resolution before we start the averaging process. For post-training, we used a variant of Finite Difference Flow Optimization (FDFO) with JEV-Image and human-in-the-loop judges. The whole release cost about $21K of compute Pretraining $ 20,348 8,139 H100-hours × $2.50 610M samples at 512², then 50M at 1024² Post-training $ 690 276 H100-hours × $2.50 FDFO with JEV-Image and human-in-the-loop judges Total $ 21,038 $ 20,348 + $ 690 · 8,415 H100-hours pretraining on 64 H100s, restarts included priced at $2.50 per H100-hour It's still early days for post-training diffusion models To be blunt, post-training is a very young discipline within diffusion models, and we've only seen the first sparks of it working in the past few months. Of course there's been a lot of work in model and schedule distillation, but when it comes to post-training in terms of improving fundamental model capabilities (like we've seen with coding in LLMs over the past 18 months), it hasn't really come to fruition just yet for diffusion. DPO has been around for a while, but tends to dramatically overfit to specific aesthetic choices. Flow-GRPO was one of the first articulations of bringing RLVR-style frameworks to diffusion, and that only came out last fall. Since then there have been a few papers like Diffusion NFT and this June's FDFO (the best articulation of diffusion post-training so far, in our opinion). We think that this difficulty in adapting techniques comes down to the fact that we don't have access to strong likelihood estimates in diffusion models like we have in auto-regressive LLMs. We'll dive more into these concerns and our full post-training stack in the coming weeks. Model Limitations This model was not trained with images of rendered text (no infographics, PDFs, pages of books, PowerPoint slides), so it cannot write text or generate posters. As we detailed in our data filtration blog , we don't consider this data useful for our ultimate goal of animation tools, so this text-heavy data has been filtered out entirely from our dataset. This is a small model (2B-parameter DiT, 4B text encoder), and accordingly there are a few areas where the model struggles: full body, many entities (e.g. 6 cars, crowds), multi-person interactions, and world knowledge. The model is capable of correctly generating these images on occasion. Training a larger model (e.g. 7B parameters) and further post-training would likely mitigate these issues. title: Download your favourite YouTube videos
body_text: You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos – The Sun and The Air The Sun and The Air Home Blog Cohost Archive About 29 Oct, 2026 What Veilguard tells me about Mass Effect 5 13 Oct, 2026 You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos 27 Sep, 2026 September Basho Wrap-up 01 Sep, 2026 September Basho preview 31 Aug, 2026 The Gameplay Loop - Zero Company You should absolutely download your favourite youtube videos 13 Oct, 2026 Signal boosting Laura's post that you should absolutely download and archive the stuff that matters to you. The corporate internet is hostile to art and the things you love do not belong to you unless you claim them for yourself. If you've been around for a while on YouTube, just look at your "liked videos" playlist and see how many of the early ones are no longer available (something you literally have to enable in the playlist settings, it's that endemic). The tools to do this in a basic way are extremely easy to get hold of, and generally have good defaults. I'm also going to talk a little about my own setup, and why it is the weird way it is, but it's definitely overkill for most setups. yt-dlp or one of it's many wrappers 1 will do most of what you need, and a folder on a bulk storage drive or NAS will be plenty sufficient to make sure you always have access to them. For me though, I had a particular need - I have unfortunately programmed myself to be almost entirely unable to fall asleep without a Many a True Nerd Let's Play on a low volume. This comes with a couple of issues. I need to be able to play it on my TV. It has to integrate into my existing NAS infrastructure. I need to be able to organise hundreds of videos across dozens of playlists. This is a bigger sticking point than it sounds. Adding new ones or placing them can't be a manual job. Again, hundreds of videos. My NAS media library is built around Jellyfin, which has a concept of Playlists but they're really not intended as a first-order organisational structure. You're expected to take a few tracks from a bunch of existing albums and place them in a playlist separate from the actual Library . No, Jellyfin has a very rigid concept of either Movies, TV Shows > Seasons > Episodes, or Artists > Albums > Songs. TV Shows is the obvious analogue here, and with some really wild finagling I was able to get a setup together that is good enough to satisfy for now 2 . My setup looks like this: Jellyfin In Jellyfin I have a Library setup in TV Shows mode called YouTube. I've turned off all metadata scrapers and the like, and have it set to prefer file data over file names. ytdl-sub This is the only yt-dlp wrapper that allowed me to properly maintain the Playlist structure to any extent, and is entirely based on a series of .yaml files. In it's self-hosted docker-compose form, it comes with a web-app VSCode IDE which is honestly super handy - bridges the tech-comfort gap nicely. I have a custom genre and list of MATN playlists I want it to collect and set metadata for. You can also see there I have a handful of Folding Ideas videos set as "Documentaries" - this is more in keeping with how ytdl-sub expects to be used. The truth is that 99% of youtubers, and 99.9% of viewers, don't particularly need to structure everything as playlists within a channel. Most have a much higher proportion of one-off to series videos that make my MATN structure utterly pointless. As such, ytdl-sub defaults to tagging videos with a Season field organised by Year, but it stores them in folders named for the Playlist. This leads to Jellyfin putting every one of those playlist videos in 2 places within the channel - a Year Series, and a Playlist Series: I only recently realised how to fix this, which is to assign the Playlist title as the Season Number in my ytdl-sub config file - it seems like it should break, but it doesn't: I could write a script to go in and fix this for all my existing series, but the issue is that once Jellyfin has Imported a video, I can't get it to update the Season Number without fully reimporting the Library, something I'm not really interested in doing for a terabyte of video. Oh, speaking of storage size... Tdarr Tdarr is a service that can automatically run through a library of videos and re-encode it in whatever way you desire - usually to some smaller, more efficient format or codec. I use it to encode everything in my media server to HEVC/H.265 as storage is my main bottleneck - processing power is the tradeoff and I have that in spades. I'm honestly not going to recommend Tdarr unless you are very comfortable looking at a massively complex and poorly designed UI and making the smart decision to do the minimum. Everyone I know who has used it has come in with grand ambitions of brilliant complex workflows and settled on just using the default one because it works fine. It has a tendency to break on anything remotely complex, and I had to manually tweak a script so that it wouldn't cry any time there was a data stream, but once it gets going it just chugs along re-encoding gigabyte after gigabyte. It does seem to cause Jellyfin to lose Thumbnail images for reasons I haven't fully figured out, but it's generally fixable either manually, with a "refresh metadata", or in your media management software of choice. It saved me about 700GB across my 2TB library, though I probably could have avoided some of that cost by just being more picky about my downloads. Again, I don't really recommend it! But if you're in a pinch, it will absolutely do the job. ✉️ Reply via email These are probably rife with vibe-coding, as yt-dlp scripts are well documented online and using the command line is daunting for most. ↩ As with all things homelab - it's never perfect, which keeps the hobby alive forever. ↩ #blog #homelab   rss | contact me Powered by Bear ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ

title: Lemmings CSS Animation
body_text: Walker Playground Star Fork Walker playground Add walkers with the button below or __walker.add() . Drag one to carry it, flick it to throw it. Resize the window and walkers ride the surface they're standing on, so a fast resize launches them. Add a walker Stairs Stairs too tall to climb Floating platforms Pit Walls Cards These wrap onto new rows as the window narrows, which shoves anyone standing on them. Card one Borders are solid. Walk the top edge or get trapped inside. Button Card two Buttons and form fields are solid too. Card three Text is a floor you can land on but walk through. Card four Throw a walker up here. Another Cage Reading Columns of text reflow a lot when the window changes size, so this is a good place to try a resize launch. Each line of text is its own floor. Walkers can drop from line to line, fall off the end of a short line, and land on whatever is below. Lines sit closer together than a walker is tall, so text never blocks them. Only borders, boxes, buttons, images and fields do. That keeps walkers from getting stuck between two lines of a paragraph. Near the bottom of the page there is one long floor to catch anything that falls all the way down.

title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
body_text: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup? | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup? 554 points by eggbrain 3 days ago | hide | past | favorite | 682 comments I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI. 1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc) - Which tiers? - Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)? 2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models. - Which models and providers? 3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses? - What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)? 4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools? - For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom. 5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse? - If you are using them, what are your main use cases? ----- I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.   help Animats 2 days ago | next [–] Embarrassingly, I don't have one yet. I'm mostly still writing code one keystroke at a time. I've used Github Copilot to translate between languages and look things up, but haven't trusted it to write new code or fix anything. Claude Fable is now good enough that I should be using it. The latest Claude version is said to be comparable to a mid-career graphics programmer, which is about what I need. Six months ago it wasn't good enough to use for such work, and probably would have made a hash of my code. There's been progress. But Anthropic's business practices are scary. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong. I'm currently stalled signing up for Claude because their verification email system can't get to my inbox. (Some problem with their using Constant Contact, a spam system, to send transactional emails to my own domain, which, long ago, I had blocked at the Constant Contact end. I think. The verification email never touches the inbound mail server.) It's very important to Anthropic that you sign up with the "right" email address, and it may not be possible to change it, so using some disposable address is not a good idea. Suggestions? reply creativeSlumber 2 days ago | parent | next [–] > But Anthropic's business practices are scary. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong. Then use open alternatives as much as possible. Something like Opencode with OpenRouter with Deepseek 4.1 from ZDR provider works very well and costs like 1/20th. reply scosman 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] It costs 1/20th the price at token pricing, but an Ultra subscription is still amazing value. reply bloppe 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I also think OAI is much better than Anthropic in this regard. They don't try to gatekeep nearly as much. But I agree that open alternatives are sort of a theoretical ideal. Just a lot harder to get those mega-subsidized. reply jpardoe 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] In practice all of these open models are more expensive than a Claude subscription. reply ggregoire 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Are they? (genuine question, i've got no experience with Claude) This month I used 1 billion tokens (including cache) with DS4.1 flash and it cost me 7% of my $10 opencode go sub. If you meant in developer time, then I don't know but it seems very fast to me (rarely thinks more than ~10sec, never more than ~30sec) and usually oneshots what I prompt it to do. I use opencode tui as harness. reply jpardoe 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] In my experience yes. Been using Claude since day one and wanted to experiment with Pi for fun, and try to get my costs down. I found the open models more expensive, eventually had to plug my Pi set up into an OpenAI subscription, that was the only way to get good value… Then I realised OpenAI is way behind Opus 5.5 and their subscription is far less generous with usage, so I’ve come full circle and am back on Claude Code. reply jeffyaw 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] i found they were until recently. mimo 2.6 flash and glm 5.3 flash seem to finally be cheaper. i find ds4.1 flash still on the high side. reply jpardoe 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I found GLM Flash competitive price wise but then my tasks took twice as long to complete. Even if it was cheaper (in my experience it still wasn’t) you then lose out on speed because of the insane amounts of inefficient reasoning. reply ChrisRR 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] You don't even need to start off with Fable. Give Opus 5.5 a try first and then then try Fable if you feel like you need to push it further reply nedt 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] I have a longer history of agents sessions and used those to benchmark the different models. Sonnet 5.5 is already pretty strong, but not always as careful (leaked secrets into the session). Opus 5.5 is already able to solve everything I'm doing. You might not need Fable for anything. Biggest different between Opus and Fable in my benchmarks was price. Also Opus 5.5 is cheaper now then previous Opus so you might also not need Sonnet as much for cost savings. reply nycdatasci 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Based on blended benchmarks from Artificial Analysis, Opus 5.5 is stronger than Fable 5.1. Are you finding use cases where Fable is superior? reply felixgallo 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] Fable can go deeper than Opus in my experience. That said one gets much more Opus for a subscription than one does Fable, so obviously benchmark your own cases and come up with your own cost benefit analysis. reply computomatic 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] You can access Claude models through any number of providers - OpenRouter, AWS Bedrock, etc. and as far as I know, Claude Code can be used with any of them. The only real benefit to going direct through Anthropic is the subscriptions. It’s worth the risk for the discount, but if you get locked out, there’s other (pricy) options to get unblocked. reply Fervicus 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] It's crazy to me that this is considered embarrassing now. People should stay up to date with current tech, but we shouldn't be ashamed of not using LLMs. Let's re-normalize coding by hand. reply 946789987649 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] I was an AI-skeptic for a while but it is embarrassing to not even try it. I'm still on the more manual end of AI use. My prompts are very small, targeted changes. I still review every line as though a human wrote it. I know exactly what I want and I've got my prompts and claude.MD at a point where it gives me that most of the time. I probably only write 5% of the code now. reply Animats 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] I did, for a long time, but we're past that point now. Someone else got something done in three months that took me years of hand coding. reply bloppe 2 days ago | root | parent | next [–] If something took 3 months, then there must have been a good deal of manual attention involved, even if it wasn't typing each character by hand. They are still your thoughts, but it's just 100x faster than coding by hand. reply steve1977 2 days ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] And thinking by brain. reply walrus01 2 days ago | parent | prev | next [–] I would suggest that based on your current level of "trust" in these things (justifiably very low, I use zero openai or anthropic products myself) that you look into self hosting locally something reasonably capable and smart on your own hardware, on llama-server or something functionally equivalent to it. They have a reputation for cancelling accounts for random reasons, offer rather bad terms, and have no customer support. I have a strong aversion to services with a reputation for cancelling services arbitrarily. They will apparently cancel based on their system's guesses as to what you're working on. Sometimes they guess wrong. What I'm doing (metaverse clients) is so far out of the mainstream they may guess wrong. From your response it does not seem like you have enough experience using LLM, and your response seem to indicate a bias from reading posts of folks who got banned. If you work without a sprint system, you'll find yourself continually reminding the AIs manually "hey, can you please work to width?", "hey, you have 10 cards ready can you please work on them now?". These things are "squishy" when worked on in LLM space, they'll kinda do it, then a few hours later forget, and by morning they're puttering along at a few cards each. But by putting everything into mechanical structure (sprint system that drives all the LLMs via push notifications), they will more reliably remember to work at width, they will not forget anything they were assigned to work on (this is stored in redis cards, not in their memory that compacts), and the whole system can work much wider and you get done a lot faster! reply drphilwinder 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Thanks. title: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome
body_text: Awesome repositories are no longer awesome Erik Gahner Larsen ← Back Awesome repositories are no longer awesome Nov 5, 2026 On GitHub, you will find a lot of repositories with the prefix 'awesome'. They usually contain curated knowledge and resources related to a certain domain, such as awesome-python (see, e.g., this repository for a list of awesome repositories). I used to see these awesome repositories as potential goldmines of good content. However, nowadays I see most of them as irrelevant and useless. There are two reasons for this, and they are both related to AI. First, as many of these awesome lists get older, they contain a lot of outdated material if they are not actively maintained. You are in most cases better off simply asking a decent AI model for inspiration or the material you need. That is, I find it difficult to believe that most of these awesome lists are of interest to people anymore. If they remain useful, it will mostly be for agents looking to find and check relevant resources. I had a quick look at the awesome-R repository. The repository was last updated more than a year ago, and most of the resources included in the overview are either outdated or will not be of general interest to people using R. One of the first links in the repository is an overview of the top 50 downloaded packages - as of 2016! This is simply not a good resource if you want to explore R in any shape or form. Second, a lot of these awesome repositories are being flooded with AI slop. Go to any random awesome repository these days and you will most likely find a lot of pull requests suggesting the most generic tools and resources. For example, take a look at this awesome-free-online-tools repository. It is a small, unknown repository with 13 stars but 91 open pull requests at the time of writing. I did not look at all of these pull requests, but the ones I looked at all suggested generic vibe-coded tools. I found this resource because of a pull request made to one of my repositories, a simple project where I store material I like related to statistics. The suggestion was to add StatOrigin ("a free, open database of industry statistics"), and once I had a quick look at the resource and the other pull requests made by the user, I could easily close the PR. This user alone has created at least six vibe-coded websites (StatOrigin, ScanChess, Sticker Printer Hub, QuizQuip, LiquidityPools, DefiLPKit) and submitted more than 100 pull requests to various awesome lists to add these websites. It did not take me long to find examples where these tools were merged into the relevant repositories (see, e.g., here , here , and here ). However, I also found examples where people did the basic work of checking out the material, such as here , where the PR was closed with the following explanation: "There is not yet sufficient evidence of qualified educator review, independent validation of the educational content, or demonstrated learning outcomes." Good stuff! My point is not that these awesome repositories are now all bad. They can still be awesome. But as a general approach to finding good resources, awesome lists are less awesome than they used to be. As AI gets better at finding and creating resources (and creating pull requests for said resources), these awesome repositories will become less relevant and less useful. title: A thousand fewer paths to root
